teile.einleitung: The compass jellyfish is a jellyfish from the Atlantic, the North Sea and the Mediterranean. It gets its name from the brown stripes on its bell, which are reminiscent of a compass rose. It can sting with its tentacles, but for people it is usually only unpleasant.
wichtigste: The compass jellyfish is called Chrysaora hysoscella in science.
It belongs to the true jellyfish and thus to the cnidarians.
On its bell it has 16 brown, V-shaped stripes like a compass rose.
Its bell usually grows to about 30 centimetres across.
It eats plankton, fish larvae and other jellyfish.
A touch stings and burns on the skin.
Its body consists for the most part of water.

abschnitte.text: The bell of the compass jellyfish is transparent, whitish to yellowish. From the centre, 16 brown, **V-shaped stripes** run to the edge, so that the pattern resembles a compass. 24 thin tentacles hang from the edge of the bell, and four long, frilly **oral arms** wave beneath it. Like all jellyfish, it has neither brain nor heart nor bones.

Compass jellyfish live in the north-east Atlantic, in the North Sea, in the English Channel and in the Mediterranean. They mostly drift near the coast in the upper part of the water. In summer and autumn they are often washed up on beaches in large numbers. In the Baltic Sea they hardly occur because of the low salt content.

The compass jellyfish is a **predator**. With its tentacles it catches small crustaceans, fish eggs, fish larvae and also other jellyfish. The prey is paralysed by **stinging cells**, which fire tiny venom threads. The oral arms then carry the food to the mouth opening under the bell.

Compass jellyfish have an **alternation of generations**. A larva turns into a small, fixed polyp on the sea floor. This pinches off many tiny young jellyfish, which swim away and grow into large jellyfish. What is special is that compass jellyfish are first male and later female.

Contact with the tentacles leads to burning, red patches of skin, which usually fade after some time. Even washed-up jellyfish can still sting, so you should not touch them. You should rinse the spot with seawater and not rub it. If symptoms are severe, a doctor or the lifeguard can help.

The compass jellyfish lives only in salt water and does not occur in Switzerland. Swiss children are most likely to meet it on holiday by the Mediterranean or the North Sea. In some Swiss lakes, however, there is a tiny **freshwater jellyfish** that grows only about two centimetres across. It is completely harmless to people.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal group with stinging cells, for example jellyfish, corals and sea anemones.
A cell that fires a tiny venom thread when touched.
A fixed life form of cnidarians that looks like a small tube.
A long, movable grasping arm.

gewusst: A jellyfish consists of about 95 per cent water or more.
Leatherback turtles like to eat jellyfish and tolerate the sting venom.
Small fish sometimes hide among the tentacles of jellyfish to be safe from enemies.

teile.einleitung: Lapland is a large region in the far north of Europe, lying for the most part north of the Arctic Circle. Here live the Sámi, a people who traditionally live with reindeer. In summer the sun does not set for weeks, and in winter it stays dark for a long time.
wichtigste: Lapland lies in the north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia.
The Sámi are the indigenous people of this area and call their land Sápmi.
Many Sámi still keep reindeer today.
A large part of Lapland lies north of the Arctic Circle.
In summer there is the midnight sun, in winter the polar night.
On clear winter nights the northern lights often glow in the sky.
Typical animals are reindeer, elk, wolverine and Arctic fox.

abschnitte.text: Lapland is not a state of its own, but a region that stretches across four countries. It includes the north of **Norway**, Sweden and Finland as well as the Kola Peninsula in Russia. In Finland there is even a region that is officially called Lapland, with the capital Rovaniemi. The Sámi themselves call their whole area of settlement **Sápmi**.

Lapland consists of wide coniferous forests, bogs, countless lakes and bare mountains, the **fjells**. Further north hardly any trees grow, and there the **tundra** begins with mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs. The winters are long and very cold, often far below minus 20 degrees. The summers are short, but bright and full of mosquitoes.

The best-known animal of Lapland is the **reindeer**, which roams here in large herds. Alongside it live elk, brown bears, wolves, lynx and the powerful **wolverine**. In the mountains you find Arctic foxes, ptarmigan and the small lemmings. Many migratory birds come in summer to breed in the bright bogs.

The **Sámi** have lived in Lapland for thousands of years. In the past many families moved back and forth with their reindeer herds between summer and winter pastures. They have languages of their own, a colourful costume and the special singing called joik. Today most Sámi live in houses and work in quite ordinary jobs, but reindeer herding remains important for their culture.

North of the Arctic Circle the sun does not set at all in midsummer, which is called the **midnight sun**. In midwinter, by contrast, it does not rise above the horizon for weeks, which is the **polar night**. In return you can often see green northern lights dancing on clear nights. For people from Switzerland this change of light and darkness is very unfamiliar.

Besides reindeer herding, people in Lapland live from timber, hydropower and mining, for example from the iron ore at Kiruna in Sweden. **Tourism** is becoming more and more important. Visitors ride in dog or reindeer sledges, watch the northern lights or visit Santa Claus Village near Rovaniemi. Many Swiss families also travel there in winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line on the Earth, north of which there are midnight sun and polar night.
A cold landscape almost without trees, with mosses and lichens.
The indigenous people of Lapland with their own language and culture.
The traditional singing of the Sámi.

gewusst: The word ‘Lapps’ for the Sámi is now regarded as derogatory, and they wish to be called Sámi.
Reindeer can smell lichens under the snow and scrape them free with their hooves.
In Finnish Lapland there are about as many reindeer as people.

teile.einleitung: ‘Maikäfer flieg’ (‘Fly away, cockchafer’) is a very old German children’s song that many children get to know as early as kindergarten. It sounds like a cheerful counting rhyme, but actually tells of war and destruction. At the same time it leads us to a beetle that used to occur in huge numbers in Switzerland.
wichtigste: ‘Maikäfer flieg’ is one of the best-known children’s songs in the German-speaking world.
In the song a cockchafer is told to fly away.
The text mentions a father at war and a mother in Pommerland, which has burned down.
Many experts suppose that the song recalls the hardship of the Thirty Years’ War.
The song was passed on orally before it was printed in song collections.
The cockchafer itself is a brown beetle that swarms in spring.
Its larvae, the grubs, live for several years in the soil.

abschnitte.text: ‘Maikäfer flieg’ is a **folk song** whose author nobody knows. Such songs were passed from parents to children over many generations. The tune is short and simple, so even small children can sing along. In the 19th century the song was written down in collections of children’s songs and so became even better known.

In the song a cockchafer flies away while the father is at war. The mother is in **Pommerland**, an area on the Baltic Sea in present-day northern Germany and Poland. This land has burned down. So the song describes a family that has been torn apart by war.

Many researchers believe that the song comes from the time of the **Thirty Years’ War** from 1618 to 1648. At that time Pomerania and many other regions were devastated. This cannot be proved with certainty, however. Later children also sang the song in other times of war, because it fitted their experiences.

The **common cockchafer** is about 2 to 3 centimetres long and has brown wing cases. Typical are its fan-like antennae, which are larger in the male than in the female. The adult beetles fly in spring, usually in May, and eat the leaves of trees. After a few weeks they die again.

The larvae of the cockchafer are called **grubs** and live three to four years in the soil. There they eat the roots of grasses and other plants. That is why in many areas there is a big **flight year** only every few years. In Switzerland, depending on the region, different flight years are distinguished, for example the Bernese or the Uri flight year.

In the 19th and early 20th centuries there were huge numbers of cockchafers in Switzerland, which caused great damage. Farmers and schoolchildren had to collect the beetles then, and they were often shaken from trees. Later poisons were used, and the beetles became rarer. Today in some areas there are more cockchafers again, and people tend to control the grubs with natural means such as a fungus.

begriffe.erklaerung: A song that was sung on by the people and whose author is mostly unknown.
A region on the Baltic Sea that today belongs to Germany and Poland.
The thick, white larva of the cockchafer that lives in the soil.
A year in which especially many cockchafers come out of the soil at the same time.

gewusst: A cockchafer pumps air into its body before take-off, which is called ‘pumping’ or ‘counting’.
In the past, collected cockchafers were sometimes fed to hens and pigs.
The cockchafer spends the greatest part of its life as a grub under the ground.

teile.einleitung: Bony fish are by far the largest group of fish. Their skeleton is made of true bone, and their gills are protected by a hard cover. Almost all fish in Swiss lakes and rivers, from perch to whitefish, are bony fish.
wichtigste: Bony fish have a skeleton of bone and not of cartilage.
Whitefish, perch, trout and pike are bony fish.
With over 30,000 species they are the most species-rich group of vertebrates.
A gill cover protects their gills.
Many have a swim bladder with which they can hover in the water.
Their skin is usually covered with thin, overlapping scales.
They live in seas, lakes, rivers and even in hot springs and caves.

abschnitte.text: Bony fish are fish with an internal skeleton of hardened tissue. In this they differ from the **cartilaginous fish** such as sharks and rays. With well over 30,000 species they make up the largest part of all fish. Their shapes range from the flat flatfish through the long seahorse to the round pufferfish.

The gills of bony fish lie under a movable **gill cover**. Many have a **swim bladder**, a gas-filled organ with which they regulate their buoyancy. In this way they can hover in the water without constantly swimming. Most have thin scales that lie over one another like roof tiles and grow with the fish.

Almost all bony fish are **ray-finned fish**; their fins are supported by thin bony rays. They include carp, salmon, perch and tuna. A small group are the **lobe-finned fish** with strong, fleshy fins, such as coelacanths and lungfish. From ancestors of the lobe-finned fish, the first land vertebrates developed around 370 million years ago.

Most bony fish lay very many small eggs, the **spawn**, into the water. The males usually release their sperm into the water as well, so that fertilisation takes place outside the body. A carp can lay hundreds of thousands of eggs. Some species such as the stickleback build nests and guard their brood, while others such as the guppy give birth to live young.

In Swiss waters live around 70 native fish species, all of which are bony fish. Especially well known are the **whitefish**, which are fished in many lakes, and the perch, the river perch. Added to these are the brown trout, grayling, pike, carp and chub. Some species such as the salmon have disappeared from Switzerland and are to be reintroduced.

The heaviest bony fish is the **ocean sunfish**, which can weigh over two tonnes. Among the longest is the oarfish, which grows to several metres long. The sailfish is one of the fastest swimmers in the sea. There are also tiny species that measure barely a centimetre when fully grown.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bony plate that protects the gills of bony fish.
A gas-filled organ with which a fish hovers in the water.
The largest group of bony fish, with fins made of thin bony rays.
The eggs of fish and amphibians.

gewusst: Strictly speaking, we humans too are descendants of bony fish, because all land vertebrates descend from lobe-finned fish.
From the scales of some fish you can tell how old they are, as with tree rings.

teile.einleitung: The European rhinoceros beetle is one of the largest beetles in Central Europe. The males carry a long, curved horn on the head that recalls a small rhinoceros.
wichtigste: The scientific name is Oryctes nasicornis.
It belongs to the scarab beetle family and to the subfamily of the rhinoceros beetles (Dynastinae).
Adult beetles are about 2 to 4 centimetres long.
Males can be recognised by the long, curved horn on the head.
Females carry only a short bump.
The beetle is active mainly at dusk and at night.
In Central Europe the beetles fly from about June to August.

abschnitte.text: The rhinoceros beetle is glossy reddish brown to chestnut brown and about 2 to 4 centimetres long. The male carries on the head a long, backward-curved **horn** and on the pronotum a ridge with three bumps. The female has only a short bump. The underside is covered with fox-red hairs, and the antennae end in a three-segmented **club**.

The rhinoceros beetle belongs to the large family of **scarab beetles**, which also includes cockchafers and rose chafers. Within this family it belongs to the subfamily of the rhinoceros beetles (Dynastinae). This group also includes the giant Hercules beetles of South America. Typical of scarab beetles are the antennae, whose ends can be fanned out like little leaves.

Originally the rhinoceros beetle lived in old forests with rotting wood. Today it is often found near people, for example in **compost heaps**, sawdust, bark mulch or old piles of wood. There the thick, white **grubs** develop, which grow to about ten centimetres long. The larvae eat rotting wood and plant remains and need several years for this.

Adult rhinoceros beetles are active mainly at dusk and at night. In Central Europe they fly from about June to August, often attracted by light. As beetles they live only a few weeks and eat hardly anything during this time. Their legs are strong digging legs with toothed tibiae, with which they burrow into rotten wood dust and soil.

The rhinoceros beetle has become rare in many areas because there is less old, rotting wood. Anyone who finds a grub in the compost in the garden should therefore not kill it. The larvae are harmless and do not harm living plants. A pile of wood chippings or leaves can be a new home for them.

begriffe.erklaerung: The thick, white larva of scarab beetles.
The hard shield between the head and the wing cases of a beetle.
The end of a beetle’s antenna, which consists of leaf-like plates.
Crumbled, crumbly wood in old trees.

gewusst: If a rhinoceros beetle is disturbed, it can make chirping sounds by rubbing its abdomen.
The beetle lives only a few weeks, but the larva several years.
Despite its heavy body the rhinoceros beetle can fly well.

teile.einleitung: The lion’s mane jellyfish is the largest known species of jellyfish in the world. It gets its name from the many long, reddish-yellow tentacles that look like a lion’s mane. In German it is also called Gelbe Haarqualle (‘yellow hair jellyfish’).
wichtigste: The lion’s mane jellyfish is the largest known jellyfish.
Its bell can reach over two metres in diameter.
Its tentacles can grow many metres long.
It lives in cool seas, for example in the North Atlantic, the North Sea and the Baltic.
Its stinging cells cause painful skin irritation.
It eats plankton, small fish and other jellyfish.
In German it is also called Gelbe Haarqualle.

abschnitte.text: The lion’s mane jellyfish has a bell-shaped **bell** that is coloured red, orange, yellow or brownish. Usually it measures about half a metre, but especially large animals grow over two metres across. Under the bell hang hundreds of thin **tentacles** in eight bundles. The largest known specimen was found in 1870 on the coast of the USA, and its tentacles were over 30 metres long.

The jellyfish lives in cool and cold seas of the Northern Hemisphere. It is found in the North Atlantic, the North Pacific, the North Sea and the western Baltic. In summer it often drifts near the coast and is sometimes washed up on beaches. Anyone who goes on holiday in northern Germany or Scandinavia may meet it there.

The lion’s mane jellyfish is a predator. With its tentacles, which hang in the water like a large net, it catches **zooplankton**, small fish, small crustaceans and above all other jellyfish. The prey is stunned with stinging cells and guided to the mouth under the bell. Some small fish, by contrast, swim between the tentacles and use them as a hiding place.

The tentacles carry countless **stinging cells** that shoot tiny venom threads into the skin on contact. For people this is painful and leads to burning, red skin. It is life-threatening only very rarely, for example in an allergy. Even torn-off tentacles and dead jellyfish on the beach can still sting, so you should not touch them.

Like many jellyfish, the lion’s mane jellyfish has two life forms. From the eggs come larvae that settle on the sea floor and become small **polyps**. These pinch off tiny young jellyfish that swim freely in the water and grow into the large jellyfish. An adult lion’s mane jellyfish usually lives only about a year.

The lion’s mane jellyfish plays a part in a detective story by Arthur Conan Doyle. In ‘The Adventure of the Lion’s Mane’ Sherlock Holmes solves a puzzling case in which the jellyfish is the culprit. In this way the jellyfish became known to many readers. In reality, however, it is far less dangerous to people than in the story.

begriffe.erklaerung: The bell-shaped body of a jellyfish.
A long, movable grasping arm.
A cell that fires a small venom thread on contact.
A fixed life form of jellyfish on the sea floor.
Tiny animals that drift in the water.

gewusst: With its tentacles stretched out, a lion’s mane jellyfish can be longer than a blue whale.
Jellyfish have neither brain nor heart nor bones.
A jellyfish consists of about 98 per cent water.

teile.einleitung: Macaques are powerful monkeys with a short muzzle that live mainly in Asia. They include well-known species such as the rhesus macaque, the Japanese macaque and the Barbary macaque. Macaques are very adaptable and live in rainforests, mountains and even in the middle of cities.
wichtigste: Macaques form the genus Macaca in the Old World monkey family (Cercopithecidae).
The genus today includes over 20 species.
Almost all macaques live in Asia, only the Barbary macaque lives in North Africa.
The Barbary macaque lives wild mainly in Morocco and Algeria.
On Gibraltar lives the only free-living monkey population in Europe.
The word ‘macaque’ came into the European languages via Portuguese.
The Barbary macaque is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List.

abschnitte.text: Macaques are medium-sized, powerfully built monkeys with a dense coat, usually in shades of brown or grey. Many have a hairless, reddish face. Tail length varies greatly depending on the species: the **long-tailed macaque** has a long tail, while the Barbary macaque has practically none. Males are usually clearly larger and heavier than females. In their **cheek pouches** macaques can collect food and eat it later in peace.

Among all monkeys, macaques have one of the largest ranges after humans. They live from Afghanistan and India through China and South-East Asia to Japan. The **Japanese macaque** even lives in areas with a lot of snow, where some animals bathe in hot springs. Many species also occur in villages and cities and get food there.

Macaques are **omnivores** and eat fruit, leaves, seeds, insects and sometimes small animals. They live in groups with several males and females. In these groups there is a clear **ranking order**, which is often inherited through the mother. Mutual grooming is important for strengthening friendships.

The **Barbary macaque** is the only macaque species outside Asia. On Gibraltar at the southern tip of Spain, a few hundred of these monkeys live free. A legend says that the British will leave Gibraltar if the monkeys disappear. That is why **Winston Churchill** had the population topped up with animals from North Africa in the Second World War. What is special is that male Barbary macaques look after young animals lovingly and carry them around.

The **rhesus macaque** has long been used in medical research, which is much discussed today. The **rhesus factor**, a feature of the blood discovered in 1940, is named after it. In some countries of Asia macaques are regarded as sacred and are fed at temples. At the same time there are conflicts when monkeys steal food in cities.

Several species of macaque are threatened because their forests are being cut down. The Barbary macaque is endangered, also because young animals are sold illegally as pets. Other species such as the rhesus macaque, by contrast, are still common. Protected areas and controls against the animal trade are meant to help preserve the threatened species.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of closely related animal species, in macaques it is called Macaca.
Skin sacs in the cheeks in which food is stored temporarily.
The fixed order of who has more say in a group.
A blood feature that was named after the rhesus macaque.

gewusst: Japanese macaques were observed washing sweet potatoes in sea water.
A rhesus monkey called Albert II flew to a great height in a rocket in 1949.
Barbary macaques are often wrongly called ‘apes without a tail’, but they are true macaques.

teile.einleitung: ‘Madagascar’ is an animated film from 2005 in which four zoo animals from New York are stranded on the island of Madagascar. Alex the lion, Marty the zebra, Melman the giraffe and Gloria the hippo have funny adventures there. King Julien, a dancing ring-tailed lemur, also became famous.
wichtigste: ‘Madagascar’ is a computer-animated film by DreamWorks from 2005.
The main characters are Alex the lion, Marty the zebra, Melman the giraffe and Gloria the hippo.
The animals first live in the Central Park Zoo in New York.
Through a mishap they end up on the island of Madagascar.
King Julien is a ring-tailed lemur and leader of the lemurs.
Four cheeky penguins became so popular that they got films and series of their own.
Two more cinema films followed in 2008 and 2012.

abschnitte.text: ‘Madagascar’ is an **animated film** that was made entirely on the computer. It was produced by the American studio **DreamWorks Animation** and came to cinemas in 2005. It was directed by Eric Darnell and Tom McGrath. The film was a great success worldwide and is still popular with children today.

Alex the lion is the star of the **Central Park Zoo** in New York and loves his comfortable life. His friend Marty the zebra, by contrast, dreams of freedom in the wild and slips away. The friends follow him, are caught and loaded in crates onto a ship to Africa. Through a prank by the penguins they are instead stranded on the island of Madagascar.

On Madagascar the zoo animals meet a group of party-loving lemurs. Their leader is **King Julien**, a vain, funny ring-tailed lemur who likes dancing best. His entourage includes little Mort, a mouse lemur, and his adviser Maurice, an aye-aye. The lemurs hope that Alex will help them against the **fossas**, the real predators of Madagascar.

The four penguins Skipper, Kowalski, Rico and Private became audience favourites. They got a television series of their own and in 2014 the cinema film ‘Penguins of Madagascar’. There are also the sequels ‘Madagascar 2’ from 2008 and ‘Madagascar 3’ from 2012. King Julien, too, later got a series of his own.

Much in the film is invented: in reality neither lions nor zebras, giraffes, hippos or penguins live on Madagascar. Real, by contrast, are the **lemurs**, which exist only on Madagascar, and the cat-like fossa. Ring-tailed lemurs really do live in groups and like to sunbathe, but of course they do not dance to party music. The film has nevertheless helped many children to know lemurs.

The film also became known for a cheerful dance song that King Julien sings with his lemurs. The film lives on quick jokes, crazy characters and friendship. Its message is that true friends stick together, even if they are very different. In Switzerland, by the way, you can see lemurs at Zurich Zoo in the Masoala Hall.

begriffe.erklaerung: A film whose pictures are drawn or made on the computer.
A species of lemur with a black and white ringed tail.
A cat-like predator that lives only on Madagascar.
A further film that continues the story of an earlier film.

gewusst: In the English original, the British comedian Sacha Baron Cohen voices the character King Julien.
The film is spelt ‘Madagascar’ with a c, as the island is spelt in English, while in German the island is written Madagaskar with a k.
For the characters the studio developed a deliberately angular, cartoonish drawing style.

teile.einleitung: An avalanche dog is a specially trained rescue dog that tracks down people under the snow. With its fine nose it smells buried people even through several metres of snow. In the Swiss Alps, avalanche dogs are a firm part of mountain rescue.
wichtigste: Avalanche dogs search for people buried by avalanches.
They smell people even deep under the snow.
A dog can search an area much faster than many people.
After an avalanche every minute counts.
Avalanche dogs are often flown to the scene by helicopter.
Today they are usually German shepherds, Labradors or Border collies.
The most famous rescue dog in Switzerland was the St Bernard Barry.

abschnitte.text: Avalanche dogs are **rescue dogs** that specialise in searching in snow. When an avalanche has buried people, they run across the avalanche debris and sniff for human scent. If they have a trace, they begin to bark and dig at that spot. Then the rescuers know exactly where they have to shovel.

Dogs have many millions more smell cells than humans. The scent of a person rises through the loose snow, and the dog picks it up at the surface. In this way it often finds buried people even at a depth of several metres. A well-trained dog searches an avalanche field about as fast as very many people with **avalanche probes** together.

Anyone lying under an avalanche has hardly any air left after a short time. In the first 15 minutes most buried people survive, after that the chances fall quickly. That is why ski tourers carry an **avalanche transceiver** with which companions can locate them at once. Avalanche dogs are especially important when someone had no such device with them.

In Switzerland the **Alpine Rettung Schweiz** (Swiss Alpine Rescue), together with partners, trains avalanche dogs and their handlers. In winter teams are ready in many mountain regions. In an alarm a helicopter, for example from Rega, often flies them directly to the scene. Dog and human train for this over years and must pass tests regularly.

Training begins playfully: a person hides in the snow, and the dog gets a reward on finding them, for example a toy. Later the hiding places become deeper and harder. An avalanche dog must also sit calmly in the helicopter and not let itself be distracted by the noise. Suitable are dogs that like to work, are brave and have plenty of stamina.

abschnitte.titel: Barry of the Great St Bernard
abschnitte.text: Over 200 years ago, dogs of the hospice on the **Great St Bernard** were already helping travellers in need. The St Bernard Barry is said to have saved over 40 people around 1800. His preserved hide stands today in the Natural History Museum of Bern. For modern avalanche searching St Bernards are too heavy, however, which is why lighter breeds are used today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dog trained to find missing or buried people.
The heap of snow that is left lying after an avalanche.
A long pole with which rescuers prod in the snow for buried people.
The person who works with the dog and leads it.

gewusst: The famous little barrel round the neck of St Bernards is a legend, real rescue dogs did not wear one.
Avalanche dogs sometimes wear their own ear protection on helicopter flights.
Barry is so famous to this day that in the Valais a foundation with his name breeds St Bernards.

teile.einleitung: Great apes are large, very intelligent apes without a tail. They include orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos. They are our closest relatives in the animal kingdom.
wichtigste: The great apes include orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos.
All great apes have no tail.
Biologically, humans also belong to the great ape family.
Chimpanzees and bonobos are the closest relatives of humans.
Great apes live in Africa and South-East Asia.
They are very intelligent and use tools.
All species are severely endangered.

abschnitte.text: The great ape family is scientifically called **Hominidae**. It includes the orangutans with three species, the gorillas with two species, the chimpanzee, the **bonobo** and humans. Gibbons are sometimes called lesser apes, but form a family of their own. All great apes lack a tail, which distinguishes them from most other monkeys. They have large brains and long arms.

Gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos live in the rainforests and savannas of Africa. Bonobos occur only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, south of the Congo River. Orangutans live in Asia, on the islands of **Borneo** and Sumatra. They spend almost their whole life in the trees. Gorillas, by contrast, live mostly on the ground.

Great apes eat mainly fruit, leaves, shoots and nuts. Chimpanzees sometimes also eat insects or hunt small monkeys. Gorillas live in groups led by a strong male, the **silverback**. Orangutans, by contrast, mostly live alone. Every evening great apes build themselves a sleeping nest from branches and leaves.

Great apes are very intelligent and can solve problems. Chimpanzees fish termites out of their mounds with little sticks or crack nuts with stones. Such **tools** are passed on within the group, which is described as culture. From 1960 the researcher Jane Goodall discovered in Tanzania that chimpanzees make tools. Some great apes in research stations have learned to communicate with signs.

All great ape species are severely endangered or even threatened with extinction. Their forests are being cleared, for example for timber or palm oil plantations. In addition there are poaching and diseases such as Ebola. Great apes have a young one only every few years, so their populations recover very slowly. In Switzerland you can watch great apes, for example, in Basel Zoo and in **Zurich Zoo**, which also work for protection in the wild.

begriffe.erklaerung: An order of mammals that includes monkeys, prosimians and humans.
An adult male gorilla with silver-grey fur on the back.
The scientific name of the great ape family.
Illegal hunting and killing of wild animals.

gewusst: The genetic material of chimpanzees and humans is about 98 to 99 per cent the same.
An adult male gorilla can weigh over 200 kilograms and is thus the largest primate in the world.
The name orangutan comes from Malay and means ‘forest person’.

teile.einleitung: Cabbage whites are white butterflies whose caterpillars like to eat cabbage and related plants. In Switzerland they flutter through gardens, over meadows and fields from spring to autumn. Best known are the large white and the small white.
wichtigste: Cabbage whites are day-flying butterflies from the family of the whites.
Their wings are white with black tips and spots.
The caterpillars eat cabbage, rape, nasturtium and other cruciferous plants.
There is the large white and the small white, which are often confused.
In vegetable gardens the caterpillars can do a lot of damage.
They usually produce two to three generations a year.
A small parasitic wasp is one of their most important natural enemies.

abschnitte.text: Cabbage whites have white to cream-coloured **wings** with black tips on the forewings. The females also carry two black spots on each forewing, the males usually only one or none. The **large white** has a wingspan of about 5 to 6 centimetres. The **small white** is much smaller and has less strong black markings.

The caterpillars eat plants from the **cabbage family** (cruciferous plants), for example white cabbage, Brussels sprouts, broccoli, rape and mustard. They also like the nasturtium in the garden. These plants contain sharp mustard oils that put off many other insects. Cabbage whites are adapted to this and even recognise their food plants by this smell.

The female large white lays yellow eggs in groups on the underside of a leaf. Its caterpillars are yellowish-green with black spots and often feed together. The caterpillars of the small white, by contrast, are velvety green and live singly. After a few weeks the caterpillar pupates, and a new butterfly emerges from the **chrysalis**.

When many caterpillars sit on a head of cabbage, they eat the leaves down to the ribs. That is why cabbage whites are considered **pests** in vegetable growing. Gardeners often protect their plants with fine nets so that the butterflies cannot lay eggs. You can also pick off the eggs and caterpillars by hand.

The caterpillars store substances from the cabbage plants and therefore taste bad to many birds. An important enemy is the tiny **braconid wasp** Cotesia glomerata. It lays its eggs in the caterpillars, and the wasp larvae eat the caterpillar from the inside. Afterwards they spin themselves into small yellow cocoons next to the dead caterpillar.

Cabbage whites live in Europe, North Africa and large parts of Asia. The small white was accidentally introduced to North America in the 19th century and later also to Australia and New Zealand. Today it is one of the most widespread **butterflies** in the world. The large white is a migratory butterfly that can fly over long distances.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant family with four petals in the shape of a cross, for example cabbage and rape.
The larva of a butterfly, which feeds and grows.
A resting stage in which the caterpillar changes into a butterfly.
A small wasp that lays its eggs in other insects.

gewusst: Cabbage whites can see ultraviolet light, and to them males and females therefore look much more different than they do to us.
A female large white can lay several hundred eggs.

teile.einleitung: Moulting is the change of feathers in birds: old, worn feathers fall out and new ones grow back. In geese this happens in an especially striking way, because they lose all their large flight feathers at once. For a few weeks they then cannot fly.
wichtigste: Moulting is the name for the regular change of plumage in birds.
Feathers wear out over time and have to be replaced.
Most birds moult at least once a year, often after the breeding season.
Geese and ducks shed all their flight feathers at the same time.
During this time geese cannot fly.
Many songbirds, by contrast, replace their feathers gradually and stay able to fly.
Moulting costs the body a lot of energy.

abschnitte.text: Feathers are made of **keratin**, the same substance as our hair and fingernails. A finished feather is dead material and cannot repair itself. Through sun, wind, water and abrasion it becomes brittle over time. That is why the bird sheds old feathers, and a new one grows from the same skin pocket. This process is called **moulting**.

Geese, swans and ducks go through what is called a **wing moult**. In it they lose all the large flight feathers of the wings almost at the same time. Depending on the species, it takes about four to six weeks until the new feathers are big enough. During this time the birds cannot fly and are easier to attack on the ground. That is why they like to stay on open water, where they can simply swim away when in danger.

Most songbirds such as the blackbird or sparrow do not moult everything at once. They lose only a few feathers at a time, usually symmetrically on both wings. In this way they stay able to fly during the whole moult. In many species the main moult takes place in late summer, after the young have been raised. Some birds also have a second moult in spring and then get a colourful **breeding plumage**.

abschnitte.titel: A feat of strength for the body
abschnitte.text: Growing new feathers takes a lot of protein and energy. A bird therefore often eats more during the moult and is calmer than usual. Breeding, moulting and the long flight to the winter quarters mostly take place at different times. In this way the body does not have to do everything at once. Young feathers are at first still supplied with blood and are called **pin feathers**.

On large Swiss lakes many waterbirds gather in summer to moult. On Lake Constance and other waters you then see large groups of ducks seeking shelter on the water. In this period male mallards wear an inconspicuous, brown **eclipse plumage** and look almost like the females. Greylag geese and mute swans also moult here. Disturbance by boats or dogs is especially stressful for birds that cannot fly.

begriffe.erklaerung: Regular change of feathers in birds.
The large, long feathers on the wing that are needed for flying.
A firm horny substance of which feathers, hair and nails are made.
An inconspicuous plumage that some birds wear after the breeding season.

gewusst: A mute swan has over 20,000 feathers, all of which have to be replaced at some point.
The German word ‘Mauser’ comes from the Latin ‘mutare’, which means ‘to change’ or ‘to alter’.

teile.einleitung: The hamadryas baboon is a monkey from north-east Africa and Arabia whose males wear a magnificent silver-grey mane. This mane looks like a cape around the head and shoulders and gave the animal its German name, Mantelpavian (‘cape baboon’). In ancient Egypt the hamadryas baboon was regarded as a sacred animal.
wichtigste: Male hamadryas baboons have a striking mane around head and shoulders.
The hamadryas baboon lives in north-east Africa and on the Arabian Peninsula.
It is the only baboon species that also occurs in Asia.
In ancient Egypt it was regarded as a sacred animal.
Hamadryas baboons live in groups with several levels.
To sleep they retreat to steep rock faces.
They are omnivores and find food even in dry regions.

abschnitte.text: Adult males wear a long, silver-grey **cape** of hair around head, shoulders and back. Their face and rump are coloured pink to red. The females are olive-brown, smaller and have no mane. Males weigh about 20 kilograms, so roughly twice as much as females.

The hamadryas baboon lives in dry, rocky areas in the **Horn of Africa**, for example in Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia and Djibouti. It also occurs in the south-west of the **Arabian Peninsula**, in Yemen and Saudi Arabia. This makes it the only baboon species that also lives in Asia. Its home is semi-deserts, savannas and mountains.

Hamadryas baboons have a society with several levels. The smallest unit is a **harem** of one male and a few females with their young. Several harems join to form larger groups that roam together. At night often over a hundred animals meet at a safe sleeping cliff.

Hamadryas baboons are omnivores. They eat grasses, seeds, roots, acacia fruit, insects and sometimes small vertebrates. In their barren homeland they often have to cover long distances by day to find enough food. Waterholes are especially important to them.

In ancient Egypt the hamadryas baboon was revered as the animal of the god **Thoth**, the god of wisdom and writing. In wall paintings and as statues it is often seen with raised arms, as if greeting the rising sun. Some baboons were even kept in temples and **mummified** after their death. In Egypt itself the hamadryas baboon no longer lives wild today.

The hamadryas baboon is currently not regarded as threatened, because it is still fairly widespread. It is sometimes persecuted, however, because it raids fields. Hamadryas baboons are kept in many zoos, including in Switzerland. There you can watch their exciting group life well on large rock enclosures.

begriffe.erklaerung: Long hair on the head and neck, as in the lion or horse.
A group of one male and several females.
An ancient Egyptian god of wisdom who was shown as a baboon or an ibis.
To treat a dead body so that it is preserved for a very long time.

gewusst: Archaeologists have found mummified baboons in Egypt that had been imported from distant countries.
A male hamadryas baboon keeps his females together by calling them back with looks and, if need be, a bite on the neck.
Hamadryas baboons sleep on rock faces because they are safe there from leopards.

teile.einleitung: Neozoa are animal species that people have brought into areas where they did not live before. Some fit in inconspicuously, while others displace native animals and cause great damage.
wichtigste: A neozoon is a non-native animal species introduced by people.
The raccoon in Europe is a well-known example.
Usually species count that were introduced after 1492.
Some were released deliberately, others travelled as stowaways.
Neozoa that cause damage are called invasive.
In plants one speaks of neophytes.
In Switzerland too there are many neozoa, such as the Asian hornet or the quagga mussel.

abschnitte.text: The word **neozoon** comes from Greek and means ‘new animal’, and the plural is neozoa. It means animal species that have reached a new area through people. As the dividing line one usually takes the year 1492, when Columbus reached America and world trade increased sharply. Non-native plants are called **neophytes**, and the two together are called neobiota.

Some animals were released deliberately, for example for hunting, for fur farming or as pets. The **raccoon** from North America was released in Germany and escaped from fur farms, and today it also lives in Switzerland. Other animals travel unnoticed with ships, lorries, plants or timber. In this way, for example, the Asian tiger mosquito came to Europe in old car tyres.

In Ticino the **Asian tiger mosquito** has lived since the early 2000s, and by now also north of the Alps. The Asian hornet has been spreading for some years and eats honey bees. In large lakes such as Lake Constance and Lake Geneva the quagga mussel is multiplying and clogging water pipes. American crayfish such as the signal crayfish transmit the crayfish plague, from which native noble crayfish die.

Not all neozoa are harmful, and many live inconspicuously alongside native species. **Invasive** species, by contrast, multiply strongly because they have no natural enemies here. They eat native animals, take their food and space away or transmit diseases. In Great Britain, for example, the American grey squirrel has displaced the native red squirrel in many areas.

Pets such as turtles, fish or crayfish must never be released into the wild. Anyone who takes a boat from one lake to another should clean and dry it, so that no mussels travel with it. Nests of the Asian hornet can be reported to the authorities so that experts remove them. In Switzerland, rules apply to especially problematic species that forbid keeping and selling them.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal species that was brought into a new area by people.
A plant species that was brought into a new area by people.
Spreading strongly and in doing so harming other species or nature.
Living naturally in an area for a very long time.

gewusst: The domestic cat and the rabbit too were introduced by people in many parts of the world.
In Australia cane toads were released against beetles and themselves became a great plague.
Some neozoa travel half the world in the ballast water of ships.

teile.einleitung: Gills are the breathing organs of fish and many other water animals. With them the animals take oxygen from the water, just as we take it from the air with our lungs. Whether salmon, trout, carp or goldfish, all fish breathe with gills.
wichtigste: Fish breathe with gills.
Gills take up the oxygen dissolved in the water.
In bony fish the gills lie protected under the gill cover.
Gills consist of many fine plates with a rich blood supply.
Water flows in through the mouth and out again over the gills.
Tadpoles, mussels and crustaceans also have gills.
In air, gills collapse and no longer work.

abschnitte.text: **Gills** are breathing organs with which animals can breathe underwater. Water contains much less oxygen than air, so gills have to be very effective. All fish breathe with them, whether salmon, trout, lake trout, carp, catfish or goldfish. Many other water animals also have gills.

In bony fish, four **gill arches** sit on each side of the head. From them hang hundreds of fine gill filaments, threaded with tiny blood vessels. Because so much blood flows through them, healthy gills are bright red. A hard **gill cover** protects the delicate gills from outside.

The fish opens its mouth and takes in water. Then it closes it and pushes the water backwards over the gills, where it leaves again under the gill cover. In the process, oxygen passes from the water into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes into the water. Because blood and water flow in opposite directions, the exchange works especially well; this is called the **counter-current principle**.

Sharks and rays have no gill cover, but usually five to seven **gill slits** at the side. Some sharks have to keep swimming so that enough water flows over their gills. Some fish can also breathe air, for example lungfish. A fish out of water still suffocates, because its gill filaments stick together.

Frog tadpoles breathe with gills first and only later get lungs. The **axolotl**, a tailed amphibian from Mexico, keeps bushy gills on the outside of its head all its life. Mussels, crustaceans and the larvae of water insects such as mayflies also have gills. They look quite different, however.

At the fish market you recognise a fresh fish by its bright red gills. Fish need clean water with enough oxygen, otherwise they gasp for air at the surface. In warm summers the oxygen in lakes and rivers can become scarce, which is dangerous for fish. That is why an aquarium too often needs a **pump** that brings air into the water.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bony arch on which the gill filaments sit.
A hard flap that protects the gills in bony fish.
A gas that living things need for breathing.
Water and blood flow in opposite directions, so more oxygen is taken up.

gewusst: A litre of water contains about thirty times less oxygen than a litre of air.
Spread out, the gills of a fish would have a much larger area than its whole body.

teile.einleitung: Damselflies are delicate dragonflies with a thin, rod-shaped body. In summer you often see them at ponds, streams and lake shores, where they whirr over the water like small coloured needles. Typical of them is that at rest they fold their wings back together over the abdomen.
wichtigste: Damselflies are one of the two big groups of dragonflies; the other is the true dragonflies.
Most damselflies hold their wings folded back over the abdomen at rest.
Their four wings are almost the same shape.
Their eyes are set far apart on the sides of the head.
The larvae live in water and breathe with three leaf-like gills at the rear end.
Damselflies are predators and catch small insects in flight.
Well-known species in Switzerland are the demoiselles, the azure damselflies and the white-legged damselfly.

abschnitte.text: Damselflies have a very slender, long abdomen, often bright blue, green, red or metallic and shiny. Their four **wings** are about the same size and narrow at the base. The two **compound eyes** sit far apart, so that the head looks like a hammer. In the true dragonflies, by contrast, the eyes often touch in the middle.

When a damselfly is perched, it usually folds its wings back together over the abdomen. True dragonflies, by contrast, hold their wings spread out to the sides at rest. An exception are the **spreadwings**, which hold their wings half open. Damselflies fly more slowly and flutteringly than the large, powerful species.

The females usually lay their eggs in plant stems in or near the water. From them hatch **larvae** that live in the water for months or up to two years. At the rear end they have three leaf-like gill plates with which they breathe. Finally they climb out of the water on a stalk, and the finished dragonfly emerges from the larval skin.

Damselflies and their larvae are **predators**. The adults catch small flying insects such as midges and aphids, often in flight or from plants. The larvae catch small animals in the water with a fold-out lower lip, the **mask**. They themselves are eaten by birds, fish, frogs and larger dragonflies.

When mating, the male holds the female by the abdomen with claspers. The female bends her abdomen forwards, and so the typical **mating wheel** is formed, which often looks like a heart. In many species the pair stays together as a tandem while the eggs are laid. That way the male can prevent other males from mating with the female.

Several dozen species of damselfly live in Swiss waters. Often seen is the **azure damselfly**, which has a blue and black pattern. At streams, the banded demoiselle and the beautiful demoiselle stand out with their dark-coloured wings. Because many species need clean water, some are threatened by the disappearance of wetlands.

begriffe.erklaerung: The other large group of dragonflies, with a powerful body and wings spread out at rest.
An eye made of many thousands of tiny single eyes, typical of insects.
The fold-out lower lip of the dragonfly larva with which it seizes prey.
The heart-shaped position of male and female when mating.

gewusst: Dragonflies existed over 300 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs.
Dragonflies can neither sting nor bite; they are completely harmless to people.

teile.einleitung: A shed snakeskin, in German a Natternhemd (literally ‘adder’s shirt’), is the old skin that a snake sheds when it moults. Often you find it as a transparent, paper-thin casing in the grass or between stones, sometimes even in a single piece.
wichtigste: The skin shed by a snake is called a Natternhemd.
Snakes moult because their outermost layer of skin does not grow with them.
Usually the skin comes off in one piece and is turned inside out in the process.
The transparent scale over the eyes is also shed.
Before moulting the snake’s eyes become milky and cloudy.
Young snakes moult more often than old ones.
From the shed skin you can often tell which snake species it was.

abschnitte.text: The **Natternhemd** is the shed outer layer of skin of a snake. The name comes from the Nattern, a large group of snakes that also includes the grass snake. The word is, however, used for the skin of all snakes. The shed skin is thin, dry and translucent, and you can still see the exact pattern of the scales on it.

The top layer of snake skin consists of dead, horny material and cannot grow with the snake. That is why the snake has to renew it regularly, which is called **moulting**. Young snakes, which grow fast, moult several times a year. Fully grown snakes moult less often, but they too renew their worn skin in this way.

A few days before moulting a new skin forms under the old one. Between them a fluid collects, so the eyes become milky blue and the colours dull. During this time the snake sees badly and mostly hides. Then it rubs its snout on stones or branches until the skin tears open at the mouth. After that it crawls out of the old skin, which turns inside out like a stocking being taken off.

In Switzerland you find shed skins, for example, of grass snakes, dice snakes, Aesculapian snakes or vipers. They often lie by sunny dry-stone walls, in heaps of stones or in tall grass. Because the **scales** can be seen well on the shed skin, experts can often identify the species from it. Even the scale over the eye, the **spectacle**, can still be recognised as a small cap.

Lizards, spiders, crustaceans and insects also moult. Lizards, however, usually lose their old skin in many small shreds and not in one piece. Insects and spiders even shed their whole hard outer shell when they moult. In us humans the skin renews itself constantly in tiny flakes that you hardly see.

begriffe.erklaerung: Shedding the old skin when a new one has grown beneath it.
A transparent scale that protects the eye in snakes, because they have no eyelids.
Small, hard plates of skin that cover the body of snakes.
A large family of mostly non-venomous snakes, for example the grass snake.

gewusst: A shed snakeskin is often longer than the snake itself, because the skin stretches as it is shed.
Snakes have no eyelids, so they always look with open eyes.
In the past some people believed that a shed snakeskin in the wallet brought luck.

teile.einleitung: Lanolin is a natural fat that sheep make in their skin and give off to their wool. That is why freshly shorn sheep’s wool usually feels a little greasy and soft. People have used this wool grease for a long time for ointments, creams and lip care.
wichtigste: Lanolin is a waxy fat from the wool of sheep.
It is made by sebaceous glands in the skin of the sheep.
Freshly shorn wool therefore feels a little greasy and soft.
The fat protects the wool and skin of the sheep from rain and drying out.
Lanolin is obtained when washing the shorn raw wool.
It is in many creams, ointments and lip balms.
Some people react allergically to wool wax.

abschnitte.text: Lanolin is a fat, more exactly a wax, that sheep make themselves. It arises in the **sebaceous glands** of the skin and lies like a thin film around every wool hair. In German it is also called **Wollwachs** (wool wax) or Wollfett (wool grease). The name lanolin comes from Latin: ‘lana’ means wool and ‘oleum’ means oil.

For the sheep the wool grease is a kind of natural raincoat. It makes the wool **water-repellent**, so that rain tends to bead off and the animal does not get wet to the skin. It also keeps skin and hair supple and protects them from wind and cold. That is why wet sheep smell so typically of wool and fat.

After **shearing**, the raw wool is full of fat, dirt and plant remains. Before it can be spun, it is washed with warm water and detergents. In the process the fat dissolves, and the lanolin is separated from the wash water and purified. So no sheep has to suffer for lanolin, it arises in wool processing.

Lanolin can bind a lot of water and makes the skin soft. That is why it is in many **ointments**, hand creams, lip balms and baby creams. It is also used for caring for leather, as rust protection and in wool detergents. From lanolin people also obtain a starting material for making **vitamin D3**.

Not everybody tolerates lanolin well. Some people get a **contact allergy** from it, with itchy, reddened skin. On packaging it often appears under the name ‘lanolin’ or ‘wool wax’. Anyone who is sensitive should read the list of ingredients closely.

In Switzerland there are several hundred thousand sheep, for example White Alpine sheep or Valais Blacknose sheep. They are usually sheared once or twice a year. Anyone who has ever touched freshly shorn wool knows the greasy feeling on the hands. Afterwards, by the way, the hands are often especially soft.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small gland in the skin that makes fat.
Another word for lanolin, the fat from sheep’s wool.
Wool straight after shearing, still unwashed.
A skin reaction when you touch something the body does not tolerate.

gewusst: Unwashed sheep’s wool can consist to a large extent of fat and dirt.
In the past sailors rubbed wool grease into their hands to protect them from salt water.
Socks made of unwashed wool keep feet drier thanks to the fat.

teile.einleitung: Mimicry means that an animal imitates another animal in order to protect itself or to deceive. Often a harmless animal looks like a dangerous one, so that enemies leave it in peace. Mimicry is a form of deception that has to be distinguished from camouflage.
wichtigste: In mimicry an animal imitates the appearance of another, usually dangerous animal.
In this way harmless animals scare off enemies.
Hoverflies look like wasps, but are completely harmless.
Two forms are named after the researchers Henry Walter Bates and Fritz Müller.
Camouflage colours, as in the mantis, are by contrast camouflage and not mimicry.
Mimicry arises through evolution over a very long time.
Many examples of mimicry can also be found in Swiss gardens.

abschnitte.text: The word **mimicry** means imitation. An animal that imitates looks very similar to another animal, although the two are not closely related. Usually the animal being imitated is poisonous, able to defend itself or bad tasting. Predators have learned to avoid such animals. The imitator benefits from this too.

The most common form is called **Batesian mimicry**, named after the English naturalist Henry Walter Bates. In the 19th century he observed in the Amazon region harmless butterflies that resembled poisonous species. A well-known example here are the **hoverflies** with their yellow and black stripes. They look like wasps, but have no sting. The hornet moth, a moth, even looks deceptively like a hornet.

In **Müllerian mimicry** several dangerous species resemble each other. It was described by the German researcher Fritz Müller, who lived in Brazil. Wasps, bees and bumblebees, for example, wear similar warning colours in yellow, black or brown. A bird that has once been stung then avoids all animals with this pattern. In this way the species protect each other.

Not every imitation is mimicry. The green or brown camouflage colour of the **mantis** means that it is seen less well by enemies and prey. That is camouflage, because it does not want to stand out at all. If an animal looks like a twig or a leaf, this is called **masquerade**. In mimicry, by contrast, the animal is meant to be seen, but to be taken for something else.

In Swiss gardens and meadows live numerous species of hoverflies that imitate wasps or bees. Some beetles, such as the wasp beetle, also wear wasp colours. The mantis occurs in warm parts of Switzerland, for example in the Valais and in Ticino. In plants too there is imitation: the **bee orchid**, an orchid, has flowers that look like a female bee. In this way it attracts males, which pollinate the flower as they do so.

begriffe.erklaerung: Imitation of another animal in order to deceive enemies.
Striking colours that show that an animal is poisonous or able to defend itself.
The animal that imitates another.
Camouflage by imitating an object such as a twig or leaf.

gewusst: Some spiders imitate ants and hold their front pair of legs up like antennae.
Some hoverflies imitate not only the appearance of wasps but also their buzzing and their movements.

teile.einleitung: Neoteny means that a living thing keeps childlike features even as an adult. The most famous example is the axolotl, but neoteny also plays a role in dogs and even in us humans.
wichtigste: Neoteny is the retention of childlike features in adulthood.
In the dog, neoteny arose through domestication.
Compared with the wolf, dogs often have shorter snouts, floppy ears and a great urge to play.
The axolotl keeps its gills all its life and stays in the water.
Even so, a neotenic animal can reproduce.
The term comes from Greek and means roughly ‘to extend youth’.
In humans too, researchers see neotenic features.

abschnitte.text: **Neoteny** means that an animal keeps characteristics of its youth although it is adult. These can be body features, for example gills or a rounded head, but also behaviours such as playing. The word is made up of Greek parts and means roughly ‘to extend youth’. The term was introduced in the 19th century by the anatomist Julius Kollmann, who did research in Basel.

The **axolotl** is a salamander from lakes near Mexico City. Normally newts and salamanders transform from a larva with gills into a land animal. The axolotl, however, stays in the water all its life and keeps its bushy **external gills**. Even so, it becomes sexually mature and has offspring. The olm from caves in Slovenia and Croatia also stays larva-like throughout its life.

Dogs descend from the wolf and were bred by people over thousands of years, which is called **domestication**. In the process many dogs kept features of young wolves: shorter snouts, rounder heads, floppy ears and a great urge to play. Their barking and their attachment also recall wolf pups. This is especially strong in breeds such as the pug or the Cavalier King Charles Spaniel.

Many researchers think that humans too have neotenic features. In some respects adult humans resemble young chimpanzees more than adult ones: a flat face, little body hair and a large, round head. The fact that humans stay curious all their lives and like to learn is also linked to this. This idea is, however, a **hypothesis**, that is, an assumption that experts are still discussing.

Neoteny shows that evolution can also produce new forms through small changes in the timing of development. In the axolotl it is linked to hormones of the **thyroid gland**. If you give an axolotl such hormones, it can still turn into a land animal. Knowledge about neoteny therefore helps us to understand the growth and development of living things better.

begriffe.erklaerung: The retention of youthful features in adulthood.
Taming and breeding wild animals into domestic animals.
The young form of an animal that looks different from the adult animal.
A scientific assumption that is still being tested.

gewusst: The axolotl can regrow lost legs and even parts of its heart.
Wild axolotls are almost extinct today, but there are many in aquariums and laboratories.
The baby schema with big eyes and a round head makes us find animal babies and many dogs especially cute.

teile.einleitung: Moulting is the change of feathers in birds: old, worn feathers fall out and new ones grow back. Almost all birds moult at least once a year. In ducks moulting is especially striking, because for a few weeks they cannot fly at all.
wichtigste: Moulting is the regular change of plumage in birds.
Feathers wear out and therefore have to be replaced.
Most birds moult once or twice a year.
Many birds change their feathers gradually so that they stay able to fly.
Ducks lose their flight feathers all at once and are then briefly unable to fly.
After the breeding season male ducks wear a plain eclipse plumage.
Moulting is controlled by hormones and the length of the day.

abschnitte.text: Feathers are made of **keratin**, the same substance as our hair and fingernails. They are dead structures and cannot repair themselves. Through sun, wind and wear they become brittle over time. In **moulting** the old feather falls out because a new one grows beneath it and pushes it out.

In most birds the **flight feathers** fall out one after another in a fixed order. In this way there are always enough feathers, and the bird can keep flying. A complete moult in songbirds often takes several weeks. Because growing new feathers costs a lot of energy, moulting usually takes place after the breeding season, in summer or autumn.

Ducks and geese lose all their flight feathers almost at the same time. That is why they are **unable to fly** for about three to four weeks. During this time they hide in the reeds or gather on large, safe stretches of water. Male mallards then wear an inconspicuous **eclipse plumage** that resembles the plumage of the females, and in autumn they wear their colourful breeding plumage again.

Some Swiss waters are important **moulting sites** for waterbirds. On Lake Constance and other large lakes thousands of ducks, for example red-crested pochards, gather in summer in order to moult there. So that they are not disturbed during this vulnerable time, there are protected areas. Boats and dogs should keep their distance.

Other animals also change their body covering, but this is mostly called something different. Mammals such as dogs, cats and deer have a **coat change** in spring and autumn. Snakes shed their whole skin at once, which is called **sloughing**. In the ptarmigan the moult even changes the colour from brown in summer to white in winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: The long feathers on the wings that are needed for flying.
A firm substance of which feathers, hair and nails are made.
The inconspicuous plumage that some male birds wear outside the courtship season.
The colourful plumage with which males court females.

gewusst: A swan has over 20,000 feathers, all of which have to be replaced at some point.
Hens often lay no eggs or only a few during the moult.
The German word ‘Mauser’ comes from the Latin word ‘mutare’, which means ‘to change’.

teile.einleitung: Dragonflies are fast and skilful flyers that you often see at ponds and streams in summer. They are insects and a very old animal group, whose ancestors lived over 300 million years ago. They spend their youth as larvae under water.
wichtigste: Dragonflies are insects and form the order Odonata.
Wings and legs sit on the thorax.
Large dragonflies fly as fast as about 50 kilometres per hour.
The larvae live in water, often for one to several years.
Adult dragonflies here usually live a few weeks to a few months.
Here most dragonflies fly from spring to autumn, above all in summer.
Dragonflies are harmless to people, they do not sting.

abschnitte.text: Dragonflies are **insects** and, like all insects, have a head, thorax and abdomen. On the head sit two huge **compound eyes** made of thousands of single eyes, with which they can see almost all round. On the thorax sit the six legs and the four wings, which they can move independently of each other. The long, slender abdomen is often coloured bright blue, red or green.

Dragonflies can hover in the air, fly backwards and change direction in a flash. Large species reach about 50 kilometres per hour. Their prey, such as midges and flies, they catch in flight with their legs, which they form into a basket. A distinction is made between **damselflies**, which fold their wings together at rest, and dragonflies proper, which hold them spread out.

Many females lay their eggs in the water or in water plants. Some have an **ovipositor** for this, with which they pierce the eggs into plant stems. From the eggs hatch larvae that, depending on the species, live one to several years in the water and hunt tadpoles, insect larvae or small fish. For this they have a **mask**, a lower lip that they shoot forward in a flash.

When the larva is fully grown, it climbs out of the water on a plant stem. Its skin splits open on the back, and the finished dragonfly squeezes out, with no pupal stage in between. Afterwards it pumps up its wings and lets them dry. The empty larval skin, the **exuvia**, often stays hanging on the stem.

The ancestors of dragonflies were already flying over 300 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs. The giant dragonfly **Meganeura** had a wingspan of about 70 centimetres. Today over 6,000 species are known worldwide, in Switzerland about 75. In old German names such as Azurjungfer or Mosaikjungfer, ‘Jungfer’ (maiden) simply stands for dragonfly.

Many species of dragonfly are threatened because pools, bogs and near-natural streams have disappeared. The best way to help them is with a near-natural **garden pond** without fish, because fish eat the larvae. In Japan dragonflies are traditionally regarded as a symbol of courage and victory. Because they need clean waters, dragonflies also show how healthy a water is.

begriffe.erklaerung: An eye made of many small single eyes, typical of insects.
The juvenile form of an animal that looks different from the adult.
The extendable lower lip of the dragonfly larva for catching prey.
The empty skin left behind after hatching.
The scientific name of dragonflies.

gewusst: Dragonflies catch the great majority of the animals they go for, far more often than lions, for example.
A dragonfly can steer each of its four wings separately.
The giant dragonflies of prehistoric times were as big as today’s pigeons.

teile.einleitung: Cranes are large, long-legged birds with a long neck, known for their loud trumpeting calls and their dances. In Europe it is mainly the common crane that lives. In autumn and spring tens of thousands of them travel across the sky in impressive formations.
wichtigste: There are 15 species of crane worldwide.
In Europe the common crane breeds, and it is about 1.2 metres tall.
Its wingspan is about two metres.
On migration, cranes often fly in a V formation.
Cranes call loudly with a trumpeting sound, and you can hear them for kilometres.
In courtship the pairs dance with leaps and wing flapping.
In Japan cranes are regarded as a symbol of good luck and a sign of long life.

abschnitte.text: The **common crane** has grey plumage, a black and white neck and a red patch on the head. It stands on long, dark legs and is about 1.2 metres tall. With its wings spread it measures about two metres. In flight it stretches neck and legs straight out, which distinguishes it from the grey heron, which pulls its neck in.

Common cranes breed in bogs, marshes and damp woods in northern and eastern Europe, for example in Scandinavia, Poland and northern Germany. In autumn they travel south-west, and many spend the winter in France and Spain. On the way they stop at **resting places**, where sometimes tens of thousands of birds gather. In the **V formation** each bird saves energy because it flies in the updraft of the bird ahead.

Cranes are omnivores. They eat grains, seeds, roots and tubers, but also insects, worms, snails, frogs and small mice. On harvested fields in autumn they look for maize left lying. With their long beak they probe in the soft ground.

Cranes often stay with the same partner for life. In **courtship** they leap into the air, bow and throw up tufts of grass. The pair calls together in a duet as they do so. Usually the female lays two eggs in a nest on the ground, and both parents incubate for about a month.

No cranes breed in Switzerland. But you can watch them in autumn and spring, when they fly across the country on migration. With a little luck you can hear their trumpeting calls high in the sky. In central Europe the populations have increased again in recent decades thanks to bog protection.

begriffe.erklaerung: The wooing of a partner before mating.
A place where migrating birds rest and feed on the way.
A flight arrangement in the shape of the letter V that saves energy in flight.
A bird that flies back and forth every year between its breeding area and its wintering area.

gewusst: In Japan people fold 1,000 paper cranes, because according to an old legend that is supposed to grant a wish.
The windpipe of the crane is coiled and very long, which is why its calls sound like a trumpet.

teile.einleitung: The least weasel (Mustela nivalis) is the smallest predator in the world and also lives in Switzerland. It is so slim that it can slip effortlessly into the tunnels of mice. There it hunts its favourite prey.
wichtigste: The least weasel is scientifically called Mustela nivalis and belongs to the mustelid family.
It is the smallest predator in the world.
Its body is about 15 to 25 centimetres long.
It hunts mainly mice and is therefore useful in agriculture.
Because of its fast metabolism it has to eat very often.
In some least weasels the fur turns white in winter.
The least weasel is native to Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The least weasel has a long, very slim body and short legs. The body measures about 15 to 25 centimetres, and there is a short tail of only a few centimetres. Depending on sex it weighs about 30 to 200 grams, and males are clearly bigger than females. The back is brown and the belly white. Unlike its relative the **stoat**, it has no black tip to its tail.

Least weasels live in large parts of Europe, Asia and North America as well as in North Africa. They like open landscapes with hedges, heaps of stones, meadows and field edges. In Switzerland they occur from the lowlands up to high in the Alps. As a shelter they often use abandoned mouse burrows or crevices in **heaps of stones**. In some northern and high-lying areas their fur turns white in winter, which camouflages them well in snow.

The most important prey are **voles** such as the field vole. Thanks to its narrow body the least weasel can follow the mice right into their underground tunnels. It sometimes also eats birds’ eggs, young birds or insects. Because it is so small and loses a lot of warmth, it has a very fast **metabolism**. It therefore has to hunt several times a day and eats about a third of its body weight or more per day.

Least weasels are very quick and curious, and when in danger they flee into a hiding place in a flash. They can hiss and squeak in order to communicate or to threaten. A female usually gives birth to four to seven young, which are at first naked and blind. After about three to four weeks the young open their eyes. The mother communicates with them through sounds and close **body contact**.

A single least weasel can catch hundreds of mice a year. In this way it helps farmers to reduce damage to fields and meadows in a natural way. Its numbers vary greatly with the number of mice: if there are many mice, there are soon more weasels too. In Switzerland hedges and heaps of branches and stones are created to encourage weasels. The least weasel is protected and may not be hunted.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that hunts and eats other animals and belongs to the order of carnivores.
All the processes in the body by which food is converted into energy.
A family of slim predators that also includes the badger, stoat and otter.
A mouse with a short tail that digs tunnels in the ground.

gewusst: A least weasel fits through a hole that is hardly bigger than a wedding ring.
The German name Mauswiesel (‘mouse weasel’) probably comes from its hunting of mice.
A small female least weasel sometimes weighs less than a bar of chocolate.

teile.einleitung: The adder, or common European viper, is a venomous snake that also occurs in Switzerland. It is easy to recognise by the dark zigzag band on its back. Although it is venomous, it is shy and bites only when it feels threatened.
wichtigste: The adder belongs to the vipers and is venomous.
Its body is stocky and relatively short, usually 50 to 70 centimetres long.
On its back it has a dark zigzag band.
Males are often grey, females more brown in colour.
It kills its prey, above all mice, with a venomous bite.
In Switzerland it lives mainly in the Alps and the Jura.
Because its habitat is disappearing, it is threatened and protected in Switzerland.
The females give birth to about 5 to 15 live young.

abschnitte.text: The adder has a stocky, relatively short body with a short tail. Its head is clearly set off from the neck and bears a dark marking on the crown, often in the shape of an X or V. Typical is the **zigzag band** on the back. Males are often grey with a black pattern, females more brown. There are also entirely black animals, which are called **black adders**.

The adder is the snake with the largest range in the world, extending from western Europe to the Pacific coast of Asia. It even lives north of the Arctic Circle. In Switzerland it is found mainly in the Alps and the Jura, often high up on mountain pastures, in bogs and at woodland edges. As hiding places it uses piles of stones, stacks of wood and dense dwarf shrubs.

The adder eats mainly mice, but also lizards and frogs. It kills its prey with a **venomous bite** and then follows it until the venom takes effect. It detects smells with its forked tongue, which carries scent particles to a smelling organ in the roof of the mouth. Because it eats many mice, it helps to regulate their numbers.

After **hibernation** in a frost-free hiding place, adders come out in spring. Then it is mating season, and the males sometimes fight in a wrestling match over the females. In late summer the female gives birth to about 5 to 15 young, which are independent right after birth. The eggs develop inside the mother’s body, which is an advantage in cold regions.

In Switzerland the adder is threatened because its habitat is disappearing through buildings, roads and intensive farming. Like all native reptiles, it is legally **protected**. When hiking it is advisable to wear sturdy footwear and not to reach blindly into grass or under stones. A bite is painful and must be treated in hospital, but is only very rarely life-threatening for healthy people.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of venomous snakes with long, movable fangs.
A resting state in winter in which the animal uses hardly any energy.
An adder that is coloured entirely black.
Cold-blooded animals with scaly skin, for example snakes and lizards.

gewusst: The adder lives further north than any other snake in the world.
Black adders warm up in the sun faster than light-coloured ones, which is handy in the mountains.

teile.einleitung: After the emperor penguin, the king penguin is the second largest penguin species in the world. The bright orange-yellow feathers on its head are reminiscent of a crown. It lives on islands in the Southern Ocean and is an excellent diver.
wichtigste: The king penguin is called Aptenodytes patagonicus in science.
It grows to about 90 centimetres tall and is thus the second largest penguin species.
Typical are orange-yellow patches on the head, neck and chest.
It breeds on sub-Antarctic islands, for example on South Georgia.
King penguins do not build a nest, and the egg lies on the parents’ feet.
They eat mainly small fish and squid.
You can watch king penguins at Zurich Zoo.

abschnitte.text: A king penguin grows to about 90 centimetres tall and usually weighs 10 to 16 kilograms. Back and head are dark, the belly is white. Striking are the **orange-yellow ear patches** and the orange colouring on the chest and beak. Its dense, multi-layered **plumage** and a layer of fat protect it from the cold water.

King penguins live on **sub-Antarctic islands** such as South Georgia, the Crozet Islands, the Kerguelen Islands, Macquarie Island and the Falkland Islands. There they form huge breeding colonies, often of tens of thousands of animals. Unlike the emperor penguin, they do not breed on the ice of Antarctica. To hunt, they swim far out into the open sea.

King penguins eat mainly small **lanternfish** and squid. They usually dive over 100 metres deep, sometimes even over 300 metres. Under water they move along with their wings like paddles. Their wings have become stiff flippers, and they cannot fly.

The female lays a single egg, which the parents incubate on their feet under a warm **brood pouch**. Male and female take turns at this while the other partner feeds in the sea.
