After about 54 days the chick hatches, wearing a thick, brown coat of down. Because raising a chick takes over a year, a pair raises at most two young in three years.

In the 19th century king penguins were killed in huge numbers to obtain oil from their fat. Since they have been protected, many colonies have recovered well. Today they are considered not threatened. **Climate change** could, however, shift their feeding grounds further south and make the search for food harder.

At **Zurich Zoo** king penguins live together with other penguin species. In winter, in cold weather, there is the popular penguin walk through the zoo. The animals waddle along ahead of the visitors of their own accord. Such walks give the penguins exercise and variety.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of animals of one species that breed together.
A sea and island region north of Antarctica with a cool climate.
A fold of skin on the belly that keeps an egg or chick warm.
Soft, fluffy feathers that keep especially warm.

gewusst: The brown, fluffy chicks are often larger and heavier than their parents and were once thought to be a penguin species of their own.
Parents and chicks find each other in the noisy colony by their unmistakable calls.
A king penguin can hold its breath under water for several minutes.

teile.einleitung: Myriapodology is the science of myriapods, the many-legged arthropods. Researchers who work in this field study animals with many legs such as centipedes, millipedes and their tiny relatives.
wichtigste: Myriapodology is the study of the myriapods.
The name comes from Greek and means roughly ‘study of the ten-thousand-footed’.
The myriapods include four groups: millipedes, centipedes, symphylans and pauropods.
About 16,000 species are known worldwide, and new ones are constantly being discovered.
No species has exactly a thousand legs.
The record is held by an Australian millipede with over 1300 legs.
Myriapodologists often work in the laboratory, in the museum and outdoors in forest and soil.

abschnitte.text: Myriapodology is a branch of **zoology**, the science of animals. It deals with the **myriapods**, which in German are called Tausendfüsser (‘thousand-footers’). The name is made up of Greek words: ‘myrias’ means ten thousand, ‘pous’ means foot and ‘logos’ means study. Researchers in this field are called myriapodologists.

The myriapods include four groups. The **millipedes** have two pairs of legs on most body segments and eat rotting leaves. The **centipedes** have one pair of legs per body segment and are quick predators with venomous claws. Added to these are the tiny symphylans and pauropods, which are often only a few millimetres in size.

Myriapodologists collect animals in leaf litter, under stones, in caves and in the soil. In the laboratory they identify the species with a magnifying glass and microscope, often from tiny body parts. Today genetic analyses are also used to clarify relationships. Many collections are kept in natural history museums, also in Switzerland, for example in Bern, Basel and Geneva.

For a long time a millipede from California with up to 750 legs was regarded as the record holder. In 2021 researchers from Australia described a new species with over 1300 legs that lives deep in the soil. This gave us, for the first time, an animal that really has more than a thousand legs. Many myriapods have not yet been discovered at all, especially in the tropics.

Myriapods break down dead leaves and wood and turn them into fertile **humus**. They are thus important helpers in the soil of forests and gardens. Anyone who studies them learns a great deal about healthy soils and the evolution of the arthropods. Some species react sensitively to environmental changes and show how a habitat is doing.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of animals.
The scientific name for the many-legged arthropods.
Myriapods with two pairs of legs on most body segments.
Dark, fertile soil made of decomposed plant remains.

gewusst: Myriapods were among the first animals to conquer the land, over 400 million years ago.
Some millipedes can release a stinking or poisonous fluid when in danger.
A giant myriapod of prehistoric times called Arthropleura was over two metres long.

teile.einleitung: The common swift is a dark bird with sickle-shaped wings that spends almost its whole life in the air. In summer it hunts in groups around the houses of Swiss towns and villages, with shrill ‘sriih’ calls. Although it resembles swallows, it is not closely related to them.
wichtigste: The common swift has narrow, sickle-shaped wings.
Its plumage is dark brown to almost black, with no white underside.
It eats, drinks and sleeps in flight.
If it lands on the ground, it often has great difficulty taking off again.
It breeds in niches on buildings and likes to use nest boxes.
A female usually lays two to three eggs.
Swifts can live for over 20 years.

abschnitte.text: The common swift is about 17 centimetres long and has a wingspan of around 40 centimetres. Its plumage is almost uniformly dark, and only the throat is slightly lighter. The wings are long, narrow and **sickle-shaped**, unlike the broad wings of a pigeon. Its tiny feet have all four toes pointing forwards, so it can cling well to walls.

Swifts are true **masters of flight**: they eat, drink, collect nesting material and sleep in the air. Researchers found that some swifts fly for up to ten months without landing. Their flight looks stiffer and faster than that of a swallow. If a swift lands on the ground by mistake, it can hardly get up again because of its long wings and short legs.

Swifts eat small insects and spiders that drift in the air, the so-called **aerial plankton**. With a wide open beak they catch their prey in flight. For their young they collect hundreds of insects in the throat pouch to form a food ball. In cold, rainy weather they often fly far away to find enough food.

Originally swifts bred in rock crevices, but today almost only in **niches** under roofs and in holes in walls. A pair often stays faithful for several years and uses the same nest again. The female usually lays two to three eggs, and both parents incubate. When young swifts leave the nest for the first time, they fly off at once on their own and do not come back.

Swifts are **migratory birds** and spend the winter in Africa south of the Sahara. In Switzerland they arrive at the end of April or the beginning of May. Already at the end of July and in August most fly away again, so they stay only about three months. In this short time they have to raise their young.

When buildings are renovated, many nesting sites are lost because niches and holes are closed up. Artificial **nest boxes** replace these lost niches in towns and cities. Bird protection organisations in Switzerland advise house owners on how to protect swifts. A young swift that falls out of the nest too early is in danger and needs help from a bird care centre.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny insects and spiders that drift through the air.
A bird that flies to warmer regions in autumn and comes back in spring.
A bird family with very long wings, which includes the common swift and the alpine swift.
An artificial little house in which birds can breed.

gewusst: In its lifetime a swift flies a distance equal to several trips to the Moon.
In bad weather young swifts can fall into a kind of cold torpor and survive several days without food.
The larger alpine swift, which has a white belly, also lives in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Spawn is the name for the eggs of fish, frogs, toads and other water animals. They are usually released into the water and fertilised there. When fish release their eggs into the water, they are said to spawn.
wichtigste: Spawn is the eggs of fish and amphibians.
When fish release their eggs into the water, this is called spawning.
The eggs are usually only fertilised by the male in the water.
Frogspawn forms clumps, toadspawn long strings.
Fish spawn is called roe in the kitchen, and in sturgeon caviar.
Many fish lay thousands or even millions of eggs.
The time in which animals spawn is called the spawning season.

abschnitte.text: **Spawn** is the eggs of animals that reproduce in water, above all fish and amphibians. The eggs have no hard shell like birds’ eggs, but a soft covering. They are often surrounded by a transparent jelly that protects them. Snails and some mussels also lay spawn.

In **spawning** the female releases her eggs into the water, and the male releases his sperm fluid, the milt, over them. In this way the eggs are fertilised outside the body. Some fish let their eggs drift freely in the water, others stick them to plants or stones. Trout and salmon bury their eggs in a spawning pit in the gravel.

In spring you often see large clumps of transparent balls with black dots in ponds, which is **frogspawn**. Toads, by contrast, lay their spawn in long strings that they wind around water plants. From each egg a tadpole hatches after a few days to weeks. You should not take spawn home from the wild, because amphibians are protected.

Most fish do not look after their eggs, so they lay a great many of them. A pike lays tens of thousands of eggs, a cod even several million. Only a tiny part of them become adult fish, as many eggs and larvae are eaten. Fish that guard their brood, such as the stickleback, lay far fewer eggs.

Every species has its own **spawning season**. Pike and common frogs spawn in early spring, whitefish and trout, by contrast, in autumn and winter. In this time **closed seasons** apply in Switzerland for many fish, in which they may not be caught. In this way they can reproduce undisturbed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The eggs of fish when they are used as food.
The salted roe of sturgeons, an expensive delicacy.
A time of year in which a species of animal may not be caught or hunted.
A transparent, slimy mass that protects eggs.

gewusst: Frogspawn first sinks and then rises to the surface, where the sun warms the eggs.
Some fish such as the salmon return to spawn at exactly the place where they themselves hatched.

teile.einleitung: Octopuses are sea animals with eight arms, a soft body without bones and a surprisingly clever brain. They can change colour in a flash and squeeze through tiny gaps. Their German name, Krake, recalls old stories about a gigantic sea monster.
wichtigste: Octopuses are cephalopods and belong to the molluscs.
There are about 300 species of octopus worldwide, and all live in the sea.
Because octopuses have no bones, they fit through very narrow gaps.
Unlike the squid, the octopus has no two long tentacles, but eight arms of the same kind.
Uncamouflaged, octopuses are usually brownish grey.
Most octopuses live only one to two years.
The female guards her eggs, eats almost nothing in the process and dies soon after the young hatch.

abschnitte.text: An octopus has a sack-like body, the **mantle**, and eight arms with suckers. It has no bones, only the beak in its mouth is hard. That is why it can squeeze through any opening that is larger than its beak. The smallest octopus is only a few centimetres across, while the **giant Pacific octopus** can measure several metres with its arms outstretched.

Octopuses live in all seas, from shallow coasts to the **deep sea**. Many hide by day in rock crevices, caves or even in empty mussel shells. In the Mediterranean the common octopus is widespread. Octopuses breathe with gills and so need the oxygen from the water.

Octopuses hunt mainly crustaceans, crabs, mussels and fish. With their suckers they can also taste and feel. They open mussels by force or drill a hole in the shell with their rasping tongue. A **venom** in the saliva paralyses the prey.

Octopuses are regarded as the most intelligent invertebrates. In experiments they opened screw-top jars and found their way through mazes. In their skin there are colour cells with which they change colour and pattern in fractions of a second in order to **camouflage** themselves. When in danger they release a cloud of ink, although they themselves can hardly hear anything.

The female lays thousands of small eggs in a cave and hangs them in clusters from the ceiling. For weeks or months she guards and cleans the eggs and fans fresh water over them. During this time she eats almost nothing. Shortly after the young have hatched, the female dies, which is why octopuses usually live only **one to two years**.

The German name Krake probably comes from old Norse tales about the **kraken**, a gigantic sea monster that dragged ships down into the depths. Behind such stories there may be sightings of giant squid. Today the octopus fascinates many people with its cleverness. In Swiss zoos and aquariums you can sometimes watch octopuses, but they do not occur in lakes.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal group in which the arms sit directly on the head.
The sack-like part of an octopus’s body in which the organs lie.
An adhesive disc on the arms for holding on and feeling.
Adapting to the surroundings so as not to be seen.

gewusst: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
A large part of an octopus’s nerve cells sits not in its head but in its arms.
The blue-ringed octopus is hardly bigger than a golf ball, but one of the most poisonous sea animals.

teile.einleitung: The hinny is a hybrid of a stallion and a female donkey. It looks similar to the better-known mule, but is usually smaller and much rarer. Like almost all such crossbreeds, a hinny cannot have offspring of its own.
wichtigste: A hinny comes from a horse stallion and a female donkey.
With the mule it is the other way round: the father is a donkey and the mother a horse.
Hinnies are usually smaller than mules because the mother is a donkey.
Hinnies are much rarer than mules.
Almost all hinnies are infertile.
They are frugal, tough and sure-footed.
Such a crossbreed is also called a hybrid.

abschnitte.text: A hinny is a **crossbreed** of a horse stallion as the father and a female donkey as the mother. Such hybrids between two species are called **hybrids**. Horse and donkey are related, but belong to different species. That is why the hinny is neither horse nor donkey, but something in between.

Hinnies are usually smaller and slighter than mules because they grow up in the womb of a smaller donkey mother. Their head often looks more like a horse’s, and the ears are shorter than in the mule. Mane and tail are often fuller than in the donkey. The voice often sounds like a mixture of a whinny and a donkey’s bray.

Horses have 64 **chromosomes**, donkeys have 62. A hinny inherits half from each parent and therefore has 63 chromosomes. This odd number means that it cannot form working reproductive cells. That is why hinnies are almost always **infertile**, and exceptions have been reported only very rarely.

A female donkey becomes pregnant by a horse stallion much less often than a mare by a donkey stallion. In addition, hinnies are smaller and can carry less than mules. That is why breeders have almost always preferred to breed mules. Today hinnies exist only in small numbers, mostly with enthusiasts.

Hinnies combine qualities of both parents: they are **frugal** and sure-footed like donkeys and often quicker to learn than these. You can ride them, harness them to carts or use them as pack animals. In the past hinnies and mules were used for transport in mountain regions such as the Alps. In everyday speech the two animals are often confused.

begriffe.erklaerung: A crossbreed of two different species.
A male horse or a male donkey.
A female horse or a female donkey.
Tiny carriers of the genetic information in every body cell.

gewusst: A memory aid in German: in the Maulesel the mother is a donkey, and the word ends in ‘Esel’ (donkey).
A zebra and a horse can also have a hybrid offspring, which is called a zorse.
A hinny can live for over 30 years.

teile.einleitung: The common wall lizard is a nimble, slim lizard that likes to sit on sunny walls and rocks. It is a reptile and one of the most common lizards in the warmer parts of Europe. In Switzerland you see it especially often in the Valais and in Ticino.
wichtigste: The common wall lizard is a reptile.
It is one of the most common lizard species in the warmer regions of Europe.
It loves dry, sunny, stony places such as walls and rocks.
In Switzerland it is especially common in the Valais and in Ticino.
Railway embankments help it to spread in Switzerland.
It lays eggs, and the mating season is in spring.
In the wild it lives for about 5 to 10 years.

abschnitte.text: Including its tail, the common wall lizard grows to about 18 to 20 centimetres long, with the tail making up almost two thirds of the length. Its body is flat and the head is pointed. It is usually brown or grey with dark spots and stripes. Males are sturdier and often more colourful, and some have an orange or reddish underside.

Common wall lizards live in **dry, sunny and stony places**. Typical habitats are dry-stone walls, rocks, vineyards, quarries and **railway embankments**. Crevices and heaps of stones are important, because they can dive into them in a flash when in danger. They also spend the winter there in **winter torpor**.

Like all reptiles, the common wall lizard is **cold-blooded**, so its body temperature depends on its surroundings. In the morning it warms up in the sun before it goes hunting. If it gets too cold, it becomes sluggish and hardly moves. With its tongue it does not only taste but also picks up scents from the air.

The common wall lizard eats insects, spiders, woodlice and small worms. In spring it is mating season, and the males defend their territory against rivals. The female usually lays 2 to 10 eggs in loose, warm soil. After a few weeks the tiny young hatch and are independent at once.

If a common wall lizard is grabbed, it can shed its tail at a breaking point. This is called **autotomy**. The shed tail wriggles for a while and distracts the attacker. The tail grows back, but afterwards it is usually shorter and a different colour.

In Switzerland the common wall lizard is found mainly in the **Valais**, in **Ticino**, on Lake Geneva and at the southern foot of the Jura. Along railway lines it has also spread into northern Switzerland. Like all reptiles, it is protected in Switzerland. If you build a dry-stone wall or a heap of stones in your garden, you help it and other lizards.

begriffe.erklaerung: Vertebrates with scaly skin, for example lizards, snakes and tortoises.
The body temperature adapts to the surroundings.
Shedding a part of the body, for example the tail, in order to escape.
A state in winter in which an animal hardly moves and eats nothing.

gewusst: The common wall lizard can run up vertical walls and even upside down.
Some common wall lizards in northern Switzerland are descended from animals that came from Italy with trains or loads of stone.
A regrown lizard tail no longer contains vertebrae, but a rod of cartilage.

teile.einleitung: Nocturnal animals sleep by day and become active only when it gets dark. Owls, bats, hedgehogs or the wels catfish are typical examples, and they have astonishing tricks for finding their way in the dark.
wichtigste: Animals that are active mainly at night are called nocturnal.
The opposite are diurnal animals, and in between there are crepuscular animals.
The wels catfish, owls, bats and hedgehogs are typical nocturnal animals.
Many nocturnal animals have large eyes, good ears or a fine nose.
A reflective layer in the eye makes cats’ eyes glow in the dark.
At night some animals are better protected from enemies and from heat.
Artificial light at night disturbs many nocturnal animals.

abschnitte.text: **Nocturnal activity** means that an animal eats, hunts and moves around mainly at night. By day it sleeps in a hiding place, for example in a cave, a tree or under stones. Animals that are on the move mainly in the morning and the evening are called **crepuscular**. The inner rhythm that controls these times is called the internal clock.

In Switzerland, for example, the tawny owl, eagle owl, bats, hedgehogs, badger, edible dormouse and many mice are nocturnal. The wels catfish in lakes and rivers also hunts mainly at night. Among the insects many moths and glow-worms fly in the darkness. The fox is often on the move at night, but can also be active by day.

Many nocturnal animals have especially large eyes, like owls or tarsiers. Behind the retina cats and many other animals have a reflective layer, the **tapetum lucidum**, which uses little light twice. Owls hear so well that they can locate a mouse under the snow. Bats give out ultrasonic calls and hear from the echo where obstacles and prey are.

At night many predators, for example birds of prey, are not on the move. In deserts it is often too hot by day, so many animals come out of their burrows only at night. In addition nocturnal animals have to compete less with diurnal species for food. Owls, for example, hunt mice at night, while birds of prey such as the common buzzard hunt by day.

Street lamps, lit buildings and advertising boards make the night ever brighter. This **light pollution** confuses many animals: insects fly around lamps until they are exhausted, and migratory birds lose their bearings. Bats avoid lit places and therefore find less food. That is why some municipalities in Switzerland switch lamps off at night or use warm light directed downwards.

begriffe.erklaerung: Active mainly in the early morning and in the evening.
A reflective layer in the eye that improves seeing in the dark.
Finding your way with calls and their echo, as in bats.
Too much artificial light at night.

gewusst: Each eye of a tarsier is as big as its whole brain.
An eagle owl can turn its head far backwards because it cannot move its eyes.
Many plants also open their flowers only at night, so that moths can pollinate them.

teile.einleitung: The leatherback turtle is the largest turtle in the world and a true giant of the oceans. Unlike other sea turtles it has no hard shell, but one that feels soft like leather. It likes best to eat jellyfish.
wichtigste: The leatherback is the largest sea turtle and the largest turtle of all.
Its shell is covered with a leathery skin instead of hard plates.
Large animals weigh several hundred kilograms.
It feeds mainly on jellyfish.
It dives deeper than any other turtle.
It swims through all the oceans, even into cool waters.
The species is threatened, among other things by plastic waste in the sea.

abschnitte.text: The leatherback usually grows to about 1.5 to 1.8 metres long and often weighs 300 to 500 kilograms. The heaviest known animal, found in Wales in 1988, weighed over 900 kilograms. Its back shell consists of many small bony plates under a thick, **leathery skin**. On it run seven lengthwise ridges that look like grooves, and the skin is dark with pale patches.

Leatherbacks eat almost only **jellyfish** and other jelly-like sea animals such as pyrosomes. Since jellyfish consist almost only of water, the turtle has to eat huge amounts of them. In its throat it has many sharp, backward-pointing spikes so that the slippery prey does not slide out again. Its sharp jaw edges cut the jellyfish into pieces as it does so.

The leatherback lives in all oceans, from the tropics to cool waters off Canada or Norway. That it can stand the cold is due to its size and a thick layer of fat that stores body heat. Every year it travels thousands of kilometres between feeding grounds and nesting sites. When diving it reaches depths of over 1,000 metres.

To lay eggs, the females crawl at night onto tropical **sandy beaches**, for example in West Africa, Central America or South-East Asia. With their hind flippers they dig a hole and lay about 80 to 100 eggs in it. They repeat this several times in a season. After about two months the young hatch and run straight to the sea, and the **sand temperature** decides whether more males or females result.

Many leatherbacks mistake floating **plastic bags** for jellyfish and swallow them, which can be fatal. They also get caught in fishing nets and long lines. On some beaches eggs are collected or the nesting sites are disturbed by buildings and light. That is why the species is on the Red List and is protected in many countries.

On many beaches conservationists and volunteers guard the nests and help the young. Less plastic in everyday life also helps the turtles, because a lot of rubbish ends up in the sea via rivers. This applies even to Switzerland, because the Rhine flows all the way to the North Sea. Leatherbacks are the last living representatives of a very old group of turtles.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hard protective covering of turtles, covered with skin in the leatherback.
A raised strip that runs lengthwise over the shell.
A list of threatened species of animals and plants.
A place where animals lay their eggs.

gewusst: Leatherbacks can keep their body temperature clearly above that of the surrounding water.
The leatherback has existed in almost unchanged form for millions of years.
The leatherback is the only living species of its family.

teile.einleitung: Cats do not speak with words, but they communicate in many ways: with sounds, with their bodies and with smells. Anyone who understands cat language soon notices whether a cat is content, frightened or annoyed. That way you can handle it better and avoid misunderstandings.
wichtigste: Cats communicate with sounds, body language and scents.
Cats use meowing mainly to communicate with people.
Purring often means well-being, but sometimes also stress or pain.
A tail held high is a friendly greeting.
If the tail swishes quickly back and forth, the cat is irritated or nervous.
Ears turned backwards often show fear or anger.
Slow blinking is a sign of trust.

abschnitte.text: Cats have many different sounds. Adult cats hardly **meow** at each other; they use meowing mainly to speak to people. **Hissing** and growling are clear warnings that say: stay away! When a cat sees a bird at the window, it often makes a soft, excited chattering.

**Purring** is a deep, even rumble that is produced in the larynx. Cats usually purr when they feel comfortable, for example when being stroked. Sometimes, however, they also purr when they are ill, injured or stressed, probably to calm themselves. Even kittens purr when feeding from their mother.

The tail is like a mood indicator. A tail held high means a friendly **greeting**. If the tail swishes quickly back and forth, the cat is irritated or nervous, and then it is better to leave it in peace. A fluffed-up tail shows great fright or fear.

Ears pointing forwards show curiosity and attention. Ears turned backwards or laid flat often show fear or anger. Very large **pupils** can mean excitement, playfulness or fear. An arched back with bristling fur is meant to make the cat look bigger and more dangerous.

Cats have **scent glands** on the cheeks, chin, paws and at the base of the tail. When a cat rubs its head against people or furniture, it marks them with its scent as familiar. When scratching trees, too, it leaves scent and visible marks. It is mainly un-neutered tomcats that mark their territory with urine.

If a cat slowly blinks at you, you can blink back just as slowly; this shows trust. **Kneading** with the front paws on a soft blanket shows that the cat feels secure. If a cat shows its belly, it is a sign of trust, but not always an invitation to stroke it. Always watch for warning signs such as hissing or a lashing tail.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cat’s hissing warning sound.
Pressing alternately with the front paws, also called making biscuits.
Communication through posture, movements and facial expression.
A smell that an animal leaves behind to mark something.

gewusst: Cats have learned that meowing works on people, which is why domestic cats meow much more than wild cats.
Some cats mix a high tone into their purr that sounds a little like a crying baby and gets people to feed them.

teile.einleitung: The mandarin duck is regarded as one of the most beautiful ducks in the world. The male wears a colourful breeding plumage with two orange feathers that stand up on the back like little sails. The duck originally comes from East Asia, but today you can also see it in parks in Europe.
wichtigste: The male mandarin duck has colourful plumage with sail-like feathers.
The female is plainly grey-brown with a white eye ring.
The mandarin duck comes from China, Japan, Korea and the east of Russia.
It breeds in tree holes, often high above the ground.
In China it is regarded as a symbol of fidelity in marriage.
Today mandarin ducks also live free in parts of Europe, especially in Great Britain.
Its closest relative is the North American wood duck.

abschnitte.text: At about 41 to 49 centimetres long, the mandarin duck is a rather small duck. The male, the **drake**, has a red beak, a broad white stripe above the eye and orange feathers on the cheeks. Especially striking are the two orange **sail feathers** on the back. The female is grey-brown and well camouflaged so that she does not stand out when breeding.

Originally the mandarin duck lives in **East Asia**, above all in China, Japan, Korea and the east of Russia. It likes quiet waters with dense bankside bushes and old trees. Because it is so beautiful, it was brought to many parks in Europe. From escaped animals, free-living populations have arisen mainly in Great Britain and Germany.

Mandarin ducks eat seeds, nuts, water plants, insects and snails. In autumn and winter they like to look for **acorns** and beechnuts under trees. Unlike many other ducks, they can sit well on branches. They are especially active at dusk.

The mandarin duck lays its eggs in **tree holes**, sometimes several metres above the ground. The female incubates alone for about a month. Shortly after hatching, the fluffy chicks jump from the hole into the depths. Thanks to their low weight they land unharmed and follow their mother to the water.

In China and Japan mandarin ducks are regarded as a sign of **love and fidelity**. Pairs of mandarin ducks are therefore often given as a wedding present or shown in pictures. In reality, however, mandarin ducks usually choose a new partner every year. In their homeland they have become rarer through the felling of forests.

In Switzerland you see mandarin ducks mainly in parks and zoos. Now and then free-living animals also turn up on lakes and rivers. These usually come from enclosures or have flown in from neighbouring countries. They do not belong to the original bird life of Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The name for the male in ducks.
The especially colourful plumage that a male bird wears in the courtship season.
A bird that builds its nest in a hole, for example in a tree.
An animal that was brought by people into a new area and lives free there.

gewusst: Mandarin duck chicks sometimes jump from their tree hole from a height of over ten metres.
In summer the drake loses his colourful plumage and then looks almost as plain as the female.
Mandarin ducks like to perch on branches, which is rather unusual for ducks.

teile.einleitung: Corals look like colourful stones or plants, but they are animals. Many tiny coral polyps together build huge coral reefs, which are among the most species-rich habitats on Earth. Tiny algae that live in their bodies help them to do so.
wichtigste: Corals belong to the animal phylum of cnidarians (Cnidaria) and to the class Anthozoa.
The reef-building stony corals form the order Scleractinia.
Their skeleton consists of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate.
A coral polyp has only a single opening for taking in food and excreting waste.
With stinging cells on the tentacles, polyps catch small prey from the plankton.
In many corals live zooxanthellae, single-celled algae from the group of dinoflagellates.
In coral bleaching the coral expels its zooxanthellae and turns white.

abschnitte.text: A coral consists of many small **polyps**, which look like tiny sea anemones. Each polyp has a tube-shaped body with a ring of tentacles around the mouth opening. In stony corals, tentacles and inner partitions are arranged in **sixes**. Many polyps are joined together and form a **colony** that grows together.

Stony corals secrete a hard skeleton of **aragonite**, a form of limestone, beneath them. When a polyp dies, the skeleton remains, and new polyps grow on it. In this way huge coral reefs arise over thousands of years. The largest is the **Great Barrier Reef** off Australia, which is over 2,000 kilometres long.

At night many polyps stretch out their tentacles and use **stinging cells** to catch tiny animals from the plankton. The food goes in through the single body opening, and leftovers are excreted through the same opening again. Reef-building corals get most of their energy, however, from their lodgers. Up to about 90 per cent of their energy needs are supplied to them by the zooxanthellae.

The **zooxanthellae** are single-celled dinoflagellates that live in the tissue of the polyps. They carry out photosynthesis and give sugar to the coral. In return they receive protection, carbon dioxide and nutrients. Because the algae need light, reef-building corals grow only in clear, shallow, warm sea water in the tropics. Such a partnership for mutual benefit is called **symbiosis**.

If the water becomes too warm, the coral expels its zooxanthellae. You can then see the white limestone skeleton through the colourless tissue, which is called **coral bleaching**. If the heat lasts too long, the coral starves and dies. Because of climate change, major bleaching events are happening more and more often, and pollution, overfishing and the acidification of the oceans do further harm.

There were once coral reefs in the area of present-day Switzerland too. About 150 million years ago there was a warm, shallow sea here in which corals grew. Their traces can be found today as **fossils** in the limestone of the Jura. Reefs are important because they protect coasts from waves and provide a habitat for a large part of all sea animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small, tube-shaped animal with tentacles, the basic building block of a coral.
Tiny algae that live in corals and supply them with food.
Two living things living together for mutual benefit.
The fading of corals when they lose their algae.
Tiny living things that float in the water.

gewusst: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest structure built by living things on Earth and can be seen from space.
Many corals of a reef release eggs and sperm into the water at the same time on the same night.
There are also cold-water corals that live without light in the deep sea, for example off Norway.

teile.einleitung: The cuckoo clock is a wall clock in which, every hour, a little wooden bird springs out of a small door and calls ‘cuck-oo’. It gets its name from this figure, which calls like a cuckoo. It comes from the Black Forest in southern Germany and is a popular souvenir worldwide.
wichtigste: The cuckoo clock became known in the Black Forest in the 18th century.
On every full hour the cuckoo calls as many times as the hour.
The call is produced by two small bellows with pipes.
The clock is usually driven by weights in the shape of pine cones.
Typical are carvings with leaves, birds and animals.
Many tourists think it is Swiss, although it comes from Germany.

abschnitte.text: A cuckoo clock is a mechanical **pendulum clock** that hangs on the wall. Above the dial there is a little door from which a small cuckoo hops on the full hour. It calls as many times as the hour, so three times at three o’clock. On many clocks it calls once at the half hour.

The clock is driven by **weights**, which often look like pine cones and hang on chains. A pendulum makes sure the clock ticks evenly. The call is produced by two small **bellows**, which push air through two pipes with different notes. You have to pull the weights up regularly, daily or once a week depending on the movement.

The cuckoo clock became known in the 18th century in the **Black Forest** in southern Germany, where many farmers built clocks in winter. Traders carried the clocks on their backs all over Europe. Around 1850 the shape of the ‘Bahnhäusle’ (railway cottage) arose in a competition at the clockmaking school in Furtwangen. This case looks like a little signalman’s house on a railway line.

The best-known style is the **hunting style** with carved leaves, birds, stag heads or hares. Other clocks look like chalets with dancing figures, mill wheels and musical movements. Many cases are still carved by hand from lime wood today. There are also modern cuckoo clocks in plain, colourful shapes.

Many people in the world associate the cuckoo clock with Switzerland. In Swiss souvenir shops, for example in Lucerne or Interlaken, they are often sold. The cuckoo clock was not invented in Switzerland, however, but in the neighbouring Black Forest. The mistake probably comes from the fact that both regions are known for mountains, wooden houses and clocks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A swinging weight that sets the even beat of a clock.
A small bag that presses air out when squeezed.
The inner workings of a clock made of gear wheels and springs or weights.
A keepsake that you bring back from a trip.

gewusst: In the Black Forest two places argue over which has the largest cuckoo clock in the world.
The cuckoo call of the clock consists of two notes, like the call of the real cuckoo.

teile.einleitung: Dogs speak with their whole body. With tail, ears, eyes, mouth and posture they show whether they feel cheerful, afraid, unsure or threatening. Anyone who understands this body language can meet dogs more safely and respectfully.
wichtigste: Dogs communicate mainly through body language, smells and sounds.
A tightly tucked tail usually means fear or submission.
Tail wagging does not always mean joy, but first of all excitement.
The play bow, in which the dog goes down on its front legs, is an invitation to play.
Yawning, licking and looking away can be signs of stress or appeasement.
Bared teeth, growling and a stiff body are clear warning signals.
Children should only touch a strange dog if the owner allows it.

abschnitte.text: Dogs descend from the wolf and live in social groups. To avoid quarrels they have developed a fine **body language**. They show their mood through posture, movements and facial expression. Added to this are sounds such as barking, growling or whining, as well as many scent signals.

A loosely wagging tail at medium height often shows joy and friendliness. A tail carried high and stiff can mean self-confidence or tension. A tail held low or **tucked** between the hind legs usually shows fear or submission. It is important to look not only at the tail, but always at the whole dog.

Ears pointing forward show attention, ears laid flat rather uncertainty or fear. A relaxed dog has a slightly open mouth and soft eyes. If a lot of white can be seen in the eye, the so-called **whale eye**, the dog often feels uncomfortable. A long, fixed stare can be a threat.

In the **play bow** the dog lowers its front legs, stretches its rear end up and wags. In this way it says: ‘Everything that happens now is play.’ With **appeasement signals** such as yawning, licking the nose, turning the head away or sniffing the ground, dogs try to calm a tense situation. They show them towards other dogs and towards people too.

Before a dog bites, it usually warns clearly. It freezes, stares, pulls up its lips, bares its teeth or **growls**. Sometimes the hair on the back also stands up, which is called hackles. You should never punish growling, because it is an important warning that prevents bites.

Always ask the owner first before you stroke a strange dog. Let the dog sniff your hand instead of reaching over its head, and stroke it rather at the side of the neck or on the chest. Never disturb dogs when they are eating, sleeping or retreating. If a dog runs towards you, stand still and calm like a **tree**, look away and fold your arms.

begriffe.erklaerung: Communication through posture, movement and facial expression.
Behaviour with which a dog wants to calm a situation.
A typical posture with which a dog invites play.
The lips of the dog.

gewusst: According to studies, dogs wag more to the right when they see something pleasant, and more to the left at something unpleasant.
A dog that shows you its belly does not always want to be tickled, sometimes it is simply unsure.
Dogs pay very close attention to our body language and often recognise whether we are cheerful or tense.

teile.einleitung: The mouflon is a wild sheep with magnificent, spirally curved horns. It is regarded as the ancestor of our domestic sheep and lives today in many parts of Europe, mainly in hilly forests.
wichtigste: The mouflon is regarded as the ancestor of our domestic sheep.
The rams carry large, spirally curved horns.
In summer the coat is reddish brown, and the males have a light saddle patch.
Wild sheep originally come from the Near East.
On Corsica and Sardinia mouflons have lived for thousands of years.
In Central Europe mouflons were released mainly for hunting.
Mouflons live in groups and are very shy.

abschnitte.text: The mouflon is smaller than most domestic sheep, and a ram weighs about 35 to 50 kilograms. Its coat is short and reddish brown in summer, and the belly and legs are light. Adult males often have a light **saddle patch** on the sides. The rams carry strong horns curved backwards and downwards, which hunters call **curls**. The females usually have no horns or only very small ones.

The wild sheep from which the mouflon descends originally lived in the Near East, for example in present-day Turkey and Iran. The European mouflons on **Corsica** and **Sardinia** probably descend from very early domestic sheep that went feral thousands of years ago. Later mouflons were brought to many countries of Europe for hunting, such as Germany, Austria and France. In Switzerland there are only a few mouflons, mainly in the Lower Valais near the French border.

Mouflons like to live in dry, hilly areas with forests and open spots. They eat grasses, herbs, buds, bark and acorns. As ruminants they chew their food a second time later. Outside the mating season females with young and rams live in separate groups.

The mating season is called the **rut** and takes place in late autumn. Then the rams fight by crashing their horns together with full force. In spring the female usually gives birth to one lamb. The lamb can walk after a short time and follows its mother.

abschnitte.titel: From wild sheep to domestic sheep
abschnitte.text: About 10,000 years ago people in the Near East began to tame and breed wild sheep. This is how the **domestic sheep** arose, which today provides wool, milk and meat. Through breeding, domestic sheep gained dense, long wool, while the mouflon kept a short coat of hair. Mouflon and domestic sheep can still mate with each other.

begriffe.erklaerung: A male sheep.
What hunters call the curved horns of the mouflon ram.
A light patch on the side of the coat that looks like a saddle.
Animals that bring up their food and chew it a second time.

gewusst: The horns of an old mouflon ram can form almost a whole circle.
Because mouflons have hard hooves and are made for rocks, on soft forest ground their hooves sometimes grow too long.
As with tree rings, you can tell from the age of the horns how old a ram is.

teile.einleitung: Sea turtles are reptiles that spend almost their whole life in the sea. With their flipper-like limbs they swim thousands of kilometres through the oceans. Only the females come onto land, in order to bury their eggs on sandy beaches.
wichtigste: There are seven species of sea turtles.
Instead of legs they have flipper-like limbs for swimming.
They have no teeth, but a horny beak.
They cannot pull their head back into the shell.
On their migrations they find their way by the Earth’s magnetic field.
The females lay their eggs on beaches, and after about two months the young hatch.
Many species are endangered today, among other things by plastic waste.

abschnitte.text: Sea turtles have a flat, streamlined **shell** with which they glide well through the water. The large front flippers are especially important for propulsion, and the hind flippers are used for steering. Unlike land tortoises they cannot pull their head and legs into the shell. Instead of teeth they have a sharp **horny beak**. On the shell small barnacles or algae sometimes grow.

The seven species are the green turtle, the loggerhead turtle, the hawksbill turtle, the leatherback turtle, Kemp’s ridley turtle, the olive ridley turtle and the flatback turtle. They live in warm and temperate seas all over the world, including the Mediterranean. The largest is the **leatherback turtle**, which can grow to over two metres long and weigh several hundred kilograms. It has no hard shell, but a leathery skin. It dives very deep and even swims into cool seas.

Every species has its own favourite food. The adult green turtle eats mainly seagrass and algae. The leatherback turtle feeds almost only on **jellyfish**. The hawksbill turtle likes to eat sponges on coral reefs. Other species hunt crabs, mussels and snails.

Females often return to lay their eggs on the beach where they hatched themselves. At night they dig a pit in the sand with their hind flippers and lay about a hundred eggs in it, which are as big as ping-pong balls. After about two months the young hatch and run to the sea, which they recognise by the brighter light above the water. The temperature in the sand decides whether males or females hatch: when it is warm, more **females** are produced. Males afterwards usually stay in the sea all their lives.

Many species of sea turtles are endangered. They get caught in fishing nets, their eggs are collected and their beaches are built on. Artificial light from hotels leads newly hatched young away from the sea. A big problem is **plastic waste**, because the animals mistake plastic bags for jellyfish and can die from them. Today many countries protect nesting beaches, and volunteers guard the clutches.

On their migrations sea turtles often cover thousands of kilometres. In doing so they find their way by the Earth’s **magnetic field**, as with a built-in compass. No sea turtles live in the wild in Switzerland. But you can do something for them by using less plastic and disposing of waste properly. For rubbish from rivers such as the Rhine ends up in the sea in the end.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cold-blooded vertebrate with scales or a shell, for example a turtle, lizard or crocodile.
A hard beak made of horn, which turtles have instead of teeth.
All the eggs that a female lays at once.
An invisible force of the Earth, which a compass also lines up with.

gewusst: Sea turtles have existed for over 100 million years, so they lived at the time of the dinosaurs.
Of a thousand newly hatched sea turtles often only about one becomes adult.
Sea turtles can excrete surplus salt from their body through salty tears.

teile.einleitung: Chickens also lose their old feathers every year and get new ones, and this change of feathers is called moulting. During this time chickens often look ruffled and a little bare. Many hens lay hardly any eggs, or none at all, during the moult.
wichtigste: Moulting is the change of feathers in birds, for example in the chicken.
Chickens usually moult in autumn, when the days become shorter.
A moult in the chicken often lasts about eight to twelve weeks.
During the moult many hens do not lay eggs.
In this time the animals need feed that is especially rich in protein.
Moulting is controlled by hormones and by the length of the day.
Mammals also change their coat, but that is called a coat change and not moulting.

abschnitte.text: In domestic chickens the moult usually begins in late summer or autumn. First the feathers on the head and neck often fall out, then those on the back, breast and wings. The new feathers grow out of the skin as thin quills and later open into finished feathers. Older hens often moult more heavily than young ones. After the moult the chickens again have a shiny, dense **plumage**.

New feathers consist to a large extent of protein. The hen now needs this protein for her plumage instead of for eggs. That is why she takes a **laying break** during the moult. Chicken keepers often give special feed with more protein during this time. As soon as the moult is over, most hens begin to lay again.

Moulting is triggered mainly by the **length of the day**. When the days become shorter in autumn, certain hormones in the body change, for example thyroid hormones. These hormones make sure that old feathers are shed and new ones grow. Stress, cold or a lack of feed can also trigger a moult. In wild birds the timing is precisely matched to the breeding season and bird migration.

Other animals also exchange their body covering. Snakes and lizards shed their old skin, which is called **sloughing**. Insects and spiders also shed their skin, because their hard shell does not grow with them. Mammals such as dogs, deer or chamois have a **coat change** in spring and in autumn. In birds, however, people speak only of moulting.

Moulting chickens are more sensitive and should be stressed as little as possible. A dry, draught-free coop helps them not to freeze. You should not pick them up unnecessarily during this time, because the growing feather quills can hurt. Good feed with grains, greens and a little animal protein supports regrowth. Feathers lying around in the coop are quite normal during this time.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the feathers of a bird together.
A time when a hen does not lay eggs.
Shedding the old skin or covering, for example in snakes and insects.
The hollow shaft of a feather that sits in the skin.

gewusst: A hen without a moult would gradually get more and more tattered feathers and be worse protected against the cold.
In autumn there are sometimes so many feathers in a chicken coop that it looks as if a fox had been raging there, when it is only the moult.

teile.einleitung: Madagascar is a huge island in the Indian Ocean that lies off the east coast of Africa. It is the fourth largest island in the world and famous for animals and plants that exist nowhere else, such as ring-tailed and other lemurs. At the same time Madagascar is a state of its own, with the capital Antananarivo.
wichtigste: Madagascar lies in the Indian Ocean off the east coast of Africa.
After Greenland, New Guinea and Borneo it is the fourth largest island in the world.
The island is about fourteen times as big as Switzerland.
Most animal and plant species of the island occur only there.
Madagascar is the home of the lemurs, for example the ring-tailed lemurs.
The capital is called Antananarivo.
Madagascar has been independent from France since 1960.

abschnitte.text: Madagascar lies in the **Indian Ocean**, separated from the African mainland by the Mozambique Channel. At its narrowest point this strait is about 400 kilometres wide. The island is about 1,600 kilometres long and about 587,000 square kilometres in area. That makes it about fourteen times as big as Switzerland.

Through the middle of the island runs a highland with mountains, rice terraces and a cooler climate. In the east grow damp **rainforests**, in the west dry forests and savannas, in the south thorn scrub. Famous are the mighty **baobab trees**, for example on the Avenue of the Baobabs near Morondava. Off the coast lie coral reefs and small islands.

Madagascar broke away from Africa and later from India a very long time ago. Since then many species have developed there quite independently, and most are **endemic**. Besides the lemurs, about half of all species of chameleon in the world live here, colourful frogs and the cat-like **fossa**. Many researchers therefore call Madagascar a small continent of its own.

The first people came to Madagascar only a few thousand years ago, many of them by boat from South-East Asia. Later people from Africa and Arab traders joined them. From the 19th century a Malagasy kingdom ruled large parts of the island, until France made it a **colony** in 1896. In 1960 Madagascar became independent.

About 30 million people live in Madagascar today (as of 2023). **Malagasy** and French are spoken. Most people live from farming, above all from growing rice. Madagascar is the most important producer of **vanilla** in the world, yet it is among the poorest countries.

A large part of Madagascar’s original forests has been cut down, for fields, charcoal and building timber. As a result many animal species, especially the lemurs, are severely threatened. National parks such as the **Masoala National Park** protect valuable areas. Zurich Zoo supports this park and shows a piece of Malagasy rainforest in its Masoala Hall.

begriffe.erklaerung: Occurring only in one particular place in the world.
A tree with a very thick trunk.
The national language of Madagascar.
An area ruled by a foreign state.
The largest predator of Madagascar, similar to a cat.

gewusst: In Madagascar there are no monkeys, lions or giraffes, but over 100 species of lemur.
The ancestors of many Malagasy come from present-day Indonesia.
The smallest known chameleon in the world lives on Madagascar and fits on a fingertip.

teile.einleitung: Gills are the breathing organs of fish and many other water animals. With them the animals take oxygen directly from the water. That is how a perch in a lake can breathe without ever coming to the surface.
wichtigste: Gills take oxygen from the water and give off carbon dioxide.
Fish such as the perch, the whitefish and sharks breathe with gills.
Gills consist of many very thin gill filaments rich in blood vessels.
In bony fish a hard gill cover protects the gills.
Most sharks have five open gill slits on each side.
Gill rakers filter food from the water in fish such as whitefish.
Tadpoles, crustaceans, mussels and many insect larvae also breathe with gills.

abschnitte.text: Gills are organs with which animals breathe in water. In fish they sit behind the head, on the left and right. Water contains much less oxygen than air. That is why gills have to be very good at extracting the dissolved **oxygen**.

In fish the gills sit on curved bony bars, the **gill arches**. From them hang hundreds of fine **gill filaments**, which lie close together like the pages of a book. Their walls are wafer-thin and full of tiny blood vessels. Because so much blood flows through, healthy gills look bright red.

The fish takes in water through its mouth and presses it out again over the gills. In the process oxygen passes from the water into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes into the water. In the gill filaments the blood flows in exactly the opposite direction to the water, which is called the **counter-current principle**. This lets the fish take up an especially large amount of oxygen.

Bony fish such as the perch or the trout have a movable **gill cover** that protects the gills and helps with pumping. Sharks and rays have no cover, but open **gill slits**, usually five on each side. Some sharks have to keep swimming so that enough water flows over their gills. Other sharks can also pump water through their gills while lying on the bottom.

On the inner side of the gill arches, many fish have small projections called **gill rakers**. They hold back food and protect the delicate gill filaments. The whitefish in Swiss lakes have especially long and dense rakers. With them they filter tiny plankton such as water fleas from the water.

It is not only fish that have gills. Tadpoles breathe with gills until they turn into frogs with lungs. The Mexican axolotl even keeps its frilly **external gills** for its whole life. Crustaceans, mussels, squid and the larvae of many insects such as dragonflies also have gills.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin, blood-rich plate of the gills through which oxygen enters the blood.
A hard bony plate that covers and protects the gills in bony fish.
Small projections on the gill arches that hold back food like a sieve.
Blood and water flow in opposite directions so that more oxygen gets into the blood.

gewusst: On land the fine gill filaments collapse and stick together, which is why a fish out of water suffocates despite all the air.
Fishermen and cooks recognise a fresh fish partly by its bright red gills.

teile.einleitung: Coprophagy means ‘eating dung’. Animals that feed wholly or partly on dung are called coprophages. What sounds disgusting to us is very useful in nature, because these animals tidy up and bring nutrients back into the soil.
wichtigste: Coprophagy literally means ‘eating dung’, and the word comes from Greek.
Animals that feed on dung are called coprophages.
Well-known coprophages are dung beetles, scarab beetles and many fly larvae.
Rabbits and hares eat a special, soft kind of dropping straight again.
Young koalas and elephants eat their mother’s dung to get useful gut bacteria.
Coprophages help to break down dung and fertilise the soil as they do so.
Dogs also sometimes eat dung, which is usually harmless but unwanted.

abschnitte.text: The term is made up of the Greek words ‘kopros’ for dung and ‘phagein’ for eating. Dung often still contains many **nutrients**, because animals do not digest their food completely. Herbivores in particular, such as cows or horses, excrete a lot of undigested plant material. Other animals use this as a source of food.

The best-known **coprophages** are beetles. The **scarab beetle** forms a ball from dung and rolls it away to lay eggs in it. Other dung beetles dig tunnels under cowpats and carry dung deep into the soil. In Switzerland there are numerous species of dung beetle, for example on alpine pastures.

Rabbits and hares produce two kinds of dropping. Besides the familiar hard pellets there is soft **caecotrope**, which they take up again directly from the anus. It contains vitamins and proteins that bacteria in the caecum have made. Only on the second pass through the gut can they absorb these substances.

Young **koalas** eat a special paste from their mother’s dung. In this way bacteria reach their gut that they need in order to digest poisonous eucalyptus leaves later. Young elephants, hippopotamuses and horses also sometimes eat the dung of adult animals. In this way they build up their **gut flora**.

Without coprophages, cowpats and other droppings would lie around much longer. The animals break the dung up, mix it into the soil and so turn it into **fertiliser**. At the same time they take away breeding places from flies and parasites. In Australia, dung beetles from other continents were therefore even introduced to break down cattle dung.

Some dogs eat the dung of cats, horses or other dogs. Mother dogs lick their puppies clean and eat their dung as they do so, which is quite normal. In adult dogs the behaviour can come from curiosity, boredom or hunger. Because **worms** and disease germs can be passed on this way, owners should stop it and ask the vet if it happens often.

begriffe.erklaerung: The eating of dung.
The droppings of animals, especially of large herbivores.
Soft, nutrient-rich droppings of rabbits that they eat again.
All the useful bacteria in the gut.

gewusst: A scarab beetle can roll a ball of dung that is much heavier than itself.
Some dung beetles find their way at night by the Milky Way in order to roll their ball in a straight line.
In ancient Egypt the scarab beetle was regarded as a sacred animal.

teile.einleitung: A cocoon is a firm covering that some animals build for themselves in order to spend an important phase of life in it, protected. Especially well known are the cocoons of moths, in which the caterpillar pupates. From the cocoon of the silkworm, people have obtained precious silk for thousands of years.
wichtigste: A cocoon is a protective covering that an animal usually builds from threads it has spun itself.
Many moth caterpillars pupate in a cocoon.
The thread for the cocoon comes from spinning glands on the caterpillar’s head.
In the cocoon the caterpillar turns into a butterfly by way of the pupa.
Silk is made from the cocoons of the silkworm.
Spiders, fleas and earthworms also form cocoons for themselves or their eggs.

abschnitte.text: A cocoon is a covering of threads, secretion or woven-in plant parts. It protects the animal from enemies, cold, wet and drying out. It is typical of insects with **complete metamorphosis**, that is, with the stages egg, larva, pupa and adult. The actual **pupa** lies inside the cocoon.

When the caterpillar is fully grown, it looks for a sheltered place, for example between leaves or in the ground. From **spinning glands** on its head it presses out a liquid that hardens in the air into a thread. In hours of work it moves its head back and forth in figures of eight and so wraps itself up. Some species also weave in hairs, bits of wood or soil.

In the cocoon the caterpillar moults one last time and becomes a pupa. After that its body is almost completely rebuilt: caterpillar legs and chewing mouthparts become wings, antennae and a sucking proboscis. This **metamorphosis** takes a few weeks or even a whole winter, depending on the species. To hatch, the moth often softens the cocoon with a liquid or cuts it open.

The **silkworm** is a moth whose caterpillars eat mulberry leaves. Its cocoon consists of a single, very long thread that can measure several hundred metres. To obtain silk, the cocoons are soaked in hot water and the thread is reeled off. Silk making comes from China, where for thousands of years it was a closely guarded secret.

It is not only caterpillars that build cocoons. Many spiders wrap their eggs in an **egg sac** of spider silk, which some females even carry around with them. Earthworms form small cocoons with their girdle, in which the young worms develop. Flea larvae and many wasps also pupate in a cocoon.

In Switzerland, silk processing was an important trade for a long time. In the 19th century Zurich was regarded as one of the most important silk cities of Europe, and in Basel silk ribbons were woven. In Ticino, silkworms were also bred in the past. In summer here you can also find the cocoons of native moths, for example on twigs or under tree bark.

begriffe.erklaerung: A protective covering that an animal builds from threads or other material.
The resting stage of an insect between larva and adult.
The change of an animal from one form into a completely different one.
A gland that makes a liquid from which a thread is formed.

gewusst: Day-flying butterflies usually do not build a cocoon; their pupae hang freely from twigs or stems.
The so-called ‘ant eggs’ you see in an anthill are in reality often cocoons with pupae inside.
For a single silk scarf you need the threads of many hundreds of cocoons.

teile.einleitung: The mule is a hybrid of a male donkey and a mare. It is big and strong like a horse, but frugal, tough and sure-footed like a donkey. For thousands of years mules have carried loads over mountain paths, including in the Swiss Alps.
wichtigste: A mule comes from a male donkey and a mare.
When a horse and a donkey mate, a mule or a hinny results, depending on the parents.
Mules are almost always infertile.
They have long ears like donkeys and a large body like horses.
Mules are very sure-footed and therefore ideal pack animals in the mountains.
They are tougher and more frugal than horses.
The Swiss Army still uses mules as pack animals today.

abschnitte.text: The mule is a **crossbreed** of a male donkey as the father and a mare as the mother. With the **hinny** it is exactly the other way round: there the father is a horse and the mother a donkey. Mules are much more common than hinnies and usually bigger too. In everyday speech people often simply say ‘Muli’.

Mules have the large, strong body of a horse. From the donkey they have inherited the **long ears**, the narrow hooves and often a short mane. Their voice sounds like a mixture of a whinny and a donkey’s bray. Depending on the breed of the mother, mules can be small or very large.

Mules are **sure-footed**, tough and need less feed than horses. They can carry heavy loads over steep, narrow paths. Like donkeys they are careful and do not go on if something seems dangerous to them. This caution is often misunderstood as stubbornness, but is actually clever.

Horses have 64 **chromosomes** and donkeys 62, and the mule has 63. Because of this odd number it cannot form healthy reproductive cells. That is why mules are almost always infertile. Every mule therefore has to be bred anew from a donkey and a horse.

In the past **pack drivers** with mules brought goods such as salt, wine and cheese over Alpine passes like the Gotthard or the Great St Bernard. To this day the Swiss Army keeps mules and Franches-Montagnes horses for the **Train**, a unit for transport in rough terrain. On some Alpine pastures and on trekking tours mules still carry loads too. They get to places where no vehicles can drive.

begriffe.erklaerung: The mating of animals of different species or breeds.
A man who in the past transported goods over the Alpine passes with pack animals.
A unit of the Swiss Army that transports equipment with horses and mules.
Safe on the feet, even on steep and stony ground.

gewusst: Mules were already bred and used in ancient Rome and by the Egyptians.
In the Grand Canyon in the USA mules still carry mail and tourists into the gorge today.
Mules often live longer than horses and can reach over 30 years.

teile.einleitung: Milking means taking milk from the udder of an animal. Cows are milked most often, but also goats, sheep and buffaloes. In the past this was done by hand, today mostly with machines or even with robots.
wichtigste: In milking, milk is taken from a cow’s udder.
A cow gives milk only after she has given birth to a calf.
A cow’s udder has four teats.
Cows are usually milked twice a day.
Today milking is mostly done with milking machines, sometimes with milking robots.
Goats, sheep, buffaloes and camels are also milked.
In Switzerland milk is important for cheeses such as Emmental and Gruyère.

abschnitte.text: A cow produces milk to feed her calf. The milk forms in the **udder**, a large glandular organ between the hind legs. The udder consists of four quarters, each with a **teat**. In milking, the milk is drawn out through the teats. For a cow to give milk, she must first have given birth to a calf, and after that she gives milk for many months.

In the past every cow was milked by hand, on a small one-legged **milking stool**. The milker grasps the teat, squeezes it shut at the top and presses the milk out downwards with the fingers. The milk then squirts into a bucket. For a single cow it takes about ten minutes or more by hand. On some Alpine pastures and with goats, milking is still done by hand to this day.

Today most farms use a **milking machine**. Four cups made of metal and rubber are attached to the teats, and a gentle vacuum sucks the milk out in a rhythm. The milk flows through tubes into a cooled tank. On many farms there are also **milking robots**: the cow walks into a box by herself when she wants to be milked. A robot arm cleans the teats, finds them with cameras or laser and attaches the cups.

Before milking the teats are cleaned so that no germs get into the milk. Calm is important, because a stressed cow gives up her milk less well. The hormone **oxytocin** makes sure that the milk lets down into the udder. Cows have to be milked regularly, otherwise the udder becomes tight and painful. An inflammation of the udder is called mastitis and has to be treated.

In Switzerland there are about half a million dairy cows (as of around 2024). Their milk is made into drinking milk, butter, yoghurt and above all **cheese**, for example Emmental, Gruyère or Appenzeller. In summer many cows are milked on the Alp, and the milk is often turned into Alpine cheese right there. Goat’s milk and sheep’s milk are also popular. In Italy genuine buffalo mozzarella is made from buffalo milk.

begriffe.erklaerung: The organ of a cow or goat in which the milk is produced.
The outlet on the udder from which the milk comes.
A machine that milks cows fully automatically.
The time in which a female mammal gives milk.

gewusst: A good dairy cow can give more than 30 litres of milk in one day.
With a milking robot the cow decides herself when she is milked, and many cows come two to three times a day.

teile.einleitung: The compost worm is a small, red earthworm that lives in compost heaps and manure. It eats rotting plant remains and turns them into nutrient-rich soil. That is why it is a hard-working helper for everyone who composts kitchen waste.
wichtigste: The compost worm is called Eisenia fetida in science and is also known as the manure worm.
It is smaller than the large lob worm and lives in rotting material instead of deep in the soil.
Typical are its red body and yellowish rings, which is why it is sometimes called the tiger worm.
It eats dead plant remains, manure and kitchen waste.
Valuable worm compost is made from its droppings.
Every compost worm is male and female at the same time.
It is used in worm bins, even on the balcony.

abschnitte.text: A compost worm usually grows to about 6 to 13 centimetres long. Its body is strongly red to reddish brown and has paler, yellowish rings between the segments. Like all earthworms it consists of many **segments** and has no eyes, but it senses light with its skin. If it is disturbed, it gives off a yellowish, strong-smelling liquid.

The compost worm lives where a lot of organic material is rotting, for example in compost heaps, leaf heaps and manure heaps. It stays near the surface and does not dig deep tunnels. In this it differs from the **lob worm**, which grows up to 30 centimetres long and digs deep, vertical tubes into the soil. Compost worms like it damp, warm and dark.

Compost worms eat dead plant parts, manure and kitchen waste such as vegetable and fruit remains. In doing so they actually eat mainly the **bacteria** and fungi that are already breaking the material down. In good conditions they can process about half their body weight every day. They tolerate meat, citrus peel in large amounts and salty things badly.

Every compost worm is a **hermaphrodite**, so it has both male and female sex organs. Even so, two worms always mate and exchange sperm. Afterwards the thickened band, the **clitellum**, forms a small cocoon in which several young worms develop. In good conditions compost worms multiply very quickly.

Compost worms turn waste into fertile soil, the so-called **worm compost**. It is rich in nutrients and well suited to garden beds and flower pots. In a worm bin you can compost in the flat or on the balcony without it smelling. Anglers also use compost worms as bait.

In Switzerland many families compost their garden waste themselves or put it in the green waste collection. In many municipalities there are also neighbourhood composts. In every healthy garden compost, compost worms usually turn up all by themselves. Worm bins with compost worms can be bought in garden centres or from specialist suppliers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Soil that is made from rotted plant remains.
A living thing that is male and female at the same time.
A thickened band on the worm’s body that forms the egg cocoon.
Dark, fertile soil made from decomposed plant and animal remains.

gewusst: The scientific name fetida means roughly ‘stinking’, because of the liquid the worm gives off when in danger.
Compost worms have no lungs, they breathe through their moist skin.
A worm bin can stand in a flat without an unpleasant smell if it is looked after properly.

teile.einleitung: Rhinoceroses are huge plant eaters with one or two horns on the nose. There are only five species left in Africa and Asia, and all are threatened by poaching.
wichtigste: There are five rhinoceros species: two in Africa and three in Asia.
In Asia live the Indian rhinoceros, the Javan rhinoceros and the Sumatran rhinoceros.
The horn consists of keratin, like our hair and fingernails.
A broken horn slowly grows back.
A rhino mother carries her young in the womb for about 15 months.
A rhino calf weighs about 40 to 65 kilograms at birth.
Rhinos smell very well, but see poorly.

abschnitte.text: Rhinoceroses have a massive body, short, strong legs and a very thick, firm skin. The largest is the **white rhinoceros**, which can weigh over three tonnes. The African species and the Sumatran rhinoceros have two horns, while the Indian rhinoceros and the Javan rhinoceros have only one. The horns are made not of bone but of **keratin**, like hair and fingernails. If a horn breaks off, it slowly grows back.

In Africa the white rhinoceros and the black rhinoceros live in savannas and bushland. In Asia the **Indian rhinoceros** lives in India and Nepal, and the Javan rhinoceros and the Sumatran rhinoceros in Indonesia. The Javan rhinoceros now exists only in a single national park on the island of Java. Of the northern white rhinoceros only two females are left.

Rhinoceroses are pure plant eaters. The white rhinoceros tears up grass with its broad lips, while the black rhinoceros plucks leaves and twigs from bushes with its pointed upper lip. They especially like to feed early in the morning and in the evening, and in the midday heat they often rest or wallow in mud. Rhinos see poorly, but their **sense of smell** and their hearing are very good.

Many rhinos live alone, and white rhinos also in small groups. Two males sometimes fight with their horns over a territory. If a rhino feels threatened, it often charges and attacks with its horn. After a gestation of about 15 months the mother gives birth to a single **calf**, which weighs 40 to 65 kilograms. Because the calf stays with the mother for a long time, she has a new young one only every few years.

Rhinos are poached because their horn is sold at a very high price in parts of Asia as a remedy or as an ornament. Yet the horn has no proven healing effect. Rangers guard the animals in protected areas, and some rhinos have their horn sawn off as a precaution. In Switzerland Basel Zoo has bred Indian rhinoceroses successfully for many years, and Zurich Zoo keeps white rhinoceroses in its Lewa Savannah.

begriffe.erklaerung: A firm horny substance of which hair, nails and hooves are also made.
Illegal hunting of animals, often to sell parts of them.
The name for the young of a rhinoceros.
Rolling in mud to cool the skin and protect it from insects.

gewusst: The name ‘white rhino’ probably comes from a misunderstanding: ‘wide’, meaning the broad mouth, was taken to mean ‘white’.
Despite their weight, rhinos can run at up to about 40 kilometres per hour.
Oxpecker birds often sit on rhinos, eat parasites and warn of danger with calls.

teile.einleitung: The nautilus, in German a Perlboot (‘pearl boat’), is a cephalopod with a beautiful, chambered shell. It is a relative of squid and octopuses and counts as a living fossil, because its ancestors lived hundreds of millions of years ago.
wichtigste: Nautiluses belong to the animal class of the cephalopods.
The family includes the living genera Nautilus and Allonautilus.
The shell is divided into many air-filled chambers.
The shell forms a logarithmic spiral, but not a golden spiral.
A nautilus has about 50 to over 90 tentacles without suckers.
Its eyes are pinhole-camera eyes without a lens.
Its blood contains haemocyanin and is therefore bluish.

abschnitte.text: The nautilus lives in a coiled limy shell with white and brown stripes, which in some species grows to about 20 centimetres. The animal itself sits only in the front, largest chamber. From the opening many **tentacles** poke out, depending on the animal about 50 to over 90, which have no suckers but are sticky. When the nautilus withdraws, a leathery **hood** closes the opening like a lid.

The shell is divided by walls into many **chambers**, which are filled with gas and a little fluid. A strand of tissue, the **siphuncle**, connects all the chambers and can pump the fluid out or let it in. In this way the nautilus rises or sinks like a submarine. To swim it expels water through a funnel and moves by jet propulsion.

Nautiluses live in the tropical Indian and Pacific Oceans, for example off the Philippines, New Guinea and Australia. By day they often stay at a depth of several hundred metres, and at night they rise up reef slopes. They eat crustaceans, dead fish and other carrion. In doing so they are helped above all by their sense of smell, with the rhinophores beneath the eyes.

The eyes of the nautilus are simple **pinhole-camera eyes** without a lens, into which seawater can enter. It has four gills, that is, two pairs, while most other cephalopods have only two. Its blood carries oxygen with the copper pigment **haemocyanin**, which colours it bluish. Nautiluses can live for over 20 years, which is very old for cephalopods.

The shell of the nautilus grows in the form of a **logarithmic spiral**, which becomes evenly wider with every turn. It is often claimed that it is a golden spiral connected with the golden ratio. Precise measurements show, however, that this is a myth. Even so, the nautilus shell is a famous example of mathematics in nature.

The ancestors of the nautiluses lived as long as about 500 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs. The extinct **ammonites**, whose fossils are also found in the Swiss Alps and in the Jura, were distant relatives. Today nautiluses are threatened by the trade in their beautiful shells. Since 2017 international trade in them has been regulated by the Washington Convention on the protection of species.

begriffe.erklaerung: Molluscs such as squid and octopuses whose arms sit directly on the head.
A strand of tissue that connects the chambers of the shell and regulates buoyancy.
A copper-containing substance in the blood that carries oxygen and colours the blood bluish.
A living thing that has hardly changed for a very long time.

gewusst: The world’s first nuclear submarine was named after the nautilus.
In Jules Verne’s novel ‘Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas’ Captain Nemo’s submarine is called ‘Nautilus’.
A nautilus lays only a few large eggs, from which the young hatch only after almost a year.

teile.einleitung: A mini pig is a pig breed specially bred to be small. Mini pigs are smaller than normal domestic pigs, but can still grow much bigger and heavier than many people think. They are very clever, sociable and need a lot of space.
wichtigste: Mini pigs are breeds of the domestic pig bred to be small.
Well known are the Göttingen minipig and the Vietnamese pot-bellied pig.
Many mini pigs weigh 40 to over 100 kilograms when adult.
Pigs are very intelligent and able to learn.
They are herd animals and should never be kept alone.
Pigs like to root with their snout and wallow in mud.
In Switzerland pigs count as farm animals, even if you keep them as a pet.

abschnitte.text: Mini pigs descend from the domestic pig, which in turn descends from the **wild boar**. Through deliberate **breeding** they were made ever smaller. A well-known example is the Göttingen minipig, which was bred from about 1960 at the University of Göttingen in Germany.
