For this, among other things, small pot-bellied pigs from Asia were crossed with other breeds. Originally mini pigs were bred for medical research.

The word mini is often deceptive. A normal domestic pig can weigh over 300 kilograms, and a mini pig is much lighter. Nevertheless many adult mini pigs weigh 40 to over 100 kilograms. Even very small piglets sold as teacup pigs usually also grow into large animals. Pigs go on growing until they are about four to five years old.

Pigs are among the most **intelligent** pets. They can learn their name, practise tricks and even solve simple puzzles. In nature pigs live in groups called a **sounder**. That is why they feel very uncomfortable alone and need at least one other pig for company. With their snout they can smell excellently.

abschnitte.titel: What does a mini pig need?
abschnitte.text: Mini pigs need a large run with soil for rooting and a warm, dry shed. Because pigs can hardly sweat, they cool off in summer in a **wallow**, that is, a mud puddle. The mud also protects against sunburn and insects. They eat almost anything, but need balanced food with plenty of vegetables and hay. A flat is not a suitable place for a pig.

In Switzerland mini pigs also legally count as **farm animals**. Anyone who keeps pigs must report this to the authorities, even if it is only one or two animals. The Animal Protection Act requires that pigs must have contact with others of their kind. In addition the animals must have a place to root. Anyone who wants a mini pig should therefore inform themselves well beforehand, because pigs can live 15 years and longer.

begriffe.erklaerung: Deliberate reproduction of animals with certain characteristics.
A group of wild boar or pigs.
A mud puddle in which pigs cool off.
An animal that people keep to obtain food or other products.

gewusst: Pigs have a much better sense of smell than humans and are used in France and Italy to search for truffles.
A pig can orient itself using a mirror and so find hidden pieces of food.

teile.einleitung: Nidifugous animals are young animals that can walk, see and follow their parents shortly after birth or hatching. Young geese, chicks or foals are typical examples.
wichtigste: Nidifugous animals leave the nest shortly after hatching or birth.
Goslings, that is, young geese, are nidifugous.
Nidifugous animals are born with open eyes and with feathers or fur.
The opposite are nidicolous animals, which are born naked and helpless.
Among birds, for example, chickens, ducks, geese and quail are nidifugous.
Among mammals, horses, cows, hares and guinea pigs belong here.
Many nidifugous animals follow the first creature they see, which is called imprinting.

abschnitte.text: **Nidifugous animals** is the name for young animals that are already well developed at birth. They have open eyes and ears, a coat of feathers or fur and can soon walk. Often they leave the nest only a few hours after hatching. They mostly eat by themselves, but are still guarded, warmed and led to food by their parents.

Typical nidifugous animals among birds are chickens, ducks, geese, swans, quail and many waders. Young geese are called **goslings** and already run behind their mother on the first day. Duck chicks swim on the water soon after hatching. Because the chicks are so well developed, the eggs of these birds are usually large and have a lot of yolk.

Many mammals too are nidifugous. A **foal** often stands on its long legs only an hour after birth. Calves, lambs, giraffes and elephants can also soon walk. Young hares are born with fur and open eyes, while baby rabbits are naked and blind. Guinea pigs are so far along at birth that after a short time they nibble solid food.

**Nidicolous animals** are born naked or almost naked, with closed eyes and helpless. They stay in the nest for a long time and are fed and warmed by their parents. Examples are blackbirds, sparrows, cats, dogs and mice. The Basel zoologist Adolf Portmann called humans ‘secondarily altricial’, because babies do have open eyes, but remain helpless for a long time.

Many nidifugous animals follow the first moving creature that they see and hear after hatching. This process is called **imprinting**. The behavioural researcher Konrad Lorenz showed it with greylag geese that ran after him as after a mother goose. Imprinting helps the chicks to stay near their mother and so be protected from dangers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A young animal that can walk right after birth and leave the nest.
A young animal that is born helpless and stays in the nest for a long time.
A young goose chick.
A fast kind of learning shortly after birth in which a young animal fixes on a parent animal.

gewusst: Young wildebeest can already run along with the herd a few minutes after birth.
Chicks of the megapode are so independent that they never get to know their parents.
Konrad Lorenz received the Nobel Prize in 1973 for his research on animal behaviour.

teile.einleitung: Melanism means that an animal has an especially large amount of dark pigment in its skin, fur or feathers and therefore looks black or very dark. The best-known case is the black panther, a dark jaguar or leopard. Melanism is a natural quirk of the genes and not a disease.
wichtigste: Melanism is a dark colouring caused by an excess of dark pigment.
This pigment is called melanin.
Black panthers are jaguars or leopards with melanism.
In black jaguars the spots can still be seen in good light.
Melanism is determined by hereditary factors, that is, genes.
The opposite of melanism is albinism.
In Switzerland there are, for example, black adders and dark squirrels.

abschnitte.text: Almost all animals have the pigment **melanin**, which colours skin, hair and feathers brown or black. If an especially large amount of it is produced, the whole animal looks black, which is called melanism. The name comes from the Greek word ‘melas’ for black. The cause is a small change in the **genes** that determine how much pigment is produced. This change can be passed on to the offspring.

There is no separate animal species called the black panther. It is **jaguars** in South and Central America, or leopards in Africa and Asia, with melanism. In black jaguars the change is dominant, so it easily prevails in inheritance. If you look at such an animal in bright sunlight, you can make out the dark rosettes in the black fur. Black leopards are especially common in dense rainforests, for example in South-East Asia.

In the Swiss Alps there are many completely black **adders**, which are sometimes called ‘Höllenotter’ (hell adders). Their dark body absorbs the warmth of the sun faster, which is an advantage in the cool mountains. In squirrels too, besides red ones there are often almost black animals. In the asp viper black animals also occur. And some domestic cats are completely black because they carry this hereditary factor.

Melanism can help or harm an animal, depending on where it lives. In the dark forest a black animal is well camouflaged, but on light sand it stands out. A famous example is the **peppered moth** in England. When tree trunks became dark from soot from factories, dark moths survived better because birds saw them less well. When the air became cleaner, the light moths increased again.

In **albinism** the body can form little or no melanin. Such animals are white and often have red or very pale eyes. Examples are white mice, rats or rabbits. Albino animals often see worse and do not tolerate strong sunlight well. Melanism and albinism show how strongly small differences in the genes can change the appearance of an animal.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dark pigment in skin, hair, feathers and eyes.
A hereditary factor that determines how a living thing is built and what it looks like.
An inborn lack of pigment, and the animals are white.
A ring-shaped dark spot in the fur of the jaguar and leopard.

gewusst: In humans too the amount of melanin determines how light or dark skin, hair and eyes are.
Black adders warm up faster in the sun than their light-coloured relatives.

teile.einleitung: The llama is a domestic animal from the Andes in South America and belongs to the camelids, but has no hump. For thousands of years llamas have carried loads and supplied wool, meat and dung. Today you can also see them in Switzerland on farms and on hikes.
wichtigste: Llamas belong to the New World camelids and come from South America.
Unlike dromedaries and Bactrian camels, they have no hump.
A llama can carry about a quarter of its body weight.
If the load is too heavy, it simply lies down.
Llamas are ruminants and chew their food a second time.
Bolivia is among the countries with especially many llamas.
Llama wool insulates well against cold and is a raw material for textiles.
Llamas often communicate with a soft humming.

abschnitte.text: A llama has a long neck, long legs and a dense, woolly coat in white, brown, black or spotted. It is about 1.1 to 1.3 metres tall at the shoulder and usually weighs 130 to 150 kilograms. Its ears are long and slightly curved inwards. On its feet it has two toes with soft **pads**, which spares the ground.

The llama was bred in the **Andes** several thousand years ago from the wild guanaco. Its relatives include the alpaca, the guanaco and the vicuña. Together they are called New World camelids, because they live in the Americas. Especially many llamas live today in Bolivia and Peru, where they live in the highlands at over 3,000 metres.

Llamas eat grass, hay, herbs and leaves. Like cows they are **ruminants**: after eating they bring the food up again and chew it once more so that it is digested better. In the upper jaw they have a hard dental pad at the front instead of a full row of incisors. Llamas need little water and manage with poor fodder.

Llamas live in herds and communicate with a soft **humming**. In quarrels they spit, but mostly at other llamas and rarely at people. After a gestation of about eleven months, one young is born, called a **cria**. Crias are usually born by day, often in the morning, so that they dry off before the cold night.

The Inca already used llamas as **pack animals** on their mountain paths. A llama carries about a quarter of its body weight, and if it gets too heavy, it lies down and goes on strike. Warm jumpers, hats and blankets are made from the wool, and the dung serves as fertiliser and fuel. In Switzerland llamas are kept for trekking tours and sometimes used as guard animals against foxes with sheep.

begriffe.erklaerung: The camelids of South America: llama, alpaca, guanaco and vicuña.
Animals that bring their food up again after eating and chew it once more.
The name for a young llama or alpaca.
A long high mountain range on the west coast of South America.

gewusst: Llamas deposit their dung in shared places, so the pasture stays clean.
In South America the llama is regarded as an important domestic animal and appears in many stories and festivals.

teile.einleitung: The sea trout is a trout that lives in the sea and swims back into rivers to spawn. It belongs to the same species as the brown trout, but spends part of its life in salt water. There it grows much bigger and gleams silver.
wichtigste: The sea trout is a migratory form of the trout and is scientifically called Salmo trutta trutta.
It belongs to the same species as the brown trout and the lake trout.
Young sea trout grow up in the river and then migrate to the sea.
To spawn they swim back into the river, which is called a spawning migration.
In doing so they often return to the water where they were born.
In the sea they become silvery and can grow to over a metre long.
Weirs and power stations block the way for many migratory fish.

abschnitte.text: The sea trout belongs to the **salmonids** and is closely related to the Atlantic salmon. Biologically it is the same species as the brown trout, which stays in the stream all its life. The difference lies in the way of life: the sea trout migrates to the sea, feeds itself big there and returns to spawn. In the sea it is silver with a few dark spots. Large animals grow to over a metre long and weigh more than ten kilograms.

Sea trout live on the coasts of northern and western Europe. They are found, for example, in the Baltic Sea, in the North Sea, around Great Britain, Ireland, Iceland and on the coast of Norway. In the sea they mostly stay near the coast and do not swim out as far as salmon. To spawn they need cool, clean rivers and streams with a **gravel bed**. Fish that migrate between the sea and fresh water are called **migratory fish**.

The young fish hatch in spring from eggs in the gravel of a river. They usually stay one to three years in fresh water and then look like small brown trout. After that their body changes: they become silvery, get used to salt water and are now called **smolts**. With the current they swim into the sea and eat crustaceans, shrimps and small fish there. After one or several years they return as adult fish.

In summer and autumn the adult sea trout swim upstream, which is called a **spawning migration**. They often find their way back exactly to the home waters where they were born. It is thought that they recognise the smell of their home river. In late autumn or winter the female beats a pit into the gravel with her tail and lays the eggs there. Unlike many salmon, many sea trout survive spawning and can migrate several times.

In Switzerland there are no sea trout, but there is a close relative with similar behaviour: the **lake trout**. It lives in large lakes such as Lake Constance or Lake Geneva and migrates to feeder rivers such as the Alpine Rhine to spawn. For it too, weirs and power stations are a big obstacle. That is why today **fish ladders** and fish passes are built, so that migratory fish can get upstream again. In the past even salmon from the North Sea swam up the Rhine as far as Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The journey of fish to the place where they lay their eggs.
A young trout or salmon that turns silvery and is ready to migrate to the sea.
A fish that migrates back and forth between the sea and a river or between a lake and a river.
A structure with small pools by which fish can overcome a weir.

gewusst: Brown trout, lake trout and sea trout are the same species, only with a different way of life.
On their migrations sea trout can leap over small waterfalls.

teile.einleitung: The salmon louse is a small crustacean that lives as a parasite on salmon and other salmonids. It feeds on the skin and blood of its hosts. Especially in large sea fish farms it multiplies strongly and so becomes dangerous for wild salmon too.
wichtigste: Despite its name, the salmon louse is not an insect but a small crustacean.
It lives as a parasite on salmon, sea trout and other salmonids in the sea.
It eats the mucus, skin and blood of its host.
Adult females grow to about one to two centimetres long.
In fish farms with many fish in a small space it multiplies strongly.
From fish farms, salmon lice can infest young wild salmon.
Against salmon lice, farmers use cleaner fish, among other things.

abschnitte.text: The salmon louse belongs to the **copepods**, a group of very small crustaceans. It has a flat body that clings like a sucker to the skin of the fish. The females carry long egg strings at the rear end. The salmon louse lives only in salt water and dies if the fish swims into fresh water.

abschnitte.titel: How does it harm the fish?
abschnitte.text: The salmon louse is a **parasite**, that is, an animal that lives at the expense of another. It rasps mucus, skin and blood off the fish. This creates wounds through which disease germs can enter. In a heavy infestation the fish is weakened and can even die.

In **fish farms** tens of thousands of salmon live in large net pens in the sea. For the salmon lice this is ideal, since they find very many hosts in a small space. Especially in Norway, Scotland, Ireland and Chile the salmon louse is a big problem for farming. Controlling it costs farmers a great deal of money every year.

Young wild salmon migrate from the rivers into the sea in spring. If their route passes fish farms, they can be infested by many salmon lice. Even a few lice can seriously harm a small young salmon. That is why experts blame lice from farms in part for wild salmon having become rare in some areas.

In the past mainly medicines were used against salmon lice, but the lice became increasingly resistant to them. Today many farms use **cleaner fish** such as wrasses or lumpfish, which eat the lice off the salmon. Other methods are warm water, freshwater baths or brushes. Some farms protect the fish with dense nets or raise them in closed tanks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that lives on or in another and harms it.
The animal on which a parasite lives.
A group of tiny crustaceans that occur in the sea and in fresh water.
A fish that frees other fish of parasites.

gewusst: Salmon lice attach themselves to the fish as tiny larvae and are hardly visible to the naked eye at first.
Fishers often recognise salmon freshly come up from the sea by the fact that salmon lice are still hanging on them.

teile.einleitung: A cat’s tongue feels rough like sandpaper. This is because of many small barbs with which the cat combs and cleans its fur. The cat’s tongue is an amazing tool for cleaning, drinking and eating.
wichtigste: The cat’s tongue is rough because it has many small barbs.
The barbs are called papillae and are made of horn, like our fingernails.
With its tongue the cat combs its fur and removes dirt and loose hairs.
The papillae take up saliva and carry it deep into the fur.
When drinking, the cat pulls up a small column of water with the tip of its tongue.
Cats cannot taste sweetness.
Cats sometimes bring swallowed hair back up as a hairball.

abschnitte.text: On a cat’s tongue sit hundreds of tiny barbs curved backwards. These **papillae** are made of keratin, that is, horn, like our fingernails. When a cat licks you, it therefore feels scratchy. In lions and tigers the papillae are so strong that they can scrape meat from bones.

Cats spend a large part of their waking time on **grooming**. The barbs work like the teeth of a comb and loosen tangles, dirt and loose hairs. In 2018 researchers discovered that the tips of the papillae are hollow and take up saliva. In this way the cat carries saliva deep into its fur, which cleans and cools.

Cats do not lap like dogs, which use their tongues like a scoop. The cat touches the surface of the water only briefly with the tip of its tongue and pulls the tongue back in a flash. This produces a small **column of water**, and the cat snaps up a mouthful from the top of it. It repeats this several times a second.

On the tongue there are also **taste buds**, but cats have far fewer of them than humans. Cats can taste well whether something is bitter, sour or salty. They cannot taste sweetness, however, because they lack the right sensory cells. As pure meat-eaters they do not need this taste either.

When grooming, the cat swallows many loose hairs. Most pass through the gut, but some collect in the stomach as a **hairball**. The cat then brings this back up. Regular brushing, especially in long-haired cats, helps against it.

Researchers in the USA studied the cat’s tongue closely and rebuilt it with a 3D printer. This gave rise to the idea for a special **hairbrush** that is easy to clean. The model could also be useful for animal care and for cleaning devices. When technology learns from nature, this is called **biomimetics**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Small bumps on the tongue, shaped like barbs in cats.
The horn substance that hair, claws and fingernails are also made of.
A sense organ on the tongue with which you taste.
Technology that copies ideas from nature.

gewusst: The chocolate sweet called a cat’s tongue is named after the shape of the tongue, not its roughness.
A cat can also use its tongue to help cool down on hot days, because evaporating saliva cools.

teile.einleitung: The common buzzard is the most frequent bird of prey in Switzerland and in all of Central Europe. You often see it sitting on a fence post or circling high over fields while it looks out for mice. Its mewing call can be heard far and wide in spring.
wichtigste: The common buzzard is the most frequent bird of prey in Switzerland.
It usually hunts from a perch and lies in wait for prey.
Its main food is voles and other small rodents.
Its wingspan is about 110 to 130 centimetres.
When circling it holds its wings in a shallow V shape.
It is a partial migrant: some leave in winter, others stay.
Young buzzards leave the nest after about 6 to 7 weeks.

abschnitte.text: The common buzzard is about as big as a large crow, but with broader wings. Its wingspan is about 110 to 130 centimetres. The plumage is coloured very differently, from almost white to dark brown, usually with a light band on the chest. With its **hooked beak** it tears up its prey, and with its **talons** it grabs it.

The common buzzard feels especially at home at **forest edges** near open fields and meadows. In the forest it builds its nest, the **eyrie**, high up in a tree. For hunting it needs open country with plenty of mice. In Switzerland it occurs almost everywhere in the Central Plateau and in the valleys.

Most often the common buzzard hunts from a **perch**, for example a post or branch, and lies in wait for prey there. It eats mainly voles, but also earthworms, insects, frogs and lizards. In winter, when fewer mice can be found, it eats more carrion and small birds. Sometimes you can also see it on foot on freshly ploughed fields, looking for worms.

High in the sky the common buzzard circles slowly in great loops. In doing so it uses **thermals**, that is, warm rising air, and hardly has to flap its wings. It holds its wings slightly raised in a shallow V shape. It often adds a loud, mewing ‘hiyah’.

Common buzzards breed in spring and usually lay two to four eggs. Both parents incubate for about five weeks. In the eyrie the young are fed mainly small rodents such as voles. After about 6 to 7 weeks they leave the nest for the first time, but are still fed by their parents for some time.

The common buzzard is a **partial migrant**: many birds from Scandinavia and north-eastern Europe fly south in winter, while most Swiss buzzards stay here. In winter you therefore often see more buzzards in Switzerland than in summer. In the past it was persecuted as a pest, but today it is protected in Switzerland. For farmers it is a helper, because it eats many mice.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that grabs its prey with its talons, such as an eagle, falcon or buzzard.
A raised seat from which a bird looks out for prey.
The large nest of a bird of prey.
Rising warm air with which birds glide upwards without flapping their wings.
A bird species in which some animals leave and others stay all year round.

gewusst: A common buzzard can eat several mice in one day.
The jay sometimes imitates the call of the common buzzard in a deceptively real way.
Hardly two common buzzards look exactly alike, so varied is their plumage.

teile.einleitung: Moths are lepidopterans that are on the move mainly at night. They are much more varied than the little clothes moths in the wardrobe.
wichtigste: Moths are the nocturnal relatives of the colourful butterflies that fly by day.
In everyday speech they are often simply called moths.
Most lepidopteran species in the world are moths.
Their antennae are thread-like or feathered, but without a club at the end.
At rest many moths hold their wings flat or roof-like over the body.
Moths pollinate many plants at night.
Artificial light attracts moths and can harm them.

abschnitte.text: **Moth** is not a strict scientific term, but a collective name for all lepidopterans that are not butterflies. It includes families such as owlet moths, geometer moths, hawk moths, silk moths and the small micromoths. Worldwide there are well over 150,000 species of lepidopterans, and by far the greatest part of them are moths. In Switzerland live over 3000 species of moths, but only about 200 species of butterflies.

Butterflies have thin antennae with a thickening at the end, a club. Moths, by contrast, have thread-like, saw-edged or **feathered antennae**. Many are rather inconspicuously coloured grey or brown and well camouflaged on tree bark. Their body is often thick and furry, which keeps them warm on cool nights.

With their feathered antennae many males smell the scents of a female from a great distance. Some moths can hear the ultrasonic calls of bats and then drop in a flash. As **pollinators** they are very important, because at night they visit flowers such as honeysuckle or evening primrose. Hawk moths suck nectar while hovering, with a very long proboscis.

Like all lepidopterans, moths develop from the egg via the **caterpillar** and the pupa into the adult. The caterpillars eat leaves, and some also eat wood, wool or stored food. The silk moth spins a cocoon of silk, from which people have made silk fabric for thousands of years. The clothes moth, by contrast, is unpopular because its caterpillars eat holes in woollen jumpers.

Moths fly to lamps because artificial light throws their orientation into confusion. Many then circle until exhaustion or become easy prey. The loss of flower meadows and the use of insecticides also cause them trouble. Anyone who wants to protect moths can plant native flowers in the garden and switch off unnecessary lamps at night.

The **death’s-head hawkmoth** has a marking on its back that recalls a skull, and can even squeak. The giant emperor moth is the largest lepidopteran in Europe. The hummingbird hawk-moth is a hawk moth that also flies by day and hovers in front of flowers like a hummingbird. The Atlas moth from Asia is among the largest moths in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: The feelers on the head with which insects smell and touch.
An animal that carries pollen from flower to flower so that fruit can form.
The larva of a lepidopteran.
A protective casing of silk threads in which the caterpillar pupates.

gewusst: Some moths have no mouth at all as adults and live only a few days.
In Switzerland the hummingbird hawk-moth is often taken for a small hummingbird.
Silk from the cocoons of the silk moth was made in China thousands of years ago.

teile.einleitung: The lion is a large big cat and is often called the ‘king of the beasts’. It lives mainly in the African savanna and is the only cat that lives together in groups, the prides. Its roar can be heard for kilometres.
wichtigste: The lion belongs to the cat family.
It lives mainly in the African savanna, with a small group in India too.
Lions live in prides of related females, their young and one or more males.
Males are larger and heavier than females and have a mane.
Over a short distance a lion runs at about 60 kilometres per hour.
Lions do not hunt successfully every day and then eat a lot at once.
Lions are considered threatened today.

abschnitte.text: After the tiger, the lion is the second largest cat in the world. Males usually weigh about 150 to 250 kilograms, females about 110 to 180 kilograms. The coat is sand-coloured, and at the end of the tail sits a dark tuft. Only the males wear a **mane**, by which you can recognise them from far away.

Lions today live mainly in the **savannas** and open woodlands of Africa south of the Sahara, for example in the Serengeti in Tanzania. They drink water from waterholes or rivers, but can also manage a few days without. A small group of Asiatic lions lives in the **Gir Forest** in India. In the past there were lions in North Africa, the Middle East and even in south-eastern Europe too.

A **pride** usually consists of several related females, their young and one or a few males. The males defend the territory and roar loudly to show others who the area belongs to. Young males must leave the pride at about two to three years old. Later they try to take over a pride themselves.

Usually the females hunt together and creep up on zebras, wildebeest, antelopes or buffalo. For a short sprint they reach about 60 kilometres per hour, but only over a short distance. When hunting they extend their sharp **claws**, otherwise they retract them so that they do not get blunt. Because not every hunt succeeds, lions do not eat every day, but eat a great deal at once.

Lions often rest and sleep for up to 20 hours a day to save energy. When they are not hunting, they walk leisurely and slowly. They are active mainly at dusk and at night, because they see much better in the dark than humans. After a gestation of about three and a half months the female usually gives birth to two to four **cubs**.

The number of lions has fallen sharply in recent decades, and they are considered **threatened**. Reasons are the loss of habitat, conflicts with livestock keepers and poaching. As a symbol of strength and courage the lion appears in many coats of arms and stories. In Switzerland the famous **Lion Monument** in Lucerne commemorates Swiss Guards who died in Paris in 1792.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large cat that hunts other animals, such as the lion, tiger or leopard.
A group of animals that live and hunt together.
Grassland with scattered trees in warm regions.
An area that an animal or a group defends against others.

gewusst: The roar of a lion can be heard up to about eight kilometres away.
In the pride, lionesses sometimes also suckle the young of other females.
The lion is the only cat species in which males and females look so different.

teile.einleitung: Rattlesnakes are venomous snakes from the Americas that warn with a rattle on the tail. When they feel threatened, they shake this rattle so fast that a loud buzzing sound is produced. With it they say: don’t come too close!
wichtigste: Rattlesnakes belong to the vipers and, among them, to the subfamily of pit vipers.
They form two genera: Crotalus and Sistrurus.
The name Crotalus comes from the Greek ‘krotalon’ and means castanet or rattle.
Carl Linnaeus described the genus Crotalus in 1758.
The rattle is made of keratin, and a new segment is added with every moult.
You cannot read the snake’s age from the age of the rattle.
Rattlesnakes live only in the Americas, from Canada to South America.

abschnitte.text: Rattlesnakes belong to the family of **vipers** and to the subfamily of pit vipers. There are two genera: the large genus Crotalus and the small genus **Sistrurus** with three species today. Sistrurus means ‘tail-rattler’, and these snakes are recognised by nine large scales on the head. The best-known species is the western diamondback, and the largest is the eastern diamondback in the south-east of the USA, which can grow to over 2 metres long.

The **rattle** is made of keratin, the same substance as our fingernails. It is built of hollow segments that fit loosely into each other and strike against one another when shaken. With every moult a new segment forms. Because the snake moults several times a year and segments can also break off, the rattle does not reveal its age.

abschnitte.titel: Seeing heat with the pit organ
abschnitte.text: Between the eye and the nostril, the rattlesnake has a small pit on each side. This **pit organ** senses heat radiation. In this way the snake can locate warm prey such as mice even in complete darkness. All pit vipers have this special sense organ.

Rattlesnakes live in North, Central and South America, with especially many species in Mexico and the south-west of the USA. They are found in deserts, prairies, forests and mountains. They eat mainly mice, rats, rabbits and sometimes birds or lizards. They kill their prey with a **venomous bite** and then swallow it whole.

Rattlesnakes do not lay eggs but give birth to live young. A newborn rattlesnake has only a ‘**prebutton**’ at the tip of the tail, which cannot rattle yet. Only after the first moults does a rattle form that makes noise. Even the young, however, have effective venom.

A bite can be dangerous for people, but with **antivenom** in hospital it is usually treated well. Rattlesnakes do not attack of their own accord, but warn first with their rattle. Anyone who hears the warning should walk slowly back. In Switzerland there are no rattlesnakes; only two native vipers live here: the asp viper and the adder.

begriffe.erklaerung: Vipers with a heat-sensing organ between the eye and the nose.
A firm horn substance that hair, nails and feathers are also made of.
The snake sheds its old skin, which has become too tight.
A medicine that cancels out the effect of snake venom.

gewusst: A rattlesnake can shake its rattle dozens of times a second without tiring quickly.
Even a freshly killed rattlesnake can still bite through reflexes, so you should never touch it.

teile.einleitung: The European garden spider is one of the best-known spiders in Europe and often lives right in our gardens. It gets its German name, Kreuzspinne or ‘cross spider’, from the pale patches on its back, which form a cross. It is famous for its skilful orb webs, which glisten in the morning dew in autumn.
wichtigste: The garden spider has four pairs of legs, so eight legs, and eight eyes.
Its body is about as big as a fingernail.
The female is usually clearly larger than the male.
It builds large orb webs to catch insects.
Its bite is harmless to people, at most like a small sting.
An adult garden spider usually lives about a year.
In winter most adults die, and only the eggs in the cocoon survive.

abschnitte.text: The **garden cross spider** is the commonest cross spider in Switzerland. Its round abdomen is brown to reddish and bears pale patches that form a cross. Like all spiders it has eight legs and eight eyes, but no wings and no antennae. The female is about as big as a fingernail, while the male stays much smaller.

The garden spider builds an **orb web** with spokes and a sticky catching spiral. A web can be over 30 centimetres across. Often it builds it anew every day and eats the old threads, to reuse the valuable silk. It does not stick fast itself, because it walks on non-sticky threads and has oily feet.

In its web the garden spider catches flies, midges, wasps and other insects. If an animal struggles in the web, it feels this through a signal thread. It paralyses the prey with a venomous bite and wraps it in silk. Then it injects digestive juice into it and sucks the prey dry.

In late summer and autumn the garden spiders are fully grown and mate. The male approaches carefully, because he is sometimes eaten by the female. Afterwards the female lays her eggs in a **cocoon** of spider silk and hides it. The adults die in winter, and in spring many tiny young spiders hatch.

Garden spiders are peaceful and mostly flee or sit still when a person comes. Their bite is at most like a small mosquito bite. They are useful for garden and house, because they catch many midges and flies. Their **spider silk** is very tear-resistant in relation to its weight and is closely studied by researchers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A round spider’s web with spokes like a bicycle wheel.
A protective covering of spider silk for the eggs.
The fine, very strong thread that spiders make from spinning glands.
An animal group with eight legs that includes spiders, scorpions and ticks.

gewusst: A garden spider often needs less than an hour for a whole orb web.
Spiders are not insects, because insects have only six legs.

teile.einleitung: The great tit is the largest and one of the commonest tits in Switzerland. You recognise it by its yellow belly with the black stripe and the black cap on its head. In winter it is a busy visitor to the bird feeder.
wichtigste: The great tit has a yellow belly and a black cap on its head.
In the male the black stripe on the belly is broader than in the female.
It lives in woods, parks and gardens and nests in tree hollows and nest boxes.
It eats mainly insects in summer and seeds in winter.
Because it eats many pests, it is popular with gardeners.
In great cold it fluffs up its plumage to stay warm.
A great tit can raise one or two broods a year.

abschnitte.text: The great tit is about 14 centimetres long and weighs around 16 to 21 grams, about as much as four sugar cubes. It has a glossy black **cap**, white cheeks and a yellow belly. A black **stripe** runs down the chest and belly. In the male it is broader and reaches down between the legs, in the female it is narrower.

Great tits live all over Europe, in parts of North Africa and far into Asia. In Switzerland they are among the commonest **breeding birds** and occur from the lowlands up to mountain forests. They are found in deciduous and mixed woods, parks, orchards and gardens in the middle of towns. Most stay here in winter too and are **resident birds**.

In spring and summer, great tits eat mainly insects, caterpillars and spiders. Larger insects they hack into pieces with the beak before eating them. In autumn and winter they eat seeds, nuts and berries. In doing so they hold a seed down with their **feet** and hack it open, and sometimes they hide seeds as a store for winter.

Great tits nest in **hollows**, for example in old woodpecker holes, cracks in walls or nest boxes. The female builds a soft nest of moss, hair and feathers and usually lays 6 to 12 eggs. While she incubates for about two weeks, the male brings her food. Both parents then feed the young with hundreds of caterpillars a day, and often a second brood follows.

In great cold the great tit fluffs up its **plumage**, so that a warming layer of air forms between the feathers. At night it often sleeps in a tree hollow or a nest box. At the bird feeder it first approaches cautiously and watches its surroundings. Then it usually takes a seed and flies off with it, to eat it in peace on a branch.

The song of the great tit sounds like ‘zi-zi-beh’ or ‘zizibe’ and can be heard from the end of January. Great tits also have many different **calls**, with which they warn of enemies, for example. They learn very easily and pick up tricks from other tits. That is why they are considered especially clever birds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that nests in an area and raises its young there.
A bird that stays in the same area all year round and does not migrate.
A small wooden box with an entrance hole in which hole-nesting birds can build their nest.
The eggs or young of a pair of birds from one nest.

gewusst: During the nestling period, a pair of great tits feeds thousands of caterpillars to its young.
In England, tits once learned to peck open the caps of milk bottles on the doorstep to get at the cream.

teile.einleitung: The saithe is a sea fish from the North Atlantic that is usually sold in shops in German-speaking countries under the name Seelachs (‘sea salmon’). Despite this name it is not a salmon, but a close relative of the cod. Its flesh is used, for example, to make fish fingers.
wichtigste: The saithe is a sea fish from the cod family.
In trade it is called Seelachs, but it is not a true salmon and belongs to the cod-like fish.
It lives in the North Atlantic, for example in the North Sea and around Norway and Iceland.
Its German name Köhler comes from its dark back, which is reminiscent of coal.
Saithe swim in large shoals and hunt smaller fish.
It usually grows to 60 to 100 centimetres long.
Its white flesh is often made into fillets and fish fingers.

abschnitte.text: The saithe has a slender, powerful body with three dorsal fins and two anal fins. Its back is dark greenish to almost black, the belly silvery pale. A pale **lateral line** along the body is clearly visible. It usually grows to 60 to 100 centimetres long, and large animals reach more than a metre.

Saithe live in the **North Atlantic**, from the North Sea via Norway and Iceland to the coast of North America. Young saithe often stay close to the coast. Older animals move into deeper water, usually down to about 200 metres, sometimes deeper. They form large **shoals** and travel long distances over the course of the year.

Young saithe eat small crustaceans. Adults are skilful **predators** and hunt herring, sprats and other smaller fish. In a shoal they sometimes drive their prey together. They themselves are eaten by larger fish, seals and seabirds.

The name **Seelachs** (‘sea salmon’) is a trade name that was meant to make the fish more popular. The saithe has nothing to do with true salmon; it belongs to the **cod-like fish** such as cod and haddock. In the past, smoked saithe flesh was dyed red and sold as a ‘salmon substitute’. The Alaska pollock, from which many fish fingers are made, is also a different kind of cod-like fish.

The saithe is an important **food fish** in Europe. It is caught mainly off Norway, Iceland and the Faroe Islands with trawl nets. Its lean, white flesh reaches the shops as fillets, frozen or in fish fingers. To stop the stocks being overfished, there are catch quotas, and some fisheries carry a sustainability label.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of sea fish that includes cod, haddock and saithe.
A sense organ along the body of a fish that senses water movements.
The name under which a product is sold in the shop.
A fixed amount of fish that may be caught in a year.

gewusst: The German name Köhler recalls the charcoal burners who used to make charcoal in the forest and were often blackened with soot.
Under the name Seelachs, shops sell two different fish species, the saithe and the Alaska pollock.

teile.einleitung: A cloven hoof (in German a Klaue) is the split hoof of animals such as the cow, goat, sheep, pig or chamois. Each foot carries two large horn shoes side by side, which together look like a divided hoof. Animals with such feet are called even-toed ungulates.
wichtigste: Cloven hooves are the horn shoes on the toes of even-toed ungulates.
A goat has two hooves on each foot, because it is an even-toed ungulate.
Hooves are made of hard horn, that is, keratin.
Underneath lie soft, elastic pads.
Because the hooves are movable, they adapt well to rock and give goats and chamois a grip.
Behind the main hooves, many animals have two small dewclaws.
In farm animals the hooves have to be cared for and trimmed regularly.

abschnitte.text: In even-toed ungulates the animals walk on the tips of two toes, the third and fourth toe. Each of these toes sits in a hard shoe of **horn**, the hoof. Together the two hooves form a split hoof. By contrast, the horse has only a single large toe with a whole hoof.

On the outside the hoof has a hard **horn wall** that keeps growing like a fingernail. Underneath lies the sole, and at the back is a soft, elastic **pad**. The pad absorbs shocks and, like a rubber sole, provides grip. A little further up the leg, cattle, goats and deer have small **dewclaws**, which usually do not touch the ground.

Goats, ibex and chamois are excellent climbers. Their two hooves can be spread a little and so adapt to rock edges and uneven ground. The hard rims grip like the edges of ski boots, and the rubbery pads stick to smooth stone. That is why chamois in the Swiss Alps can climb safely on steep rock faces.

In the barn the hooves often wear down less than on stony ground. That is why a **hoof trimmer** usually trims them in cows once or twice a year. Hooves that are too long or diseased hurt the animals and make them limp. Good hoof care is therefore important for the animals’ welfare.

Well known is **foot-and-mouth disease**, a very contagious viral disease of even-toed ungulates. It causes blisters in the mouth and on the hooves. In Switzerland it has not occurred for many decades, but it is strictly monitored. More common are inflammations between the hooves, caused by wet and dirty floors.

The German word Klaue is sometimes also used for the pointed **claws** of predators or birds of prey. People speak, for example, of the claws of an eagle or a bear. In zoology, however, Klaue mainly refers to the split hooves of even-toed ungulates. That is also where the German name Klauentiere (cloven-hoofed animals) for cattle, sheep, goats and pigs comes from.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals that walk on two toes, each with a hoof, for example the cow and goat.
A small extra toe behind the main hooves that usually does not touch the ground.
The soft, springy part at the back of the hoof.
A professional who trims and cares for the hooves of farm animals.

gewusst: The horn wall of a cow’s hoof grows about half a centimetre a month.
Thanks to their hooves, chamois can dare leaps of several metres onto narrow rock ledges.

teile.einleitung: Malaria is a dangerous disease that is transmitted by mosquitoes in warm countries. It is caused by tiny parasites that invade the blood cells and cause high fever. To this day malaria is among the diseases of which most children die worldwide.
wichtigste: Malaria is transmitted by mosquitoes of the genus Anopheles.
The disease is caused by single-celled parasites called Plasmodia.
Only the female mosquitoes bite and transmit the germs.
Typical are bouts of fever, shivering and headaches.
Most cases occur in Africa south of the Sahara.
Mosquito nets and medicines protect against infection.
Since 2021 there has been, for the first time, a vaccine against malaria recommended by the WHO.

abschnitte.text: Malaria is an **infectious disease** caused by single-celled parasites of the genus **Plasmodium**. The name comes from Italian and means ‘bad air’, because it was once believed that the air over marshes made people ill. Today we know that mosquitoes transmit the germs. In German the disease is also called Sumpffieber (marsh fever) or Wechselfieber (intermittent fever).

The carriers are females of the **Anopheles mosquito**, which need blood for their eggs. If a mosquito bites a sick person, it takes up the parasites. At the next bite it passes the germs on to another person. In the body the parasites first travel to the liver and then infect the **red blood cells**.

Typical of malaria are high fever, shivering, sweating and headaches. The fever often comes in bouts, because the parasites destroy the blood cells at regular intervals. The most dangerous form is caused by Plasmodium falciparum and can be fatal without treatment. According to WHO estimates, about 600,000 people died of malaria worldwide in 2023, most of them small children in Africa.

In the past malaria was treated with **quinine** from the bark of the South American cinchona tree. Today medicines with **artemisinin** are especially important, an active substance from a wormwood plant. The Chinese researcher Tu Youyou received the Nobel Prize for it in 2015. Mosquito nets, insect repellents and vaccines also help to prevent infections.

The French doctor Alphonse Laveran discovered the parasites in the blood of sick people in 1880. The British doctor **Ronald Ross** proved in 1897 that mosquitoes transmit the disease. Both received the Nobel Prize in Medicine for it. In the past there was malaria in many marshy areas of Europe too, until these were drained.

In Switzerland there are no malaria infections through mosquitoes today. Travellers can, however, become infected in warm countries and return ill. That is why many people seek advice before a trip to the tropics. In Basel the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute has been researching malaria for decades.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that lives in or on another and harms it.
The single-celled germ that causes malaria.
The genus of mosquitoes that transmit malaria.
Measures meant to prevent you from becoming ill.

gewusst: Mosquitoes are regarded as the most dangerous animals in the world because they transmit so many diseases.
You can recognise Anopheles mosquitoes by the fact that they stretch their abdomen obliquely upwards when sitting.
Only female mosquitoes bite, the males drink plant juices.

teile.einleitung: The Cuculiformes are an order of birds to which our well-known cuckoo belongs. Worldwide there are over 140 species, living mainly in warm countries. Not all of them lay their eggs in strange nests, and many raise their young themselves.
wichtigste: The cuckoo belongs to the bird group of the Cuculiformes.
Worldwide there are over 140 species of Cuculiformes.
Most species live in the tropics and subtropics.
Cuculiformes have feet with two toes pointing forwards and two backwards.
Only some of the species are brood parasites.
They also include the roadrunner from North America.
In Switzerland only one species breeds, the cuckoo.

abschnitte.text: The **Cuculiformes** form an order of their own in the bird world. They include cuckoos, coucals, anis and roadrunners. The birds differ greatly in size, from sparrow-sized to crow-sized species. Many have a long tail and a slightly curved beak.

Cuculiformes have so-called **zygodactyl feet**: two toes point forwards and two backwards. In this way they can sit and climb well on branches. Their plumage is often grey, brown or black, and some species shine green or blue. Many Cuculiformes eat insects, especially caterpillars.

Many people think all cuckoos are **brood parasites**. But only some of the species lay their eggs in strange nests, for example the cuckoo or the koel from Asia. Many other species build their own nests and feed their young themselves. The anis of South America even breed in groups in a shared nest.

The **roadrunner** lives in the deserts of North America and can run very fast. It hunts lizards, insects and even small snakes. As the cartoon character Road Runner it has become world famous. The coucals in Africa and Asia live in dense undergrowth and are reluctant to fly.

In central Europe and Switzerland only a single species breeds, the **cuckoo**. In the Mediterranean region the great spotted cuckoo also lives, which lays its eggs mainly in the nests of magpies. Rarely, a great spotted cuckoo also strays north of the Alps. Most species of the order, however, are found in Africa, Asia, Australia and America.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of related animal families in biology.
A bird’s foot with two toes pointing forwards and two backwards.
An animal that has others raise its young.
The hot regions of the Earth around the equator.

gewusst: The roadrunner would rather run than fly.
The turacos of Africa were once counted among the Cuculiformes, but today form a group of their own.

teile.einleitung: The cockchafer is a brown beetle that usually appears in May and has its German name, Maikäfer or ‘May beetle’, for that reason. It buzzes around trees mainly at dusk and eats their leaves. Its larvae, the grubs, live for several years in the soil.
wichtigste: The cockchafer is called Maikäfer in German because it usually appears in May.
Its wing cases are usually brown.
It is active mainly at dusk and in the evening.
Its larvae, the grubs, live three to four years in the soil.
Adult cockchafers live only a few weeks.
With their fan-shaped antennae they mainly smell.
Cockchafers are harmless to people.

abschnitte.text: The cockchafer grows to about two to three centimetres long. It has brown **wing cases**, a black thorax shield and white triangles on the sides of the abdomen. At the rear end it has a pointed extension that was once wrongly taken for a sting. Its **antennae** end in a fan of small plates, and in the males they are larger because they use them to smell the females.

Cockchafers usually appear from the end of April to June. By day they sit in trees, at dusk they fly around buzzing. They eat the leaves of oaks, beeches, maples and fruit trees. Adult beetles live only a few weeks, in which time they mate and the females lay their eggs in the soil.

From the eggs hatch whitish, curved larvae, the **grubs**. They live three to four years in the soil and eat plant roots. In winter they dig deeper so that they do not freeze. Afterwards they **pupate** in the soil, and the finished beetle overwinters there once more and comes out in spring.

Cockchafers and grubs are important food for bats, birds, hedgehogs, moles and wild boar. When you touch a cockchafer, it often plays dead or lets itself drop. For people it is harmless, it does not bite or sting dangerously. In large numbers, however, grubs can damage meadows, fields and fruit trees, which is why they are regarded as **pests**.

Because the development takes several years, in one area especially many cockchafers usually fly every few years. This is called **flight years**. In Switzerland different regions are distinguished for this, for example the Bernese, the Uri or the Basel flight year. In the past farmers and schoolchildren had to collect cockchafers in such years to reduce the damage.

In the 20th century cockchafers were heavily controlled with **insecticides**, and many habitats were lost. That is why they became rare in some areas. For some decades now they have been occurring more often again in many places. The cockchafer is also known from the story ‘Max and Moritz’ by Wilhelm Busch, in which the boys put cockchafers into Uncle Fritz’s bed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The larva of the cockchafer, which lives in the soil.
Hard front wings that protect the delicate hind wings.
To turn into a pupa from which the adult insect hatches.
A year in which especially many cockchafers fly in an area.
An animal that damages people’s plants or supplies.

gewusst: Before a cockchafer takes off, it pumps itself up with air, which is called pumping or counting.
In times of need, cockchafer soups were even cooked in the past.
In Switzerland there is the forest cockchafer as well as the common cockchafer.

teile.einleitung: Salmon are powerful fish that live in the sea but return to spawn in the rivers where they hatched. On this journey they even leap over waterfalls. Their pink flesh is also a popular food in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Salmon travel from the sea upstream to spawn there.
They find their home river mainly with their sense of smell.
There is the Atlantic salmon and several species of Pacific salmon.
After spawning many salmon are badly weakened, and Pacific salmon all die.
Their dead bodies supply nutrients to animals and plants along the rivers.
In the past salmon swam up the Rhine as far as Switzerland.
A large part of the salmon in shops today comes from fish farms.

abschnitte.text: Salmon have a slim, powerful body with silvery, shiny scales. Like all **salmonids**, they have a small adipose fin on the back in front of the tail fin. An Atlantic salmon can grow to over a metre long. At spawning time many salmon turn red or brown, and in Pacific salmon often bright red.

abschnitte.titel: A life between river and sea
abschnitte.text: Salmon hatch in the gravel of a river and usually stay there for one to three years. Then they migrate to the sea, where they find plenty of food and grow quickly. After a few years they return to exactly the river where they were born. This migration is called **anadromous**, and they find the way mainly with their sense of smell.

On the way upstream the salmon eat nothing more and live off their fat reserves. They swim against strong currents and leap over rapids and small waterfalls. In North America **grizzly bears** often wait at such places and catch the leaping fish. At the destination the female lays her eggs in a spawning pit in the gravel.

After spawning many salmon are badly weakened. In Pacific salmon all the animals die, and only some Atlantic salmon can spawn several times. The dead fish are important for nature: their bodies supply **nutrients** for bears, birds, insects and even for the trees on the bank. In this way salmon carry nutrients from the sea deep inland.

Until the 19th century salmon swam up the Rhine as far as Basel and on into the Aare and Limmat. Because of power stations, pollution and overfishing, the salmon disappeared from Switzerland around the middle of the 20th century. Today the countries along the Rhine are trying to bring it back with **fish ladders** and clean water. Most salmon in Swiss shops come from fish farms, for example in Norway or Scotland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The name for fish that live in the sea and migrate into rivers to spawn.
The laying and fertilising of eggs in fish.
A staircase of pools with which fish can get past a power station or weir.
A small fin without rays between the dorsal fin and the tail fin.

gewusst: On their migration salmon can leap over obstacles about three metres high.
The pink colour of salmon flesh comes from pigments in the small crustaceans that the salmon eat.

teile.einleitung: The cowbell is a bell that cows wear on a leather strap around the neck. In Switzerland its sound belongs to the Alps as much as the mountains themselves. In the past it helped above all to find the animals again on wide pastures.
wichtigste: Many alpine cows in Switzerland wear a bell around the neck.
From the sound the herdsman knows where his animals are grazing.
A distinction is made between cast bells and forged Treicheln.
At the Alpaufzug and Alpabzug, cows wear especially large, decorated bells.
The straps are often skilfully embroidered or decorated.
In some villages there are arguments about the noise of cowbells.
Cowbells are also a popular souvenir and gift.

abschnitte.text: A cowbell is a sound instrument that hangs on a wide **bell strap** around a cow’s neck. Inside swings a clapper that strikes the wall with every movement. In this way you can hear the cow from far away. Goats and sheep also sometimes wear smaller bells.

In Switzerland a distinction is made between two kinds. A **bell** is cast from bronze or brass and sounds bright. A **Treichel** is forged from sheet iron and has a deeper, rough tone. Treicheln are often very large and heavy and are worn mainly on special occasions.

On the alp the cows graze in summer over large areas, often without a fence. In fog, in the forest or on steep ground you cannot always see them. From the sound of the bells the Senn, the alpine dairyman, knows where his herd is at the moment. Experienced herdsmen can even recognise individual animals by the tone of their bell.

At the **Alpaufzug**, the procession up to the alp in early summer, and at the Alpabzug in autumn, the cows wear especially large and beautifully decorated bells and Treicheln. The animals are also decorated with flowers and wreaths. At festivals, groups of Treichler also walk through the villages in traditional costume with large Treicheln. For the Silvesterchläuse in Appenzellerland, bells and rolls are an essential part of the custom.

Today some people ask whether heavy bells bother the cows. That is why many animals wear lighter bells in everyday use, and the large ones only on festive days. In some villages residents complain about the jingling at night, and municipalities then look for solutions. For many farmers, though, the bell is an important piece of tradition.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large cowbell forged from sheet metal with a deep sound.
The movable part inside the bell that produces the sound.
The festive journey of the cows up to the alp in early summer.
A herdsman on the alp who looks after the cows and often makes cheese.

gewusst: Large festival Treicheln can weigh several kilograms.
Cowbells are sometimes also used as a musical instrument in orchestras or at football matches.

teile.einleitung: The mustelids are a large family of predators that includes not only martens but also weasels, badgers and otters. Almost all of them have a long, slim body and short legs. They live on every continent except Australia and Antarctica.
wichtigste: The mustelids (Mustelidae) are the family of predators with the most species.
The family includes about 60 species worldwide.
The stone marten belongs to the mustelids.
The badger, otter and stoat also belong to this family.
The smallest member is the least weasel, one of the smallest predators in the world.
Many mustelids have scent glands at the rear.
Several species live in Switzerland, including the pine marten, polecat and otter.

abschnitte.text: The mustelids form a **family** within the predators, and their scientific name is Mustelidae. Typical features are a slim body, short legs, a small head and short, round ears. Many species have strong claws and sharp teeth. Almost all have **anal glands** with which they leave strong-smelling scent marks.

The smallest member is the **least weasel**, which often weighs only about 50 to 100 grams. The largest species are the sea otter and the South American giant otter. The **wolverine** in the far north is especially strong and can even catch reindeer. The African honey badger also belongs to the family and is known for its courage.

Mustelids have very different ways of life. Otters live on and in the water, have webbed feet and very dense fur. Badgers dig huge underground setts. Pine martens climb skilfully in the treetops, and stoats even hunt mice in their tunnels.

In Switzerland live **stone martens**, pine martens, polecats, stoats, least weasels, badgers and otters. The **otter** was regarded as extinct in Switzerland from the 1980s. For some years now it has been back and is breeding again, for example on the Aare and the Inn. The badger is widespread in forests but is seldom seen, because it is active at night.

In the past many mustelids were hunted for their valuable fur, such as sable, mink and stoat. The white winter coat of the stoat adorned the robes of kings. The **ferret**, a tamed form of the polecat, has long been kept as a pet and for hunting rabbits. Today some species such as the European mink are severely threatened.

begriffe.erklaerung: In biology, a group of related genera, for example the mustelids.
An order of mammals with sharp canine teeth, which also includes cats and dogs.
A gland at the rear that produces a strong-smelling scent.
The tame form of the polecat, kept as a pet.

gewusst: Skunks used to be counted among the mustelids, but today they form a family of their own.
The sea otter has the densest fur of all animals, with over 100,000 hairs on one square centimetre of skin.
The stoat wears a white coat in winter, and only the tip of the tail stays black.

teile.einleitung: The common woodlouse is a small, grey creepy-crawly that is often found under stones, in compost or in damp cellars. Although it lives on land, it is not an insect but a crustacean. It helps to turn dead plant material into fertile soil.
wichtigste: Common woodlice like to live in cellars and in damp, dark places.
They are crustaceans and related to crabs and lobsters.
Common woodlice have 14 legs, that is, seven pairs of legs.
They need moisture, because otherwise they dry out.
They eat mainly dead plant material.
The females carry their eggs in a brood pouch on the belly.
Common woodlice are harmless to people.

abschnitte.text: The **common woodlouse** belongs to the woodlice and so to the **crustaceans**. Its ancestors lived in the sea, but land woodlice have managed to live on land. Common woodlice grow to just under two centimetres long. Their body is flat and grey and covered with an armour of plates.

Common woodlice have seven pairs of legs, so 14 legs, and two pairs of antennae, one pair of which is tiny. Their armour is rough and grainy. At the back of the body sit two short projections. Unlike the related **pill woodlouse**, the common woodlouse cannot roll itself up into a ball.

Common woodlice need it damp and dark, because otherwise they dry out quickly. You find them under stones, boards, leaves and bark, in compost and in damp cellars. During the day they hide, at night they go looking for food. They live in Europe and have been carried to many other parts of the world.

Common woodlice eat mainly dead plant material such as leaves, rotting wood and fungi. They are **decomposers**, which means they help to turn plant remains into humus. In compost and in the garden they are therefore useful. They only rarely eat healthy plants.

Because woodlice descend from sea animals, they breathe with gill-like organs on their rear legs. Common woodlice also have fine breathing tubes there, called **pseudotracheae**, with which they breathe air. These only work, however, if they stay moist. That is why woodlice avoid dry, sunny places.

The female carries her eggs in a fluid-filled **brood pouch** on the underside of her body. In it the young develop and hatch as small, pale woodlice. Because the armour does not grow with them, woodlice have to moult. They moult in two steps, first the rear half of the body and later the front half.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of armoured animals that includes crabs, lobsters and woodlice.
Living things that break down dead plants and animals.
Shedding the old skin or armour in order to grow.
A pocket on the belly in which the eggs develop in safety.

gewusst: The common woodlouse is more closely related to a crab than to a beetle.
A half-moulted woodlouse looks two-coloured, grey at the front and pale at the back.

teile.einleitung: The Ensifera are grasshopper relatives with very long antennae, which are often longer than their whole body. They include the great green bush-cricket and the crickets. In summer you can hear their chirping in meadows and gardens, especially in the evening.
wichtigste: The great green bush-cricket belongs to the Ensifera.
You recognise Ensifera by their very long antennae.
They include bush-crickets and crickets.
They chirp by rubbing their forewings together.
Their ears sit on the front legs.
Many females have a sabre-shaped ovipositor.
Unlike grasshoppers, many Ensifera also eat insects.

abschnitte.text: The **Ensifera** are one of the two large groups of grasshopper relatives. The other group is the Caelifera, which includes the grasshoppers. Ensifera have thin antennae that are often longer than the whole body. They include bush-crickets such as the **great green bush-cricket**, but also crickets and the mole cricket.

The males chirp by rubbing their **forewings** together, with a kind of file on one wing and an edge on the other. Grasshoppers, by contrast, make their sounds with their hind legs. Each species has its own song, which is how males and females find each other. The ears of the Ensifera lie on the tibiae of the front legs and look like small slits.

Ensifera live in meadows, hedges, woods, gardens, and some also in caves or houses. Many are active mainly at dusk and at night. They eat plants, but often also insects such as caterpillars and aphids. The great green bush-cricket is a real hunter and can bite hard with its mouthparts.

The females of many species have a long, sabre-shaped **ovipositor** at the rear of the abdomen. With it they lay their eggs in the ground or in plant stems. In many species the eggs overwinter, and in spring small larvae hatch. These already look like the adults and moult several times until they get wings.

In Switzerland there are over 100 species of grasshopper and relatives, and a large part of them are Ensifera. Common are the great green bush-cricket, the **field cricket** and the upland green bush-cricket. In spring the field cricket sits in front of its burrow and chirps loudly. Because species-rich meadows are disappearing, some grasshopper species are threatened.

begriffe.erklaerung: Long sense organs on the head of insects for feeling and smelling.
A long extension on the abdomen of females for laying eggs.
Grasshopper relatives with short antennae, for example grasshoppers.
The juvenile form of an insect.

gewusst: In some crickets you can roughly estimate the air temperature from the number of chirps per minute.
The great green bush-cricket can be longer with wings and antennae than a child’s finger.

teile.einleitung: Oxpeckers are African birds that climb about on large animals such as buffalo, rhinos, giraffes or zebras. There they pick ticks, insects and skin remains out of the coat. They are often regarded as the ‘cleaners’ of the savanna, but are not only useful.
wichtigste: Oxpeckers are songbirds from Africa south of the Sahara.
There are two species: the red-billed and the yellow-billed oxpecker.
They often sit on buffalo, rhinos, giraffes and antelopes.
They eat ticks, insects and other parasites.
Sometimes they also peck at wounds and drink blood.
With warning calls they alert their host animals to dangers.
With strong claws and stiff tail feathers they hold on to the coat.

abschnitte.text: Oxpeckers are about as big as a starling and have brown plumage with a paler belly. The **red-billed oxpecker** has a red beak and a yellow ring around the eyes. The **yellow-billed oxpecker** has a yellow beak with a red tip. Their closest relatives are the starlings and mockingbirds.

Oxpeckers spend almost the whole day on large mammals, their **host animals**. They climb about like woodpeckers on neck, back and legs, even into the ears and nostrils. Sharp claws and stiff tail feathers, which they use for support, help them in this. They sit especially often on buffalo, rhinos, giraffes, zebras and impalas.

The main food of oxpeckers is **ticks** that have sucked themselves full of blood. They also eat flies, larvae and dead skin flakes. With their flat beak they comb through the coat. However, they also peck at wounds, keep them open and drink blood.

For a long time oxpeckers were regarded as perfect helpers because they rid the animals of parasites. Today we know that the relationship is not only to the benefit of the hosts, because the birds also peck open wounds. People therefore speak of a mixed relationship between **symbiosis** and parasitism. Most host animals tolerate the birds nevertheless, while elephants usually chase them away.

When people or predators approach, oxpeckers give loud, hissing **warning calls**. Researchers have observed that black rhinos, which see poorly, notice people much sooner as a result. In the Swahili language the bird is therefore also called the ‘guard of the rhino’. In this way oxpeckers may even help rhinos to escape poachers.

Oxpeckers breed in **tree holes** or holes in walls. They line their nest with hair that they pluck from their host animals. Often older young birds from earlier broods help to feed their siblings. Where wild animals disappear or cattle are heavily treated with anti-tick products, the oxpeckers also become rarer.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal on which another animal lives and finds food.
A small arachnid that sucks blood.
Two species living together, from which both benefit.
A living thing that lives at the expense of another.

gewusst: Oxpeckers sometimes even sleep on their host animals at night.
A single oxpecker can eat very many ticks in a day.
Oxpeckers take their nest lining straight from the backs of living animals.

teile.einleitung: A caterpillar becomes a butterfly: this astonishing transformation is called metamorphosis. In a pupa the caterpillar’s body is almost completely broken down and rebuilt. In the end a winged butterfly emerges that looks and lives quite differently from the caterpillar.
wichtigste: The transformation from caterpillar to butterfly is called metamorphosis.
A butterfly develops from the egg via caterpillar and pupa into the adult.
The caterpillar eats a great deal and moults several times.
In the pupa the body is rebuilt.
The caterpillar chews leaves, and the butterfly sucks nectar with a proboscis.
Beetles, bees and flies also transform via a pupa.
Depending on the species the transformation takes a few weeks to several years.

abschnitte.text: A female butterfly usually lays her eggs on one very particular **food plant**. The peacock butterfly, for example, lays its eggs on stinging nettles. After a few days tiny caterpillars hatch and begin to eat at once. Often they first eat their eggshell. The caterpillar is a kind of eating machine whose main task is growing.

Caterpillars grow very fast, but their skin does not grow with them. That is why they have to **moult** several times, usually four to five times. In doing so the old skin splits open and the caterpillar crawls out in a new, bigger skin. Some caterpillars are well camouflaged, while others are brightly coloured and warn enemies that they are poisonous. Some have hairs that can itch on the skin.

When the caterpillar is big enough, it turns into a **pupa**. Butterflies that fly by day form a hard pupal case, which often hangs from a twig. Many moths also spin themselves into a **cocoon** of silk, as does the silk moth. Inside the pupa the caterpillar’s body is dissolved into a kind of soup. From small groups of cells that were already laid down in the caterpillar, wings, legs, antennae and proboscis are formed anew.

When the transformation is finished, the pupal case splits open and the **butterfly** crawls out. Its wings are at first soft and crumpled. The butterfly pumps blood into the veins of the wings until they unfold and dry. After about one to two hours it can fly. As a butterfly it sucks nectar from flowers with its proboscis and looks for a partner to reproduce.

In Switzerland there are about 200 species of butterflies that fly by day, for example the peacock, the small tortoiseshell and the swallowtail. The caterpillars of the swallowtail like to feed on carrot tops or fennel in the garden. With stinging nettles, wild flowers and little poison in the garden you help butterflies. In some schools caterpillars are reared and the whole **metamorphosis** is observed. Afterwards the butterflies are set free again.

begriffe.erklaerung: The transformation of an animal from a larva to an adult animal.
The larva of a butterfly.
A casing of silk threads that some caterpillars spin around themselves.
Another word for an adult lepidopteran.

gewusst: A caterpillar can increase its weight many times over in a few weeks.
Silk for clothes is obtained from the cocoons of the silk moth caterpillar.

teile.einleitung: A mahout is a person who looks after an elephant, steers it and works with it. Mahouts are found mainly in South and South-East Asia, for example in India, Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand. Often mahout and elephant spend their whole life together.
wichtigste: A mahout leads and looks after a working elephant.
The word comes from Hindi.
Mahouts are found mainly in India, Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand.
The occupation is often passed from father to son.
A mahout usually sits on the elephant’s neck and steers it with voice and feet.
In the past elephants worked mainly transporting timber in the forest.
Today many mahouts work in tourism, in temples or in conservation projects.

abschnitte.text: A mahout is an **elephant handler** who is responsible for a particular elephant. He feeds and bathes it, looks after its health and works with it every day. The word comes from **Hindi** and goes back to an old Sanskrit word. In the individual countries there are also names of their own for it in the national language.

Often a boy is entrusted with a young elephant as a child, and the two grow up together. Since elephants can live to 60 years and older, this partnership sometimes lasts a lifetime. In many families the occupation is passed on through generations. A good mahout knows his elephant’s moods exactly and builds **trust**.

Usually the mahout sits on the elephant’s **neck**, just behind the head. He steers it with commands in his language and by light pressure with his feet behind the ears. Many mahouts carry a stick with a hook, the **ankus**, which is controversial, however, because it can hurt elephants. An elephant can learn dozens of commands.

abschnitte.titel: Work in the past and today
abschnitte.text: For centuries elephants with their mahouts dragged heavy **tree trunks** out of the forests where no machines could go. Elephants were also used in wars, at ceremonies and as mounts for kings. In 1989 Thailand banned the felling of most forests, and many mahouts lost their work. Today many work in tourism, in temples such as in Kerala or at festivals such as the Perahera in Kandy in Sri Lanka.

Animal welfare campaigners criticise that young elephants are sometimes tamed with violence. **Elephant riding** for tourists is also controversial, because it can harm the animals. Good elephant camps therefore rely on gentle methods, plenty of exercise and no riding offers. The Asian elephant is **endangered**, so good treatment of every animal is important.

In some national parks, for example in India, mahouts patrol through the forest on elephants to deter poachers. They also help to keep wild elephants away from villages. In zoos such as Zurich Zoo with its Kaeng Krachan Elephant Park, keepers usually work in **protected contact**, that is, through a barrier. In this way the elephant stays freer, and keepers are safer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who leads and looks after an elephant.
A stick with a hook with which some mahouts steer elephants.
An elephant that carries or pulls loads for people.
Caring for an elephant through a protective wall without direct bodily contact.

gewusst: An elephant can recognise its mahout by his voice among many people.
In Myanmar elephants still work with mahouts in the forest today.
Young mahouts often first learn how to bathe and feed an elephant before they ride it.

teile.einleitung: A sewage treatment plant cleans the dirty water from houses, schools and factories before it flows back into rivers and lakes. In Switzerland it is usually called an ARA, which stands for Abwasserreinigungsanlage (wastewater treatment plant). Thanks to sewage treatment plants, Swiss waters are clean again today, and fish and other water animals can live in them well.
wichtigste: A sewage treatment plant cleans wastewater so that rivers and lakes stay clean.
In Switzerland almost all households are connected to a sewage treatment plant.
The water is cleaned mechanically, biologically and chemically.
In biological cleaning, tiny bacteria eat the dirt.
The building of sewage treatment plants helped the Swiss lakes to recover.
Many plants are getting an additional stage against residues of medicines and chemicals.
Biogas can be obtained from sewage sludge.

abschnitte.text: **Wastewater** is all the water that we have used: from the toilet, shower, washing machine and kitchen. Added to this is water from factories and often also rainwater from roads and roofs. It flows through the sewer system, a network of underground pipes, to the sewage treatment plant. Without cleaning it would badly pollute streams and lakes.

First a **screen** holds back coarse things, for example wet wipes, plastic or leaves. In the grit chamber, sand and small stones sink to the bottom. In the primary settling tank the water flows very slowly, so that further particles of dirt can settle. After that the water is already clearer, but still contains many dissolved substances.

In the **aeration tank**, billions of tiny bacteria and other micro-organisms are at work. They eat the dissolved pollutants, in a similar way to what happens in nature. So that they have enough oxygen, air is blown into the tank. In the secondary settling tank the bacterial flocs settle as sludge, and the cleaned water flows on.

abschnitte.titel: Chemical cleaning and the fourth stage
abschnitte.text: With the help of chemicals, **phosphate** in particular is removed from the water. In a lake, phosphate acts like fertiliser and makes algae grow strongly. For some years now, Switzerland has been equipping many large sewage treatment plants with a fourth cleaning stage.
