It removes **micropollutants**, that is, tiny residues of medicines, plant protection products and cosmetics, for example with ozone or activated carbon.

In the 1960s and 1970s many Swiss lakes were badly polluted, and often you were not allowed to swim. Too much phosphate made algae run wild, and when the dead algae broke down, oxygen was lacking in the deep water. Fish such as whitefish suffered from this. Through the building of sewage treatment plants and a ban on phosphate in detergents in 1986, the lakes have recovered.

abschnitte.titel: What happens to the sewage sludge
abschnitte.text: A lot of **sewage sludge** is produced during cleaning. In large digester towers, bacteria break it down without oxygen, producing biogas. With it, the plant can generate electricity and heat. In Switzerland sewage sludge may no longer be spread on fields as fertiliser; it is burned instead.

begriffe.erklaerung: Short for Abwasserreinigungsanlage, which is what a sewage treatment plant is called in Switzerland.
An underground network of pipes that carries wastewater to the sewage treatment plant.
A tank in which bacteria clean the wastewater with the help of oxygen.
Sludge that settles during the cleaning of wastewater.
Tiny residues of medicines or chemicals in the water.

gewusst: Wet wipes do not belong in the toilet, because they do not dissolve and cause blockages in pumps and pipes.
The cleaned water from a sewage treatment plant is clean enough for fish, but still not drinking water.
The largest sewage treatment plant in Switzerland is the Werdhölzli plant in Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Lantern sharks are small sharks that live in the dark deep sea and can glow themselves. On their underside they carry tiny light organs that give off a faint blue light. In this way they are like living lanterns in the eternal darkness of the sea.
wichtigste: Lantern sharks form a family of their own among the sharks, with dozens of species.
They live in the deep sea, usually several hundred metres below the surface.
Many species hardly grow longer than half a metre.
On their belly sit thousands of small light organs.
The glow helps them to camouflage themselves from enemies below.
They include one of the smallest sharks in the world.
They give birth to live young.

abschnitte.text: Lantern sharks belong to the order of **dogfish sharks**, which have a spine in front of each dorsal fin. About 50 species are known worldwide. Most are smaller than half a metre, so much smaller than a great white shark. The dwarf lanternshark grows to only about 20 centimetres long and is among the smallest sharks of all.

Lantern sharks have thousands of tiny **light organs** in their skin, called photophores. In them a chemical reaction produces a faint blue light, which is called **bioluminescence**. The sharks can control the light with hormones and make it brighter or dimmer. In some species the spines on the dorsal fins also glow, perhaps as a warning to enemies.

Seen from below, an animal stands out as a dark outline against the faint remaining light from above. The glowing belly of the lantern shark evens out this shadow, so that it becomes almost invisible. This camouflage is called **counter-illumination**. Many deep-sea fish and squid also use this trick.

Lantern sharks live in all oceans, mainly on continental slopes and around undersea mountains. They usually stay at depths between about 200 and 1,500 metres, and some species even deeper. There it is cold, pitch dark and the water pressure is enormous. Some species rise a little higher at night to hunt.

Lantern sharks eat small fish, **squid** and crustaceans such as shrimps. Some species probably hunt in small groups. The females do not lay eggs in the water, but the young develop inside the mother and hatch from the egg case there. Afterwards they are born as fully formed small sharks.

Because lantern sharks live so deep, they are hard to observe. Many species were discovered only in recent decades, often because they ended up as **bycatch** in deep-sea nets. Researchers study their glow to learn more about camouflage and communication in the dark. The deep sea is still one of the least explored habitats on Earth.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability of living things to make light themselves.
A small light organ in the skin of an animal.
Camouflage in which a glowing belly makes the animal’s own shadow disappear.
The part of the sea below about 200 metres, which hardly any sunlight reaches.
Animals that end up unintentionally in fishing nets.

gewusst: A fully grown dwarf lanternshark fits on a human hand.
The light of lantern sharks is blue because blue light travels furthest in water.
In the deep sea very many animals make their own light.

teile.einleitung: Masquerade is a special kind of camouflage: an animal looks like an object that is uninteresting to enemies, for example a twig, a leaf or a stone. The stick insect is a master of it, resembling a dry twig. In this way it is simply overlooked by hungry birds.
wichtigste: Masquerade means that an animal imitates a lifeless or uninteresting object.
The stick insect camouflages itself perfectly as a twig.
The leaf insect looks like a leaf.
Many looper caterpillars look like small twigs.
Masquerade often also includes suitable behaviour, such as keeping still or swaying.
Masquerade protects from enemies, but can also help in hunting.
Masquerade is not the same as mimicry.

abschnitte.text: In **masquerade** an animal imitates something that an enemy does not want to eat or does not notice at all. These can be twigs, leaves, bark, stones or even bird droppings. The enemy does see the animal, but takes it for something boring. The word comes from the Greek ‘mimesis’ and means imitation. Masquerade is one of the many forms of **camouflage** in nature.

**Stick insects** have a long, thin body and long legs that look like dry twigs. By day they sit motionless in the bushes, and sometimes they sway gently like a branch in the wind. The largest species grows to over half a metre long with its legs stretched out. Even more astonishing is the **leaf insect** from South-East Asia. It is flat and green and even has lines that look like leaf veins.

The caterpillars of many **geometer moths**, a family of moths, stand stiffly away from a twig and then look like a little twig themselves. These looper caterpillars can also be found in Switzerland. The dead leaf butterfly Kallima from Asia looks like a withered leaf with its wings folded together. Some caterpillars look like bird droppings and are therefore left in peace. In the sea the leafy seadragon, a relative of the seahorse, resembles a drifting piece of seaweed.

Masquerade helps not only prey animals, but also hunters. The **stonefish** lies on the seabed and looks like a stone overgrown with algae. When a small fish comes past, it snaps at it in a flash. Some mantises look like flowers or leaves and lie in wait for insects in this way. For the prey the predator is then almost impossible to spot.

The two words sound similar, but mean something different. In masquerade the animal does not want to be recognised as an animal at all, and pretends to be an object. In **mimicry**, by contrast, an animal imitates another animal that is, for example, poisonous or able to defend itself. A harmless hoverfly looks like a wasp and is therefore avoided. Both strategies arose through long **evolution**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Camouflage in which an animal imitates an uninteresting object.
When an animal looks the way that it is not recognised, or recognised only poorly, by others.
A family of moths whose caterpillars move along in loops as they walk.
The slow change of living things over many generations.

gewusst: Some stick insects lay eggs that look like plant seeds.
Good masters of camouflage often stay completely motionless for hours, because even a small movement could give them away.

teile.einleitung: Moray eels are eel-like sea fish with a long, snake-like body and a powerful set of teeth. They hide in rock crevices and coral reefs and snap in a flash at prey swimming past.
wichtigste: Moray eels are eel-like sea fish with powerful jaws.
There are around 200 species, and most live in warm seas.
A moray also lives in the Mediterranean, the Mediterranean moray.
Moray eels have no pectoral fins and no scales.
They constantly open and close their mouth in order to breathe.
In the throat they have a second jaw that can shoot forwards.
The largest morays grow to up to three metres long.

abschnitte.text: Moray eels have a long body flattened from the sides, without scales. Their skin is covered with a protective **layer of mucus**. Pectoral fins are missing, and the dorsal and anal fins form a continuous fin fringe. Many species have striking patterns, spotted or striped. The giant moray can grow to up to three metres long, while many other species are only about half a metre long.

Moray eels live in tropical and temperate seas all over the world. Especially many species are found in the **coral reefs** of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. In the Mediterranean lives the spotted Mediterranean moray. By day morays mostly hide in caves and rock crevices, so that only the head peeks out.

Moray eels eat fish, squid, crustaceans and shrimps. They hunt mainly at night and find their prey with their very good sense of smell. When they bite, a second set of jaws in the throat shoots forwards, the so-called **pharyngeal jaw**, and pulls the prey into the stomach. Some morays even hunt together with groupers: the moray drives fish out of crevices, and the grouper catches them in open water.

Moray eels often look as if they were about to bite, because they open and close their mouth. In reality they are **breathing** this way, for they pump water over their gills. Morays are mostly not dangerous to divers as long as you leave them in peace. But anyone who puts a hand into their cave can be bitten painfully.

The ancient Romans already kept moray eels in fish ponds and ate them as a delicacy. In diving paradises such as the Red Sea or the Maldives, moray eels are among the most popular photo subjects. Morays often let themselves be cleaned by **cleaner shrimps** and cleaner fish, which even swim into their mouths. The meat of some tropical species can be poisonous, because toxins from the food chain accumulate in it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A second jaw in the throat that pulls prey inwards.
Breathing organs of fish that take oxygen from the water.
A small shrimp that eats dead skin and parasites off larger fish.
A large structure made of the limestone skeletons of tiny coral animals in warm sea.

gewusst: The moray’s second jaw recalls the monster from the film ‘Alien’.
Moray eels are not snakes, but true fish with gills.
The green moray is actually bluish, and the green colour comes from a yellow mucus on the skin.

teile.einleitung: The kiwi is a flightless bird from New Zealand, about as big as a chicken. It is nocturnal, sniffs for worms with its long beak and has many features that you would otherwise expect more from mammals. For the people of New Zealand it is the most important national symbol.
wichtigste: The kiwi belongs to the flightless birds called ratites.
Its genus name Apteryx means ‘without wings’ and comes from George Shaw in 1813.
Today five living kiwi species are distinguished, all found only in New Zealand.
It is the only bird in the world with its nostrils at the tip of the beak.
Its feathers have no little hooks and therefore look like hair.
According to DNA studies, the extinct elephant bird of Madagascar is its closest relative.
Kiwis lay huge eggs in proportion to their body size.
Many kiwis are threatened by introduced predators.

abschnitte.text: A kiwi has a plump body, strong legs and a long, thin beak. Its wings are tiny and hidden under the brown plumage. The **feathers** have no little hooks joining their branches, and therefore feel like fur. The breastbone lacks the **keel** to which the flight muscles are attached in flying birds. The kiwi also has no preen gland, with which almost all birds oil their plumage.

The bones of most birds are hollow and filled with air so that they are light. The bones of the kiwi, by contrast, contain **bone marrow** as in mammals. Its body temperature is about 38 °C, which is lower than in most birds. The female also has two working ovaries, whereas in most birds only one works.

Kiwis live only in New Zealand, in forests, scrubland and grassland. Five species are distinguished, for example the **brown kiwi**, the little spotted kiwi and the Okarito kiwi. They belong to the flightless birds, like the ostrich, emu and rhea. DNA studies surprisingly showed that their closest relative is the extinct elephant bird of Madagascar.

Kiwis are nocturnal and see poorly. In return they have a very good **sense of smell**. Because their nostrils sit right at the tip of the beak, they can smell worms and insect larvae in the ground. They probe the earth with the beak and also eat spiders, fruit and seeds.

A kiwi egg is enormous compared with the bird and weighs up to a fifth as much as the female. In many species it is mainly the **male** that incubates the eggs. Incubation lasts about two and a half months, which is very long. The chicks hatch already covered in feathers and are soon independent.

In the past there were no mammals in New Zealand apart from bats. Introduced animals such as stoats, cats and dogs now kill many kiwis, above all chicks. That is why several species are **threatened**. New Zealand protects them with reserves, traps for predators and rearing stations for chicks.

begriffe.erklaerung: Large birds that cannot fly and get around by running, for example the ostrich, emu and kiwi.
An animal that is out and about at night and sleeps by day.
A gland at the base of the tail whose oil most birds use to care for their plumage.
A bony ridge on the breastbone of flying birds to which the powerful flight muscles attach.

gewusst: The people of New Zealand like to call themselves ‘Kiwis’.
The kiwi fruit was named after the bird, because its brown, hairy skin is reminiscent of its plumage.
Shortly before laying, a female kiwi carries an egg inside her that fills almost her whole belly.

teile.einleitung: The raven is the largest member of the crow family and at the same time the largest songbird in the world. It is completely black, very clever and can even use tools. After being rare in Switzerland for a long time, it can now be seen again in many regions.
wichtigste: The raven belongs to the crow family and to the genus Corvus, like the carrion crow and the rook.
It lives mainly in the Northern Hemisphere, in Europe, Asia and North America.
Ravens eat almost anything, for example carrion, small animals, eggs and fruit.
They are considered very intelligent and can use tools to get at food.
Pairs often stay together for life, and only the female incubates the eggs.
In human care a raven can live to over 40 years old.
Ravens traditionally live at the Tower of London, and a legend has grown up around them.

abschnitte.text: A raven is about 55 to 65 centimetres long and thus clearly larger than a carrion crow. Its wingspan can be well over a metre. Typical are the mighty beak, whose base is covered with **short, bristle-like feathers**, and the shaggy throat feathers. In flight you can recognise it by its **wedge-shaped tail** and its deep call ‘krock’.

The raven occurs in deserts, on sea coasts, in forests and in the high mountains. It lives in Europe, Asia, North America and parts of North Africa, even in the Arctic. In the Alps it often nests on rock faces. It needs large territories and mostly avoids densely built-up cities.

Ravens are **omnivores**. They eat carrion from dead animals, catch mice, insects and young birds and raid nests. Fruit, grain and rubbish are added to this. They often discover carcasses before other animals and sometimes lure foxes or wolves with them, which tear open the hide.

Ravens solve difficult tasks and use **tools**, for example little sticks to get food out of crevices. In experiments they even planned ahead and remembered who had treated them well or badly. They can imitate noises and sometimes human words. Young ravens like to play, for example by sliding in the snow or throwing objects through the air.

Raven pairs mostly stay together for life. In the **courtship season** they perform acrobatic flights with loops, rolls and dives. Early in the year, often in February or March, the female lays about 4 to 6 eggs in a large nest of branches. She incubates alone while the male brings food, and both then feed the young.

Because it ate carrion, in the Middle Ages the raven was often called the **gallows bird** and was thought to be a bringer of bad luck. In Norse legend the god Odin had two ravens called Hugin and Munin. Ravens are still kept at the Tower of London today, because according to legend the kingdom will fall if they leave the castle. In Switzerland the raven was rare for a long time because it was persecuted, and has only been spreading again for a few decades.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird family with ravens, crows, magpies and jays.
The flesh of dead animals.
An animal that eats both plants and animals.
Behaviour with which animals woo a partner.

gewusst: Ravens are songbirds, even though their croaking does not sound like singing at all.
Ravens can roll onto their backs in flight and glide upside down for a stretch.
Young ravens often join together in groups before they find a territory of their own.

teile.einleitung: A spawning pit is a small hollow in the gravel at the bottom of a river or stream into which fish lay their eggs. Trout and salmon in particular dig such pits. In them the eggs are well hidden and bathed by fresh water.
wichtigste: The pit in which a trout lays its eggs is called a spawning pit.
Trout lay their eggs in a pit of gravel on the river bed.
The female digs the pit with powerful strokes of her tail fin.
The male fertilises the eggs directly in the pit.
Afterwards the eggs are covered with gravel.
The eggs need clean gravel through which oxygen-rich water flows.
In Switzerland, brown trout usually dig their spawning pits between October and January.

abschnitte.text: A **spawning pit** is a shallow hollow in the gravel bed of a water that a female fish digs herself. Depending on the size of the fish, it is about the size of a plate up to the size of a bathtub. From above you can recognise it as a pale patch, because the gravel has been freshly turned over. Experts count such spots to find out how many fish are spawning in a stream.

The female lies on her side and beats powerfully against the bottom with her **tail fin**. In this way she stirs up sand and gravel, which are carried away by the current. This creates a hollow with clean, coarse gravel. The male guards the spot during this time and drives away rivals.

When the pit is ready, the female lays her eggs in it. At the same time the male releases his sperm fluid and **fertilises** the eggs. Afterwards the female digs a little further upstream and covers the eggs with gravel as she does so. In this way the eggs lie protected between the stones.

Between the stones fresh, oxygen-rich water flows through constantly. Depending on the water temperature, the eggs develop over several weeks to months. The hatched **yolk-sac larvae** stay at first in the gravel and live off their store of yolk. Only in spring do the young fish swim out of the gravel.

If a lot of fine silt gets into the stream, it clogs the gaps in the gravel. This is called **colmation**, and the eggs then suffocate because no more oxygen reaches them. Power stations that suddenly change the water level can also leave spawning pits dry. That is why in Switzerland new gravel is tipped in on some rivers, so that trout can find good spawning grounds again.

begriffe.erklaerung: The stony bottom of a river or stream.
A store of food on the belly of freshly hatched fish.
The clogging of the gaps in river gravel by fine silt.
The fusion of egg and sperm from which a new living thing arises.

gewusst: When laying her eggs, a female trout can make several spawning pits one after another.
Fishers and walkers should not walk through the gravel banks of trout streams in winter, because eggs may lie beneath them.

teile.einleitung: Hummingbirds are tiny, often iridescently coloured birds that occur only in the Americas. They can hover in the air like a helicopter and are the only birds that can even truly fly backwards. With their long beaks they drink nectar from flowers.
wichtigste: Hummingbirds form a bird family of their own with over 300 species.
They live only in North, Central and South America.
The smallest bird in the world is the bee hummingbird, a hummingbird from Cuba.
Hummingbirds can hover in the air and even fly backwards.
They often beat their wings more than 50 times a second.
Their most important food is sugary flower nectar, plus small insects.
In Switzerland there are no hummingbirds in the wild.

abschnitte.text: Most hummingbirds are only 6 to 12 centimetres long and weigh a few grams. The **bee hummingbird** measures about 5 to 6 centimetres and weighs around 2 grams, less than a sugar cube. The largest is the giant hummingbird from the Andes, at a good 20 centimetres. Many males have feathers that **shimmer** metallic green, red or violet depending on how the light falls.

Hummingbirds live only in the Americas, from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego. Most species are found in the tropical rainforests and mountain forests of South America, for example in Ecuador and Colombia. Some species live high in the Andes at over 4,000 metres. The **ruby-throated hummingbird** flies from North America to Central America in autumn and even crosses the Gulf of Mexico on the way.

Hummingbirds drink mainly **nectar**, a sugary liquid from flowers. To do so they put their beak deep into the flower and lick very fast with their long, forked tongue. For protein they also catch small insects and spiders. Because they use so much energy, they visit hundreds of flowers every day.

In hovering flight, hummingbirds rotate their wings at the shoulder and beat them back and forth in a lying figure of eight. In this way they can hover in front of a flower and fly sideways and backwards. Small species manage 50 to 80 **wingbeats** a second, which produces the typical hum. Their heart can beat over 1,000 times a minute in flight.

Hummingbirds are mostly loners and bravely defend their flowers against their own kind. The female builds a tiny nest alone from plant down and spider webs, which stretches as the chicks grow. In it she usually lays two white eggs that are hardly bigger than peas or beans. On cold nights hummingbirds fall into a stupor called **torpor** to save energy.

When they drink, pollen sticks to the head and beak. In this way hummingbirds **pollinate** many plants, which often have red, tube-shaped flowers. Some flowers and hummingbirds fit together as well as a key and a lock. Some species are threatened by the destruction of forests.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sweet juice in flowers that attracts animals.
Flight on the spot with very fast wingbeats.
A stupor in which body temperature and heartbeat drop sharply to save energy.
The transfer of pollen so that a plant can form seeds.

gewusst: What some people in Switzerland take for a hummingbird is usually the hummingbird hawk-moth, a moth that likewise hovers in front of flowers.
In proportion to its body size, a hummingbird has one of the largest hearts of all birds.
A hummingbird can drink more nectar in a day than it weighs itself.

teile.einleitung: Konrad Lorenz was an Austrian zoologist and is regarded as one of the founders of behavioural research. He became famous because young greylag geese followed him as if he were their mother. For his research he received the Nobel Prize in 1973.
wichtigste: Konrad Lorenz lived from 1903 to 1989 and came from Vienna.
He is regarded as one of the founders of comparative behavioural research, ethology.
He researched imprinting, in which young animals accept the first moving creature as their mother.
Gosling chicks that saw him after hatching followed him like their mother.
In 1973, together with Karl von Frisch and Nikolaas Tinbergen, he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
His books about animals became very well known.
His attitude during the time of National Socialism is viewed critically today.

abschnitte.text: Konrad Lorenz was born in Vienna in 1903 and grew up in Altenberg near Vienna. Even as a child he kept many animals, including ducks, geese and jackdaws. He first studied medicine and then **zoology**. Later he headed, among other things, a Max Planck Institute for Behavioural Physiology in Seewiesen in Bavaria.

Lorenz observed that freshly hatched gosling chicks follow the first moving creature they see. When he himself was there, the chicks ran after him as if he were their mother. He called this quick, lasting learning in a short span of time **imprinting**. The greylag goose Martina, who regarded him as her mother, became especially well known.

Lorenz wanted to understand why animals behave as they do. He observed animals as far as possible in their natural surroundings and compared the behaviour of different species. In this way he researched inborn behaviours, which he called **instinctive actions**. This made him a founder of **ethology**, the science of animal behaviour.

In 1973 Lorenz received the **Nobel Prize** in Physiology or Medicine together with the bee researcher Karl von Frisch and the Dutchman Nikolaas Tinbergen. He also became known through books for a wide public, such as ‘King Solomon’s Ring’ from 1949. In ‘On Aggression’ from 1963 he wrote about aggression in animals and humans. Later he also campaigned for environmental protection.

Konrad Lorenz joined the Nazi party in 1938 and in that period wrote texts that fitted the racial doctrine of the National Socialists. After the war he distanced himself from this, but many find his explanations inadequate. Some honours were therefore later taken away from him. That is why he is seen today as an important researcher, but also as a **controversial** person.

Imprinting is now an established term in biology and psychology. Findings from it help, for example, in raising young animals in zoos and rescue centres. In some reintroduction projects, chicks are raised in such a way that they do not imprint on humans. Konrad Lorenz died in 1989 at the age of 85.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science that researches the behaviour of animals.
Quick learning in a short phase of life that can hardly be undone.
Inborn behaviour that an animal does not have to learn.
A famous prize for outstanding achievements in science, literature and peace.

gewusst: In his parents’ house in Altenberg, Lorenz kept a colony of jackdaws whose birds flew freely in and out.
Lorenz researched not only geese but also jackdaws, fish and dogs.
The 1973 Nobel Prize was one of the first to be awarded for research into animal behaviour.

teile.einleitung: Ladybirds are small, round beetles that are often red with black spots. Children regard them as lucky charms, and gardeners like them because they eat huge numbers of aphids. There are thousands of species worldwide.
wichtigste: Ladybirds are insects with six legs and hard wing cases.
They are well-known predators of aphids.
A ladybird can eat up to 50 aphids in one day.
You see them most often in spring and summer.
In autumn they look for a sheltered hiding place, often under bark or in leaf litter.
Ladybirds are harmless to people.
In organic farming they are used deliberately against aphids.

abschnitte.text: Ladybirds have an almost hemispherical body and six short legs. Their hard **wing cases** are often red or yellow with black spots. The best-known species in Switzerland is the **seven-spot ladybird**. The number of spots depends on the species and does not reveal the beetle’s age.

Before take-off the ladybird first folds its hard wing cases to the side. Underneath it unfolds its thin, transparent **hind wings**, with which it actually flies. After landing it carefully folds them up again. The wing cases protect the delicate wings like a case.

Most ladybirds and their larvae eat **aphids**. An adult beetle manages up to 50 a day, and a larva several hundred during its development. That is why ladybirds are used in **organic farming** and in greenhouses to fight aphids without poison. Some species also eat fungi or plants.

The female lays her yellow eggs in small groups on leaves, usually near aphid colonies. From them hatch long, dark **larvae** that do not look like beetles at all. After a few weeks the larva attaches itself to a leaf or stem and turns into a pupa. From the pupa the finished beetle finally emerges, which is called complete metamorphosis.

The bright colours warn birds that ladybirds taste bad. If a ladybird feels threatened, it draws in its legs and plays dead. In addition it can release a yellow, bitter liquid from its leg joints, which is called **reflex bleeding**. Ladybirds are harmless to people, and at most they can give a very slight nip.

In autumn ladybirds look for sheltered hiding places under tree bark, in piles of leaves or in cracks in walls. They often spend the winter there together in large groups. Since about 2004 the **harlequin ladybird** has been spreading in Switzerland and can displace native species. For many children the ladybird is a lucky charm, and in Swiss German it is also called ‘Himmelsgüegeli’.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hard front wings of a beetle, which protect the flight wings.
The young form of an insect, which looks quite different from the adult animal.
When a beetle releases a bitter liquid from its joints as a defence.
An animal that helps people, for example by eating pests.

gewusst: There are about 6000 species of ladybirds worldwide.
The German name Marienkäfer (‘Mary’s beetle’) recalls Mary, the mother of Jesus.
There are also ladybirds that are black with red spots or yellow with black spots.

teile.einleitung: Rodents are the group of mammals with the most species. They include mice, hamsters, guinea pigs, squirrels and beavers, and all of them have special gnawing teeth that keep growing throughout their lives.
wichtigste: Rodents form the largest order of mammals, with over 2000 species.
Guinea pigs, hamsters, mice, squirrels, dormice and beavers are rodents.
Typical are two large gnawing teeth each at the top and bottom.
The gnawing teeth keep growing constantly throughout life.
If a hamster gets too little gnawing material, its teeth can become too long.
The largest rodent is the South American capybara.
Rodents live almost everywhere on Earth, except in Antarctica.

abschnitte.text: Rodents are an **order** of mammals with the scientific name Rodentia. Almost half of all mammal species belong to it. Most are small, like mice or hamsters, but some also grow large like the beaver. The largest rodent is the **capybara** from South America, which can weigh over 50 kilograms.

Rodents have two large **gnawing teeth** each at the top and bottom. These teeth have open roots and therefore keep growing. Only the front is covered with hard, often orange tooth enamel, and the back wears down faster. In this way the teeth sharpen themselves as they gnaw, like a chisel. Canine teeth are missing, but there is a gap between the gnawing teeth and the cheek teeth.

Rodents live in forests, meadows, deserts, mountains and even in towns. Some dig burrows underground, others climb in trees or swim like the beaver. Many eat seeds, nuts, grass and roots, and some also eat insects. Some species such as the marmot or the dormouse have a long **hibernation**.

In Switzerland live, among others, squirrels, marmots, dormice, hazel dormice, various mice and voles. The **beaver** was wiped out in Switzerland in the 19th century. From 1956 it was reintroduced, and today again several thousand beavers live on Swiss rivers and lakes. The Alpine marmot whistles loudly when it spots an eagle or a fox.

Guinea pigs, hamsters, gerbils, rats and chinchillas are popular pets. They need branches, hay and wood for **gnawing**, so that their teeth do not grow too long. In Switzerland, under the Animal Protection Act, sociable animals such as guinea pigs may not be kept alone. The golden hamster, on the other hand, is a loner and likes best to live alone.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of related animals, for example all rodents.
The large, chisel-shaped front teeth of rodents.
A deep, long sleep in winter in which the body uses very little energy.
The hardest layer of the body, which protects the teeth.

gewusst: The gnawing teeth of a rat can even bite through cables, wood and soft metals.
A beaver can fell a small tree with its teeth in one night.
Rabbits and hares look like rodents, but belong to a group of their own, the lagomorphs.

teile.einleitung: The mole is a small mammal that spends almost its whole life underground. With its shovel-like front paws it digs long tunnels and hunts earthworms there. Although it sees almost nothing, it finds its way around superbly in the dark.
wichtigste: The mole spends almost its whole life underground.
It digs its tunnels with its strong front paws.
Its eyes are tiny, and it sees very badly.
It eats mainly earthworms and insect larvae.
A mole weighs about as much as a bar of chocolate.
Its fur feels as soft as velvet.
The mole is not a rodent but an insectivore.

abschnitte.text: The European mole is about 12 to 16 centimetres long and usually weighs between 60 and 120 grams, so roughly as much as a bar of chocolate. Its cylindrical body is ideal for life in narrow tunnels. The front paws are as broad as **shovels** and carry strong claws. The black, **velvety fur** has no lie, so it can run forwards and backwards in the tunnel without any trouble.

The mole’s eyes are tiny and hidden in the fur, and it can tell little more than light from dark with them. In return it has an excellent sense of touch and smell. On its snout sit thousands of tiny touch organs, the **Eimer’s organs**. With its short tail it also feels what is happening behind it in the tunnel.

The mole eats mainly **earthworms** and insect larvae, as well as snails and centipedes. Every day it needs roughly as much food as it weighs itself. For hard times it builds larders in which it stores earthworms. To do this it bites them in the head, so that they are paralysed but do not die.

A mole digs a **tunnel system** that can be over a hundred metres long. The surplus soil it pushes upwards, which is how molehills are formed. It is active all year round and does not hibernate. Moles are loners and defend their territory against others of their kind.

In spring the males search for females. Gestation lasts about four weeks. The mother builds her nest in a soft chamber padded with grass and leaves, deep underground. Usually three to four naked, blind young are born, and they are independent after about two months.

In Switzerland the mole lives in meadows, in gardens and in forests, up to high in the mountains. It is useful because it loosens the soil and eats many pests. In some cantons it is protected. Because it can be confused with the water vole, it is important to tell the two animals apart.

begriffe.erklaerung: Mammals such as the mole, hedgehog and shrew that mainly eat small animals.
Tiny touch organs on the mole’s nose.
A network of underground tunnels.
A space in which an animal stores food for later.

gewusst: In one mole’s larder over a thousand earthworms have been found.
A mole can dig several metres of tunnel in an hour.
On its front paws the mole has an extra sickle-shaped bone that works like a sixth finger.

teile.einleitung: The mandrill is a large monkey from the rainforests of West Africa that, with its bright red and blue face, can hardly be mistaken. It is regarded as the largest species among the Old World monkeys. Mandrills live in large groups that sometimes comprise hundreds of animals.
wichtigste: The mandrill belongs to the Old World monkey family (Cercopithecidae).
Its scientific genus name is Mandrillus.
Its closest living relative is the drill.
It is related to the baboon and has a strikingly colourful face.
Genetically it is more closely related to the white-eyelid mangabeys than to the baboons.
Mandrills live in the rainforests of Cameroon, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and the Republic of the Congo.
The Swiss naturalist Conrad Gessner already depicted the mandrill in the 16th century.

abschnitte.text: Adult males have a bright red nose that is framed by blue, grooved **ridges**. The rear end is also coloured brightly in red, blue and violet. The higher a male stands in the ranking order, the more strongly his colours glow. Females and young animals are coloured much paler.

Male mandrills can weigh over 30 kilograms and are thus about three times as heavy as the females. Such a large difference between the sexes is called **sexual dimorphism**. Mandrills have a short stub of a tail and very long canine teeth. They move mostly on all fours on the ground, but also climb trees.

The mandrill lives in the **tropical rainforest** of Central Africa, north of the Congo River. It is an omnivore and searches on the ground for fruit, seeds, fungi, insects and small animals. In its **cheek pouches** it can collect food. Because mandrills spread many seeds, they are important for the forest.

Mandrills live in very large groups called **hordes**. In Gabon hordes with several hundred animals have been observed, one of the largest groups of any monkey. The core is formed by females with their young, and the adult males join mainly at mating time. For communication they use sounds, gestures and showing their teeth.

Carl von Linné described the mandrill scientifically in 1758 under the name Simia sphinx. Later mandrill and **drill** were counted among the baboons (Papio), until the separate genus Mandrillus was created in 1824. The lines of mandrill and drill separated about 3 million years ago. No fossils of the genus have been found so far, and subspecies are mostly not distinguished today.

The mandrill is listed as **vulnerable** on the IUCN Red List. Its forests are being cut down, and it is hunted for its meat. In national parks such as the Lopé National Park in Gabon it is protected. Zoos also take part in breeding programmes in order to preserve the species.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large family of monkeys in Africa and Asia that includes baboons and macaques.
Clear differences in appearance between male and female.
A large group of animals that roams together.
The closest relative of the mandrill, with a black rather than colourful face.

gewusst: The wise monkey Rafiki from the film ‘The Lion King’ has features of a mandrill.
Conrad Gessner from Zurich already showed the mandrill in his great animal book of the 16th century.
When a mandrill shows its teeth, it can also be a friendly greeting.

teile.einleitung: The Muscovy duck is a large duck from Central and South America. It does not quack like our mallard, but rather hisses, and its face is covered with red, warty skin.
wichtigste: The Muscovy duck comes from Central and South America.
It hardly quacks, but makes mainly hissing sounds.
The males have red, warty skin on the head.
Drakes are much bigger and heavier than females.
Muscovy ducks can fly well and like to sit in trees.
The indigenous peoples of the Americas already kept the Muscovy duck as a domestic animal.
The domestic form is often called the warty duck or flying duck.

abschnitte.text: The wild Muscovy duck is black with green shimmering feathers and large white patches on the wings. On the head, mainly the males have bare, red skin warts, which are called **caruncles**. The drakes are almost twice as heavy as the females. Domestic forms come in many colours, for example white, black and white or blue-grey. Their feet have sharp claws with which they hold on to branches.

In the wild the Muscovy duck lives from Mexico to the north of Argentina. It inhabits rivers, swamps and lakes in wooded areas. Unlike most ducks it likes to sleep in trees. Through human activity there are today also feral Muscovy ducks in North America and Europe.

Muscovy ducks eat plants, seeds, roots, but also insects, worms, small fish and crustaceans. They look for their food in shallow water and on land. Instead of quacking, the drakes **hiss** when they are excited or want to impress a female. The females make soft, peeping sounds.

The female often builds her nest in a **tree hole**. She lays about 8 to 15 eggs and incubates them for around 35 days. That is a week longer than in many other duck species. The ducklings are nidifugous and soon follow their mother into the water.

The Muscovy duck was **domesticated** by the indigenous peoples of the Americas long before the arrival of the Europeans. Spanish and Portuguese sailors brought it to Europe. Today it is also kept in Switzerland on farms and in hobby flocks. It is regarded as calm and likes to eat snails in the garden. Its meat is leaner than that of domestic ducks, which descend from the mallard.

begriffe.erklaerung: The name for a male duck.
Bare, red growths of skin on the head of some birds.
To turn wild animals into domestic animals over many generations.
Young animals that can walk and leave the nest right after hatching.

gewusst: The Muscovy duck is not a relative of the domestic duck, which descends from the mallard, but a quite separate species.
If you cross a Muscovy duck with a Pekin duck, hybrids result that cannot have offspring themselves.
Despite their weight, domestic Muscovy ducks can often still fly and sometimes land on roofs.

teile.einleitung: The mimic octopus is an octopus famous for imitating other sea creatures. It can, for example, look and move like a poisonous lionfish, a sea snake or a flatfish. In this way it protects itself from enemies.
wichtigste: The mimic octopus is scientifically called Thaumoctopus mimicus.
It imitates other, mostly dangerous sea creatures.
It lives in the Indo-Pacific, above all around Indonesia.
It was discovered only in 1998.
It lives on sandy sea floor in shallow water.
Like all octopuses it has eight arms, three hearts and blue blood.
It can change its colour and shape very quickly.

abschnitte.text: The mimic octopus is an **octopus**, that is, a cephalopod with eight arms. With its arms stretched out it is about 60 centimetres long. Normally it is striped brown and white. Its arms are long and thin, and its body is small. It is soft and has no shell, so it needs good tricks against predators.

The mimic octopus lives in warm, shallow coastal waters in the western **Pacific** and in the Indian Ocean. It is especially well known from Indonesia, for example off the island of Sulawesi. There it was discovered by divers in 1998. It was scientifically described only a few years later. It lives on open sand and mud bottom, where there are hardly any hiding places.

Because there are no rocks on the sandy bottom, the mimic octopus imitates dangerous animals. It spreads out its striped arms and then looks like a poisonous **red lionfish**. It hides in the sand, stretches two arms out in opposite directions and so looks like a poisonous **sea snake**. It holds its arms close and glides flat over the bottom like a flounder. Depending on which enemy comes, it apparently chooses a suitable disguise.

In the skin of octopuses sit thousands of pigment cells, the **chromatophores**. The octopus can enlarge or shrink them in a flash with muscles and so change its colour. Because it has no bones, it can also change its body shape. Added to this is suitable behaviour, for example a certain swimming movement. Only this combination makes the deception so convincing.

The mimic octopus is active by day and searches the sand for prey. It eats small crabs, fish and worms. In doing so it pokes its arms into holes and tubes in the ground. Like many octopuses it lives only about one to two years. After reproducing the animals usually die.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mollusc with eight arms and suckers.
Imitation of another, often dangerous animal.
Pigment cells in the skin with which cephalopods change their colour.
A poisonous fish with striking stripes and long fin rays.

gewusst: The mimic octopus is one of the few known animals that can imitate several different animals.
A large part of an octopus’s nerve cells sits not in the head but in its arms.

teile.einleitung: Merle is a special coat pattern in dogs in which the coat looks irregularly patched and marbled. It occurs, for example, in the Border Collie, the Australian Shepherd or the dachshund. The merle gene variant can, however, also be linked to eye and hearing problems.
wichtigste: Merle is a patched, marbled coat pattern in dogs.
It is caused by a change in a particular gene.
In it the coat colour is lightened in places, with dark patches left in between.
Common colours are called blue merle and red merle.
Merle dogs often have blue or differently coloured eyes.
If two merle dogs are mated with each other, puppies can be born deaf or blind.
Responsible breeders therefore never mate two merle dogs.

abschnitte.text: Merle is not a colour of its own, but a **pattern** that alters a base colour. Parts of the coat are lightened, while others keep their dark colour. This produces irregular patches that look marbled. In a black dog this produces a grey-blue coat with black patches, which is called **blue merle**. In a brown dog the pattern is called red merle.

Merle is triggered by a change in a gene that is involved in the production of pigment. Every dog has this gene twice, once from the mother and once from the father. If a dog has the merle variant only once, it shows the typical pattern. If it has it twice, this is called **double merle**. Such dogs are often almost white and frequently have severe damage to the eyes and ears.

Merle occurs in many breeds, especially in **herding dogs**. Well-known examples are the Australian Shepherd, Border Collie, Rough Collie and Shetland Sheepdog. In the dachshund the pattern is called dapple (in German, ‘Tigerdackel’). In the Great Dane the black and white **harlequin** pattern is related to merle. The pattern is also found in some crossbreeds.

The merle gene affects not only the coat, but also pigment cells in the eyes and inner ear. That is why merle dogs often have blue eyes or two differently coloured eyes, which is called **heterochromia**. In dogs with only one merle copy, problems occur less often. In double merle dogs, on the other hand, deafness, blindness or very small eyes are common. That is why mating two merle dogs counts as breeding that causes suffering.

Anyone who would like a merle dog should look for a reputable breeder. A good breeder always mates a merle dog only with a dog without the merle gene. With a gene test you can find out whether a dog carries the merle variant, even if it is hardly visible in the coat. Animal welfare organisations strongly advise against breeding dogs only for a striking colour. In several countries such matings are forbidden.

begriffe.erklaerung: A patched, marbled coat pattern in dogs.
A dog that has inherited the merle gene from both parents.
When an animal has two differently coloured eyes.
Breeding in which animals suffer or become ill because of certain features.

gewusst: No merle dog looks like another, because the patches are unique in every animal.
Sometimes the merle pattern is so faint that it is hardly visible, and such dogs are called cryptic merles.

teile.einleitung: The kype is a hook-shaped outgrowth on the lower jaw of male salmon and trout. It forms mainly at spawning time. With it the males look especially fierce and show others how strong they are.
wichtigste: The kype grows on the lower jaw of male salmonids.
Male lake trout often develop it especially clearly at spawning time.
It is a sign of a fully grown male ready to spawn.
In fights over females it can serve as a weapon.
Often the male can no longer quite close his mouth because of the hook.
Together with the hook, the males get a coloured spawning dress.

abschnitte.text: The **kype** is an upward-curved extension of the lower jaw. It occurs in males of salmon, lake trout, sea trout and other salmonids. The hook arises because bone and tissue on the jaw grow strongly before the spawning season. Females usually have no hook or only a small one.

The hook grows when the males become sexually mature and move into the rivers at spawning time. In lake trout this is in autumn, when they ascend from the lakes into the inflowing streams. At the same time the fish change strongly in other ways too and get a coloured **spawning dress**. In Atlantic salmon that survive, the hook partly shrinks back again afterwards.

At spawning time the males fight for the best places near the females. They threaten, bite and ram each other. The kype makes the males larger and better able to defend themselves. For the females, a large hook is also a sign of a strong **male**.

Besides the hook, many salmonids change their appearance at spawning time. Lake trout become darker, salmon get reddish patches, and some Pacific salmon glow bright red. In the **pink salmon** the males even grow a high hump on the back. These changes cost a lot of energy, because the fish hardly eat during the spawning migration.

The **lake trout** lives in large Swiss lakes such as Lake Constance, Lake Geneva or Lake Lucerne. In autumn it migrates into the rivers and streams to spawn. Large males with a mighty kype are then an impressive sight. Because weirs and power stations block its way, the lake trout is threatened in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time of year in which fish reproduce.
The special colours that fish get at spawning time.
Grown up enough to be able to reproduce.
A large trout that lives in lakes and migrates into rivers to spawn.

gewusst: In some large male salmon the kype is so long that it fits into a pit in the upper jaw.
Fishers can easily tell from the kype whether they have caught a male or a female.

teile.einleitung: Metamorphosis means transformation: an animal changes its shape completely during its development. A caterpillar becomes a butterfly, a tadpole becomes a frog. In insects a distinction is made between complete and incomplete metamorphosis.
wichtigste: Metamorphosis is the transformation of a larva into an adult animal.
In complete metamorphosis there are four stages: egg, larva, pupa and the finished insect.
Bees, beetles, flies and butterflies undergo complete metamorphosis.
In incomplete metamorphosis the pupal stage is missing.
The larvae of grasshoppers already resemble the adult animals.
Frogs, toads and newts also undergo metamorphosis.
The transformation is controlled by hormones.

abschnitte.text: The word **metamorphosis** comes from Greek and means transformation. Many animals look quite different as young from the adults. The young animals are then called **larvae**. Larva and adult animal often live in different places and eat quite different food. In this way young and old do not compete with each other.

In complete metamorphosis an insect goes through four stages: egg, larva, **pupa** and the finished insect. A bee, for example, develops from an egg that the queen lays in a honeycomb cell. From it hatches a white, maggot-like larva, which is fed by worker bees. Then it pupates in the sealed cell and is rebuilt into the finished bee. In a worker all this takes about three weeks.

In grasshoppers, dragonflies, bugs and cockroaches there is no pupal stage. Here we speak of **incomplete metamorphosis**. The larvae already resemble the adult animals, but do not yet have finished wings. They grow and moult several times, and with each moult they become more like the adults. At the last moult the finished wings appear.

In frogs and toads too there is a metamorphosis. From the frogspawn hatch **tadpoles**, which live in the water, breathe with gills and have a paddle tail. Gradually first the hind legs grow, then the front legs. The tail shrinks back, and the gills turn into lungs. In the end the young frog can go onto land.

Metamorphosis is controlled by **hormones**. In insects the moulting hormone ecdysone triggers every moult. Another hormone, the juvenile hormone, makes sure that the larva first stays a larva. Only when little of it is present does the transformation into the adult animal begin. In frogs a hormone of the thyroid gland is responsible for metamorphosis.

begriffe.erklaerung: The young form of an animal that looks different from the adult animal.
A resting stage of insects in which the body is completely rebuilt.
Shedding skin or covering that has become too tight.
The larva of frogs and toads, which lives in water.

gewusst: About four out of five insect species undergo complete metamorphosis with a pupa.
A queen bee develops faster than a worker because she gets especially rich food.

teile.einleitung: Heat, or being in season, is the time when a bitch is ready to mate and can have young. It normally comes about twice a year and lasts roughly three weeks. In other animals this time is called oestrus, in cats for example being on heat.
wichtigste: Heat is the fertile time of the bitch.
It normally occurs about twice a year.
A heat usually lasts around three weeks.
The first heat usually comes at the age of about six to twelve months.
Typical are a swollen vulva and bloody discharge.
Male dogs can smell a bitch in heat from far away.
Neutering ends the heats.

abschnitte.text: In dogs, heat is the time in which the female, the **bitch**, produces eggs and can become pregnant. It is controlled by **hormones**, that is, messenger substances in the body. In this time not only the body changes, but often also the behaviour. Many bitches are more clingy, more restless or mark more often with urine.

Most bitches come into heat about twice a year, so roughly every six months. Small breeds are often in heat for the first time at six months, large breeds sometimes only after a year. The interval between two heats is a little different for every bitch. There is no menopause as in humans in dogs, the intervals only get longer with age.

The heat has several stages. First comes **proestrus** of about nine days with bloody discharge, in which the bitch still turns male dogs away. Then follows **standing heat**, in which she lets herself be mated, usually also for about a week. Afterwards the body calms down again until the next heat.

A bitch in heat gives off scents that male dogs can smell over long distances. Some males then become very excited, howl, eat less or try to slip away. If the bitch is mated, she is **pregnant** for about nine weeks, so around 63 days. Afterwards usually several puppies are born.

During heat you should keep the bitch on the lead and away from strange male dogs. Against bloodstains in the home there are special protective pants. Anyone who does not want puppies can have the bitch **neutered** by the vet. In Switzerland you should discuss this well with the vet, because neutering has advantages and disadvantages.

Other mammals also have fertile periods, which are generally called **oestrus**. In cats it is called being on heat, in mares being in season and in deer the rut. In deer you can hear the loud roaring of the males in autumn. Each species has its own rhythm for this.

begriffe.erklaerung: A female dog.
A male dog.
Messenger substances that control processes in the body.
The word for an animal that carries young in its belly.
An operation after which an animal can no longer have young.

gewusst: Female wolves are in heat only once a year, domestic bitches usually twice.
The Basenji is a dog breed whose bitches often come into heat only once a year.
Some bitches have a false pregnancy after the heat and mother toys like puppies.

teile.einleitung: The American alligator, also called the Mississippi alligator, is a large armoured reptile from the south-east of the USA. It lives in swamps, rivers and lakes, for example in Florida and Louisiana. In the past it was almost wiped out, but today there are again very many of these animals.
wichtigste: The American alligator is scientifically called Alligator mississippiensis and belongs to the family Alligatoridae.
The genus Alligator includes only two living species: it and the Chinese alligator.
It lives in the south-east of the USA, on the Atlantic coast from about North Carolina southwards.
Males can grow to over four metres long.
Because of hunting for leather it was severely threatened in the 20th century.
In 1967 it was classed as an endangered species, and in 1987 its population was regarded as recovered.
Today it is classed by the IUCN as least concern.

abschnitte.text: The American alligator has a massive, dark, almost black body with hard horny scales and bony plates on the back. Males usually grow to three to over four metres long, while females stay clearly smaller. Its snout is broad and rounded at the front like a U. When the mouth is closed, the teeth of the lower jaw are hardly visible, while in **crocodiles** they are. That is a good trick for telling alligators and crocodiles apart.

The American alligator lives in fresh water, above all in swamps, rivers, lakes and marshes. Its range stretches from **North Carolina** on the Atlantic coast to Texas. Especially many live in Florida and Louisiana, for example in the **Everglades**. There alligators dig water holes that also serve other animals as watering places in dry periods. In winter they can even survive short cold spells by lying in the water and sticking out only their nose.

Alligators eat fish, turtles, birds, mammals and snails. They lie in wait in the water and snap in a flash. The female builds a large nest mound from plants and mud and lays dozens of eggs in it. The warmth of the rotting plants incubates the eggs, and the **temperature** decides whether males or females hatch. The mother guards the nest and helps the young to hatch.

The American alligator was scientifically described in 1802 by the French naturalist François Marie Daudin. The word **alligator** comes from the Spanish ‘el lagarto’, which means the lizard. Spanish sailors called the large reptiles this when they saw them in America. Its only living relative in the genus is the much smaller Chinese alligator. Both belong to the family **Alligatoridae**, which also includes the caimans of South America.

In the 19th and early 20th centuries alligators were hunted intensively, above all for their leather for shoes and bags. Numbers fell sharply, so in 1967 the alligator was classed in the USA as an endangered species. Thanks to strict protection laws it recovered so well that the authorities declared it fully recovered in 1987. It nevertheless remains formally listed, because it looks similar to endangered crocodile species and so their leather cannot be traded under a false name. In the species protection agreement **CITES** it is in Appendix II, so trade is allowed, but controlled.

Today well over a million American alligators again live in the south-east of the USA. In Louisiana eggs are collected in the wild and the young are raised on farms. Some of the young alligators are later released back into nature. The alligator is the official state reptile of Florida and the mascot of many sports teams. Anyone who lives in Florida sometimes has to reckon with an alligator in the garden pond or on the golf course.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cold-blooded vertebrate with horny scales, for example a lizard, snake or crocodile.
An international agreement that regulates trade in endangered animals and plants.
The world conservation organisation that keeps the Red List of endangered species.
A huge swamp area in the south of Florida.

gewusst: An alligator can use up thousands of teeth in the course of its life, because lost ones keep growing back.
Young alligators call to their mother with squeaking sounds while still in the egg.

teile.einleitung: Cnidarians are an ancient group of aquatic animals that includes jellyfish, corals and sea anemones. What they all share are tiny stinging cells with which they paralyse their prey and defend themselves.
wichtigste: Jellyfish belong to the large animal group of the cnidarians.
Close relatives of jellyfish are corals and sea anemones.
All cnidarians have stinging cells containing venom.
There are two basic forms: the sessile polyp and the swimming medusa.
Cnidarians have no brain, but a simple nerve net.
Most live in the sea, some also in fresh water.
About 10,000 species are known worldwide.

abschnitte.text: Cnidarians, scientifically **Cnidaria**, are animals of very simple build. Their body is like a sack with only one opening, which is mouth and anus at the same time. Around this opening sit **tentacles** with many stinging cells. Cnidarians have no brain and no eyes in the usual sense, but a nerve net that runs through the whole body.

Cnidarians occur in two forms. The **polyp** sits fixed to the bottom, with the tentacles upwards, like a sea anemone or a coral. The **medusa** swims freely as a bell or umbrella with tentacles downwards, like a jellyfish. In many species the two forms alternate during life: small jellyfish bud off from polyps and later lay eggs again.

The cnidarians include the **anthozoans** such as corals and sea anemones, which live only as polyps. Then come the true jellyfish such as the moon jellyfish and the lion’s mane jellyfish. The box jellyfish in tropical seas are among the most venomous animals in the world. Another group are the hydrozoans, which also include the Portuguese man o’ war, a floating colony of many individual animals.

Stony corals build huge **coral reefs** of limestone over thousands of years. The Great Barrier Reef off Australia is so large that it can even be seen from space. Coral reefs are home to countless fish and other sea animals. Through the warming of the seas many corals bleach and die.

Cnidarians also live in Swiss waters. The freshwater polyp **Hydra** is only about one centimetre in size and sits on water plants in ponds and lakes. In warm summers small, transparent freshwater jellyfish, which originally come from China, appear in some lakes. They are harmless to people, because their stinging cells do not penetrate our skin.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sessile form of a cnidarian, with tentacles upwards.
The freely swimming form of a cnidarian, that is, a jellyfish.
Long, mobile catching arms.
A large structure made of the limestone skeletons of corals.

gewusst: A small jellyfish called Turritopsis can turn back into a polyp when in danger and is therefore regarded as ‘immortal’.
Cnidarians have existed for over 500 million years.
The tentacles of the Portuguese man o’ war can grow many metres long.

teile.einleitung: Mako sharks are slim, powerful sharks that are among the fastest fish in the sea. They hunt in the open ocean for tuna and mackerel and can even leap metres out of the water. There are two species, the shortfin mako and the longfin mako.
wichtigste: The mako shark is among the fastest fish in the sea.
There are two species: the shortfin mako and the longfin mako.
Mako sharks belong to the mackerel shark family, like the great white shark.
They live in warm and temperate seas all over the world.
Mako sharks can keep their body warmer than the water around them.
They give birth to live young.
Both species are considered endangered today.

abschnitte.text: Mako sharks have a **torpedo-shaped** body that is metallic blue above and white below. Their snout is pointed, and the teeth are long, narrow and clearly visible. The shortfin mako usually grows to about 2 to 3 metres long, with large animals reaching around 4 metres. The **tail fin** is almost symmetrical, shaped like a crescent, which helps in fast swimming.

The mako is known for its enormous speed. For short sprints, values of 50 to over 70 kilometres per hour are estimated, but exact measurements are difficult. Its skin is covered with tiny scales that reduce water resistance. Mako sharks can leap several metres out of the water when hunting.

Mako sharks live in the **open ocean**, far from the coasts. They are found in the Atlantic, the Pacific, the Indian Ocean and also in the Mediterranean. They often travel thousands of kilometres. Because they can keep their muscles warm, they also hunt successfully in cooler water.

Mako sharks eat mainly fast fish such as **tuna**, mackerel and swordfish, as well as squid. After a long gestation the females give birth to live young. The unborn sharks feed inside the mother on unfertilised eggs. At birth the young are already about 70 centimetres long.

Mako sharks are caught for their meat and fins and often end up as **bycatch** in fishing nets. Because they reproduce only slowly, their populations have fallen sharply. On the IUCN Red List both species are considered endangered. Since 2019 trade in mako sharks has been regulated internationally by the **Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES)**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A shark family of fast swimmers that includes the great white shark.
Animals that get into the net unintentionally along with other fish.
The open sea far from any coast.
Tiny tooth-like scales on shark skin that make swimming easier.

gewusst: Mako sharks are closely related to the great white shark.
Because mako sharks leap so powerfully, they have even jumped into fishing boats.
The skin of a shark feels smooth in one direction and rough like sandpaper in the other.

teile.einleitung: The red panda is a reddish-brown, climbing animal from the mountain forests of the Himalayas and south-west China. With its thick fur, white face and long, ringed tail, it looks almost like a soft toy. Although it is called a panda, it is not closely related to the giant panda.
wichtigste: The red panda is slightly larger than a house cat.
Its fur is mainly reddish-brown, the tail long and ringed.
It lives in the Himalayas and in south-west China.
It belongs to an animal family of its own, not to the family of the giant panda.
It is active mainly at dusk and at night.
Its main food is bamboo.
The red panda is endangered.

abschnitte.text: The red panda grows to about 50 to 65 centimetres in head and body length, plus a bushy tail of 30 to 50 centimetres. It usually weighs 3 to 6 kilograms. Its fur is **reddish-brown** on top, the belly and legs are dark, and the face has white markings. The tail is patterned with light and dark rings.

Red pandas live in cool mountain forests with dense bamboo undergrowth, often between 2,000 and 4,000 metres above sea level. They occur in Nepal, Bhutan, India, Myanmar and in south-west China. They spend most of their lives in the **trees**. In the cold they curl up and cover themselves with their tails like a blanket.

The red panda eats mainly the tender leaves and shoots of **bamboo**. Now and then it also eats fruit, berries, mushrooms, eggs or insects. Because bamboo provides little energy, it sleeps a lot and moves rather slowly. Like the giant panda, it has an enlarged wrist bone, a kind of **false thumb**, with which it can hold bamboo stalks.

Red pandas are active mainly at **dusk** and at night. During the day they usually rest on branches high up in the trees. They live as loners and mark their territory with scents. In summer, after a pregnancy of four to five months, usually one or two young are born.

The red panda was already described in 1825, long before Europeans knew the giant panda. It was therefore the first ‘panda’. For a long time researchers argued about whether it belongs to the bears or the raccoons. Today it stands in a family of its own, the **red panda family** (Ailuridae), and is only distantly related to the giant panda.

The red panda is classed as **endangered**. Its forests are being cut down, and sometimes the animals are poached or caught as pets. In the wild there are probably fewer than 10,000 adult animals. Zoos all over the world, including in Switzerland, take part in breeding programmes to preserve the species.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal family of its own, which today includes only the red panda.
An elongated bone at the wrist that helps like a sixth finger when gripping.
An animal that is out and about mainly in the evening and early morning.
An animal that mostly lives alone and not in a group.

gewusst: The English name ‘red panda’ simply means a panda that is red, and in China the animal is also called the ‘fire fox’.
The red panda can climb down tree trunks head first, because it can turn its hind feet backwards.

teile.einleitung: New World camelids are the camels of South America. They include the llama, the alpaca, the guanaco and the vicuña. Unlike their relatives in Africa and Asia they have no hump.
wichtigste: The New World camelids include the llama, alpaca, guanaco and vicuña.
The closest relatives of the alpaca are the llama, guanaco and vicuña.
They come from South America, above all from the Andes.
Guanaco and vicuña live wild, while llama and alpaca are domestic animals.
New World camelids have no hump.
Their wool is very soft and warm.
In Switzerland too, many llamas and alpacas are kept.

abschnitte.text: The **guanaco** and the **vicuña** are the wild New World camelids. The llama was bred from the guanaco thousands of years ago. The alpaca descends from the vicuña. The llama, at up to about 150 kilograms, is the largest species, and the dainty vicuña the smallest.

New World camelids live mainly in the **Andes**, a long mountain range in the west of South America. Vicuñas and alpacas occur there up to over 4000 metres above sea level. At this height the air is thin and the nights are icy cold. Guanacos also live in lower areas, all the way down to Patagonia in the south.

New World camelids belong, like the dromedary and the Bactrian camel, to the camel family. The common ancestors lived millions of years ago in North America. One part migrated to Asia and Africa, another to South America. All camelids are **even-toed ungulates** and walk on soft pads on their feet.

New World camelids eat grass and other plants. They are **ruminants** and chew their food through several times. They live in herds and communicate with humming sounds. When they get annoyed, they can spit stomach contents, but mostly at others of their kind and not at people.

The Incas already used llamas as **pack animals** and alpacas for their wool. Alpaca wool is soft, warm and hardly itches. The wool of the vicuña is among the finest and most expensive animal hair in the world. In the Andes the animals still provide meat and fertiliser today.

In Switzerland several thousand llamas and alpacas live today. Many farms offer **llama trekking**, in which you hike with the animals. Alpacas are kept as wool suppliers and sometimes even as flock guards for sheep. They cope well with the climate in the Alps.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long high mountain range in the west of South America.
An animal that brings its food back up from the stomach and chews it once more.
Mammals that walk on two toes per foot.
Taming and breeding wild animals into domestic animals.

gewusst: Llamas and alpacas leave their droppings together in a few places, like a shared toilet.
The blood of vicuñas can take up oxygen especially well, which is why they cope with the thin mountain air.
A llama carries only a load that is not too heavy, otherwise it simply lies down.

teile.einleitung: Cormorants are a family of dark, fish-eating water birds found all over the world. They are excellent divers and in Switzerland also eat popular food fish such as whitefish and grayling. That is why nature lovers admire them and fishers often view them critically.
wichtigste: The family of cormorants, or shags, includes about 40 species.
They occur on coasts and waters on every continent except Antarctica.
All cormorants are good divers and eat mainly fish.
In Switzerland the cormorant, Phalacrocorax carbo, is the commonest species.
The cormorant also eats whitefish, an important food fish of the Swiss lakes.
The Galápagos cormorant is the only species that cannot fly.
Many cormorants spread their wings to dry after diving.

abschnitte.text: Cormorants, also called **shags**, form the family Phalacrocoracidae with about 40 species. Most are black or black and white, and some have brightly coloured facial skin. Typical are a long neck, a hooked beak and feet on which all four toes are joined by webbing. The smallest species weigh under a kilogram, the largest over three kilograms.

Cormorants live on sea coasts, lakes and rivers almost everywhere in the world. Many species, such as the **shag**, live only by the sea, others inland as well. In Europe, besides the cormorant, the shag and the pygmy cormorant occur. There are especially many species in New Zealand and on the coasts of the Southern Hemisphere.

Cormorants hunt under water and drive themselves along with their feet as they do so. Sometimes they hunt in groups and herd **shoals of fish** together. They eat mainly fish that they can catch easily, that is, common species. Their plumage gets wet when diving, so afterwards they dry their wings in the sun.

On the Galápagos Islands lives the **Galápagos cormorant**. It has only small stub wings left and can no longer fly. Because there were no predators on the islands for a long time, it did not have to flee and found enough food in the sea. It is one of the rarest seabirds in the world.

In Switzerland cormorants also eat **whitefish**, perch and the threatened grayling. Professional fishers complain that the birds reduce their catches and damage fish in nets. Nature conservationists point out that over-fertilisation, climate change and river engineering also change fish stocks. The Confederation and the cantons try to take both interests into account with rules on regulation.

In China and Japan there has been **cormorant fishing** for over a thousand years. In it, trained birds catch fish for their keepers. In Japan it is still demonstrated as a tradition on the Nagara River today. On the coast of Peru, cormorants and other seabirds once supplied the valuable fertiliser guano with their droppings.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another name for cormorants.
A salmon-like fish from Swiss lakes that is popular to eat.
Fertiliser from the dried droppings of seabirds.
A large group of fish swimming together.

gewusst: The Galápagos cormorant is the only cormorant in the world that has lost the ability to fly.
Cormorant chicks put their whole head into their parents’ throat to be fed.
In winter there are clearly more cormorants in Switzerland than in summer, because birds from the north spend the winter here.

teile.einleitung: The Kodiak bear is an especially large subspecies of the brown bear. It lives only on Kodiak Island and the surrounding islands in the south of Alaska. Together with the polar bear, it is one of the largest predators that live on land.
wichtigste: The Kodiak bear is a subspecies of the brown bear.
It lives on Kodiak Island and neighbouring islands in Alaska.
Together with the polar bear, it is one of the largest land predators in the world.
Large males can weigh over 600 kilograms.
Standing upright, a large Kodiak bear is around 3 metres tall.
It eats salmon, berries, grass and roots.
In winter it spends the cold months in winter dormancy in a den.

abschnitte.text: The Kodiak bear is one of the largest **subspecies** of the brown bear. Males usually weigh 300 to over 600 kilograms, females are much lighter. When a large male stands on its hind legs, it is around 3 metres tall. That makes it much bigger than the brown bears in Europe, such as those that occasionally migrate into Switzerland from Italy.

Kodiak bears live only in the **Kodiak Archipelago**, a group of islands in the Gulf of Alaska. The landscape consists of mountains, meadows, forests and many rivers. Since the end of the last ice age about 12,000 years ago, the bears there have been separated from other brown bears. That is why they have developed into a subspecies of their own.

Kodiak bears are **omnivores**. In spring they eat grass and roots, in summer mainly salmon, which swim up the rivers to spawn. In late summer and autumn many berries are added. In this way they build up a thick layer of fat for the winter.

In winter the bears withdraw to a den and go into **winter dormancy**. They eat and drink nothing for months and live off their fat reserves. In the den the female usually gives birth to two or three very small cubs. The cubs stay with their mother for about three years.

Today about 3,500 Kodiak bears live on Kodiak Island. A large part of their habitat belongs to a **nature reserve**, the Kodiak National Wildlife Refuge. Hunting is strictly regulated, and the population is considered stable. For tourists there are guided trips on which you can watch the bears fishing from a safe distance.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals of one species that has developed slightly differently in a particular area.
A group of islands that lie close together.
An animal that eats both plants and meat.
A long resting state in winter from which the animal can wake up easily, however.

gewusst: A newborn Kodiak bear weighs less than half a kilogram, even though it later becomes so huge.
Kodiak bears sometimes stand on their hind legs, not to attack but to be able to smell and see better.

teile.einleitung: The cuckoo is a bird that almost every child recognises by its call ‘cuck-oo’. It is famous for laying its eggs in the nests of other birds. These foster parents then raise the strange, much larger chick.
wichtigste: The cuckoo is about as big as a pigeon, but slimmer.
It is a migratory bird and spends the winter in Africa south of the Sahara.
The female lays her eggs in the nests of other bird species.
Worldwide the cuckoo uses over 100 different species as host birds.
The cuckoo chick pushes the other eggs out of the nest with its back.
It likes best to eat caterpillars, including poisonous and hairy ones.
In Switzerland, for example, the reed warbler often raises young cuckoos.

abschnitte.text: The cuckoo is about as big as a pigeon, but slimmer, and has a long tail. Its back is grey, its belly pale with dark cross stripes. In flight it looks like a **bird of prey**, a bit like a sparrowhawk, which is why small birds are sometimes afraid of it. Only the male calls the familiar ‘cuck-oo’, while the female has a trilling call.

The cuckoo lives at woodland edges, in bogs, in reed beds and in open landscapes with bushes. It is a **migratory bird** and spends the winter in Africa south of the Sahara. In April it returns to Europe. The young cuckoos later fly to Africa entirely alone, without anyone showing them the way.

The female cuckoo does not build a nest of her own. She lays one egg at a time in the nest of another bird, often when that bird is not there. This way of reproducing is called **brood parasitism**. The cuckoo egg often looks very similar to the eggs of the host birds, so that it does not stand out.

The chick hatches after about two weeks, often earlier than the other young. After a short time it pushes the other eggs or chicks out of the nest with its back.
